speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Earlier this week the CRTC granted BC Tel a 5 per cent rate increase for residential phone rates bringing to 18 per cent the total in residential rate increases given to BC Tel by the commission this year. This increase was granted even though the CRTC concluded in their decision that many areas of B.C. are receiving unsatisfactory service, and in spite of the fact that several exchanges in the Lower Mainland are already paying the highest residential rates in the country. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen):
That cabinet send this decision back to the CRTC with instructions to roll back this unearned rate increase, and further that the Minister of Communications immediately issue a policy directive to the CRTC that no further rate increases be granted to telephone companies within the commission's jurisdiction until such time as the companies provide acceptable levels of service to all of their residential customers.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I was saying before I was interrupted by the hon. member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith) who decided to practise counting, what we are really concerned with here today is the impact of the loss of Alsands on Canada. Canada desperately needed the economic stimulus this project would have given. It would have provided about 4,800 permanent jobs, about 7,000 temporary construction jobs, and by "temporary" we mean anywhere from four to seven years. It would have provided 14,000 jobs indirectly. In total, including the spin-off effect, we could be looking at in the neighbourhood of 200,000 jobs. That becomes very significant when you consider we have roughly 1,200,000 unemployed. In other words, this project meant that one unemployed person in six may have had an opportunity for a job.
The irony of this situation is that a few short months ago we were worried about how to train all the skilled people we were going to need for these projects. We were worried about the 12,500 engineers that would have been needed. Today we do not have to worry about them or the welders, the carpenters or the pipefitters. That is really ironic in light of what has been happening in my own region where we have in Grande Prairie UIC offices a 64 per cent increase in unemployment insurance applications. Unemployment has tripled in less than a year. This project, had it gone ahead, would have created a great deal of spending in Canada, roughly 38 per cent of it in Alberta. Twenty-eight per cent of that money would have ended up in Ontario: $1.5 billion in iron and steel; $600 million in metalworking firms; $550 million in transportation. In total, this project would have injected roughly $450 billion into the Canadian economy, which it so desperately needs.
We all know investment in Canada has taken a beating recently because of things like the National Energy Program and the budget. In 1980, investment in Canada by non-Canadians was around $585 million. In 1981 we find it is a negative $5.3 billion. In 1980, investment by Canadians in foreign companies was $2.78 billion; it almost doubled to $4.9

May 6, 1982
billion in 1981. Money is leaving Canada at an unprecedented rate and that works against the Canadianization policies this government has talked so much about. Since the 1981 budget it has become no longer profitable to invest in Canada. Our last budget was anti-entrepreneur and anti-business. That, coupled with the NEP, has resulted in a double-whammy which has hurt our manufacturing and economic sectors. And now Alsands, which formed the cornerstone of the budget and the NEP, has been cancelled. What is going to happen now? Will the government consider rewriting the NEP and the budget? The NEP was designed to achieve these goals:
-provide Canadians with energy security, the opportunity to participate in energy development, and fairness in the manner in which the benefits of the nation's rich resources are shared.
We now have an NEP without an Alsands. We have no energy development and no energy security. The NEP has already succeeded in decreasing drilling activity by 25 per cent in 1981 over 1980; 226 drilling rigs have left Canada. Of the rigs still here, they were 33 per cent less active in 1981 over 1980. Seismic crews-without which there can be no exploration-are down 25 per cent in 1981 over 1980. The NEP went on to say that it:
-includes made-in-Canada prices which are designed to provide attractive returns to new sources when they come on-stream, and to provide new certainty to the industry.
The only thing we are left with now is uncertainty. This government, through its ignorance of the industry and the jobs that can be created, has destroyed Alsands. What now? What about the tar sands project in Peace River? Will the minister now try to get that project on-stream which, while it is roughly a third of the size of Alsands, is still worth $5 billion. It is a manageable size, and it can still create jobs and economic spinoffs throughout Canada. Will the minister approve that project? Will he give us some hope, something to look forward to? I challenge the minister to give that project the go-ahead and do all in his power to bring it into the mainstream of the Canadian economy.
I want to talk about the potential we have in this country. We have a lot of resources: oil, gas; we have tremendous potential in forestry, agriculture and manufacturing. A few short years ago a Dutch economist came to the Peace River region and said he had never before seen so many resources in such abundance in one place. He was overwhelmed by our potential. He was overwhelmed by our opportunity. He predicted that we would experience massive success. He predicted that we had a golden opportunity to create jobs. He predicted that we had a great opportunity to create Canadian and national wealth.
Let us stop a few years later and look at the same potential and see what we have now. If we look at the oil industry, we find the oil sands projects cancelled. We find that our rigs are moving to the United States. We find jobs which the oil industry should have created in Canada are now being created south of the border. We are importing oil into this country. All
the indications are that in the next decade and maybe the next one again we will still be importing oil into Canada. If we look at the natural gas situation, we find our gas is shut in the ground. Exploration has virtually ceased.
Let us take a look at the forest industry. All over Canada we have lumber mills shutting down. Our retail lumber outlets are closing. People are losing their jobs. Take a look at the housing construction industry. Construction of homes has virtually stopped.
What about the agricultural industry? Agriculture today is being slaughtered by high interest rates, and our high energy taxes have affected fertilizer costs as well as fuel costs.
What about the manufacturing sector? People are being laid off in that sector right across the country. Plants are being closed and there are production cutbacks.
If that Dutch economist were to come back to this country today, he would be met with a very grim picture, a picture that would show all that potential wasted. He would see all that opportunity gone and all that hope turned into despair. Why has that happened? Is it because of a lack of demand for our products? Is it because of a lack of initiative on the part of the Canadian people? I do not think so. I still say there is a demand for our products. There is still a demand for our oil. There has to be. Today we are importing about 400,000 barrels of oil per day. It would take at least three Alsands projects to provide us with that oil. There is still a demand for gas. Look at our unemployment situation. We are not creating any jobs. We are not creating any spin-offs in the manufacturing sector. We are not creating any spin-offs in housing construction. We are not creating any spin-offs in the forestry industry.
Our energy sector could be the trigger to prosperity. It could be the beginning. It could be the comeback to a strong economy. But instead of that, this government of 15 tax increases on fuel, this government of high interest rates, this government of the National Energy Program and this government of the 1981 budget just continues on blindly. It is blind at a time when there is no need to be, a time when there is still opportunity and, a time when everything is still possible.
I want to close by saying that all it takes is a change in the government's attitude. Failing that, all it takes is a dozen of those silent Liberal backbenchers to stand up for what is right, to stand up for the unemployed in their constituencies and to stand up for our country; because that is what we need.

Why is it that we have agreed now by unanimous consent in this House today that we should continue with this special debate? The reason is that we on this side of the House feel that it is appropriate to focus the country's attention on a particular topic. The topic is not the failure of a particular megaproject per se, but the failure of the government's economic strategy, the failure of this government's ability to introduce any program that will result in economic recovery in this country. It is the failure of an economic strategy, and one that is dependent upon megaprojects. I know the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said earlier that he did not necessarily agree with that, but the individual in the cabinet responsible for economic development, the senator from Alberta-

The senator had a vision that the future of this country economically in the 1980s and 1990s would be the large megaprojects, primarily the energy megaprojects in western Canada. I suspect another motive might be that since these were high profile projects they were sexy projects, that they would capture the imagination of western voters so that western voters would fall over themselves to vote Liberal in the next federal election. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, that is not going to happen at all. The reason is that this particular strategy has fallen flat on its face.
I want to comment briefly on the other disappointment, not Alsands but the pipeline, the pipeline that we in the New Democratic Party felt right from the beginning was somewhat of a fraud, that it was an effort by the oil companies in cooperation with American colleagues to encourage the Canadian government to approve the pre-build so that we could export natural gas from Canada at a relatively cheap rate, and some day in the future the northern pipeline would be built to provide Canadians with natural gas.
We wanted to have some ironclad guarantees that that would be taking place. We in the New Democratic Party said that we were not prepared to support that project unless those ironclad guarantees were in place. We were concerned about the jobs that this program would have created in Canada. Something like 11,783 jobs would have been created, and

something in the neighbourhood of $40 billion to $60 billion would have been generated by this project. We wanted to see that project go ahead. We asked for a guarantee. As a matter of fact, 1 would like to read the motion that we proposed on July 22, 1980. It reads:
That before the House adjourns for a summer recess, the House calls on the government to declare that it will not proceed with the construction of the prebuild portion of the northern gas pipeline until complete financial guarantees for the whole pipeline have been obtained and an agreement has been reached between the government of Canada and the government of the United States that the Canadian gas exported through the southern portion of the proposed pipeline will be replaced by Alaska gas at an equivalent price.
That was the motion we put forward in this House on July 22, 1980. It is interesting to note who did not support it. I know there is a member in this House who says he represents the Yukon. In common parlance he is often referred to as "Yukon Eric". He says he is interested in Yukon jobs and investment in the Yukon. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the point raised. I was simply raising a question about an hon. member's whereabouts. I will refrain from referring to it any further.
I should like to refer to an article which was published in The Globe and Mail two days after the vote had taken place. On the issue of guaranteeing jobs for Canadians and investment in Canada, it indicated that the New Democratic Party stood alone, that only the New Democratic Party made a determined effort to defend Parliament, the law and the people. I wanted to read that comment into the record. I think it is important because of the accusations of a number of members regarding our positions on the natural gas pipeline and on the Alsands project.
It is well known that in cabinet the minister responsible for manufacturing development in Canada was overruled by his cabinet colleagues and was replaced by the visionary senator from Alberta. The megaprojects were to be the saviour of the Canadian economy. He wanted to continue with a policy which would make western Canada susceptible to the boom and bust syndrome, to the vagaries of the international marketplace-in this case the price of oil on the world market-and to the continuation of the western theme of being hewers of wood and drawers of water. Essentially that is what the Alsands project and the megaprojects do. This is why we in the NDP feel that as well as the development of these projects, we must make significant effort to develop a long-term job-creation strategy

May 6, 1982
which would result in a sound economic base for western Canada. Of course, that is the manufacturing sector which must be developed alongside megaprojects in energy or resource development.
Why did the Alsands project collapse? We heard speakers earlier in the debate mention that it was because of the downturn in world markets. Others referred to the fact that interest rates were too high and too volatile. I think the real reason was the uncertainty and the lack of confidence which exists in Canada in terms of the political leadership of the country. Investors in the country are afraid of what is to come, of the uncertainty, and are hesitant to go ahead particularly with any long-term commitments. The two foreign oil companies involved in the Alsands project decided that enough was enough and that they would not continue within the atmosphere of uncertainty about interest rates and downturning oil prices. The Liberals saw this happening and panicked. They felt that more concessions should be made to the oil companies to keep them in the act, which would allow Alsands to proceed, because of its symbolism to the people of Canada.
I ask members of the Progressive Conservative Party what is their position. The impression one receives is that they want this project to proceed at almost any cost to Canadian taxpayers. We in the NDP looked at the offer where Canadians would put up 85 per cent of the financing and would receive a 50 per cent equity in the project. I do not know what businessman would consider that to be a reasonable deal. On top of it, we would provide royalty holidays and tax concessions to the two multinational oil companies. What kind of a deal was it? Even under those conditions the oil companies turned it down. This should be a clear signal to everyone in the House that the project is uneconomical and that at this point in time it must not proceed. If the time comes when the economics of the project become realistic and viable, then I say that if Canadians are to put up 85 per cent of the financing, let us go the other 15 per cent and obtain a 100 per cent equity, rather than only a 50 per cent equity. This would turn the project into a public utility in the best interests of Canadians.
It is too risky to proceed, so let us learn a lesson. Whether we agree on what we should do in the future in terms of Alsands, let us at least agree today that if the two multinational oil companies are not prepared to continue, it is an unwise decision at this point to proceed with the Alsands project.
Is all lost? Must we in the House perpetuate doom and gloom because of this failure? What is the silver lining in this particular cloud? We must look at whether or not a total reevaluation is required in terms of meeting Canada's goal of oil self-sufficiency by 1990. Perhaps we should turn our attention from the Gulfs and the Shells and direct it to small, independent Canadian oil companies which are not necessarily operating in frontier lands or particularly involved in the Alsands project. They are involved in western Canadian sedimentary basins in traditional recovery programs. They are the hundreds and hundreds of small Canadian companies which have been overlooked by the government. The government's attention has
been directed to the multinational companies, but what about small Canadian producers in western sedimentary basins?
If we were prepared as Canadians to place that amount of money in the Alsands project, it seems to me that we should now shift that investment into upstream projects and say to small independent Canadian oil companies that now is the time for a review of the potential for enhanced recovery. We know that 30 per cent of the oil is still sitting in western basins and that now is the time for new research and development of technology to draw up that 30 per cent. There would be no risk involved at all. All we require is the technology to move it to the surface.

Yes, let us give the small guy a chance; let us give the small oil companies in western Canada a chance and stop being preoccupied with the multinationals.
These are examples of upstream projects which we could now begin to support. What about downstream projects such as heavy oil upgrading plants in Saskatchewan? This would be an opportunity to take the heavy oil, move it through the plants, and refine it in central and eastern Canadian refineries rather than American ones. Funds could be reallocated to this downstream project. Even within the oil industry itself the failure of the Alsands project will perhaps provide a challenge and opportunity for Canadian oil companies and Canadian refiners, two groups which have been incensed and overlooked by the National Energy Program and by the efforts to move ahead in frontier areas and on projects such as Alsands.
Another opportunity which perhaps has been provided by the cancellation of the Alsands project is to develop alternate forms of energy. We should take more initiative in developing alternate energy forms such as geothermal energy, particularly in western Canada, hydrogen, biomass, wind, solar, tidal, and non-conventional propulsion such as propane and alcohol. As well, we should develop heat pumps and coal technologies and so on.
These are alternate forms of energy which have had to take a back seat while so much attention and money from the private and public sector was being focused on the megaprojects. We should see this as an opportunity to move funds from the private and public sector into developing alternate forms of energy which could complement the recovery programs of our traditional energy fields.
Another opportunity which we should take advantage of is the development of conservation practices. It has been said that the cheapest barrel of oil is the one that you do not have to buy. Here is our opportunity to experiment with new forms of conservation. We now have an opportunity to conduct research and develop into such things as new building forms and new building designs. We should develop new conservation programs because I believe this is where the long-term job security opportunities will be. Canadian manufacturers will
May 6, 1982

have the opportunity to develop and build new types of windows and doors and other conservation related materials.
This brings me to my main concern, and that is, how can we as Canadians-especially in western Canada-move away from the "boom and bust"scenario and from our dependency on the vagaries on the international market? One step would be to develop the manufacturing sector which would provide long-term security for jobs and investment. The manufacturing sector is essential to any mature and sound economy. Our nation is presently experiencing a deficit in our manufacturing trade balance of $21 billion a year and this is increasing. It has cost Canadians 200,000 jobs. It seems that now is the time to introduce a manufacturing strategy for Canada and for western Canada particularly.
As a first step in developing this strategy we would ask foreign companies operating in Canada to build in Canada what they sell here. I ask hon. members, is that an unrealistic request? We would tell foreign manufacturers that if they have a particular market in Canada we would like them to source and assemble their products in Canada for that market. For example, if Japanese automakers were selling 185,000 Japanese vehicles in this country, we would ask them to source and assemble those vehicles in this country. In other words, we would say: "If you want to make profits in this country, you must at least create jobs in this country." In my opinion, that is not an unrealistic request. But it will take some courage and leadership from the government, and quite frankly, I do not think that those of us on this side of the House will hold our breath to wait for that action.
We have seen the collapse of the Alsands project and the northern gas pipeline shelved, at least temporarily. We have seen the economic strategy which has been espoused by the government collapse. Where is this country headed? May I suggest that we should not view this time as one for bitterness and depression. We must face the economic reality of these megaprojects. Let us seize this time as an opportunity and a new challenge for Canadians. It is a challenge to support for the first time in many years our independent Canadian-owned and controlled western oil companies. It is an opportunity to move into the research and development field in order to support the area of conservation. It is an opportunity to move into new areas where we can develop a manufacturing structure which will relieve us from the branch plant mentality that we find ourselves in today.
Why is there not more research and development? Why are Canadian entrepreneurs not aggressively seeking new markets? The answer is obvious. Why should they? Why should a small Canadian branch plant company actively compete with its parent companies or other branch plants? Why should a small branch plant operating in Canada have a sophisticated research and development program when there already is one in the head office in Germany, Britain or the United States? The continuation of our branch plant economy is one of the fundamental problems we face in this country. I am afraid that
we continue to have a branch plant mentality as well. It is time that we move ourselves from being renters in our own house to being masters of our own house.

When they drill in that area they are never sure of getting gas or oil so they must drill more wells for more oil and they must consume the gas so that they can move toward oil self-sufficiency.
The Americans believe in free enterprise, Mr. Speaker, but this government does not, even though the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) kept on yelling "We are private entrepreneurs". The government has put private entrepreneurs out of business.
The Alaska pipeline will never be built, Mr. Speaker. I do not believe it was just delayed for two years; it will never be built. The Americans will put it over their own soil. With the attitude that we show toward the Americans, how do we know that they will not say: "We don't want anything more to do with Canada; they have hurt enough of our corporate citizens and investors, and we want to get away from that?"
Representatives of the Consumers' Association of Canada appeared before the committee and I was shocked by what they said. I think they wrote the National Energy Program. I think they got Ed Clark in a corner and wrote the National Energy Program with him. Their only comment was to the effect that private enterprise cannot do it and the state must do it. Mr. Speaker, the state does not do very much in the private sector very well. A couple of recent examples are Canadair which got $1,350,000 to bail them out and Eldorado which got $400 million to bail them out.
How much more do we have to give for state ownership to pacify the red rump and then keep bailing them out? All they can do is talk and yell and get upset. Why do they not believe in what built this country, namely private enterprise?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say at the beginning of my remarks that I am genuinely pleased this debate is being resumed. I think it is appropriate to say that common sense, tradition and good judgment have prevailed, and I am very pleased about that.
This is a very necessary and timely energy debate. It is of the utmost importance to all of my constituents and to myself as their member of Parliament that I participate. Indeed, it is my duty and my responsibility to participate today and I am eager and privileged to do so on behalf of my Medicine Hat constituents.
This emergency debate was triggered by last weekend's double whammy of the collapse or demise of the two giant megaprojects, one being Alsands in the Alberta northern oil sands, and the other project, the northern natural gas pipeline, particularly the financing of it by the United States. This is an appropriate occasion to discuss some of the serious consequences of the National Energy Program on the oil and natural gas industry in southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan. I am reasonably well acquainted and familiar with both of those areas.
I propose to direct my remarks to this aspect of the energy debate. I deliberately used the slang expression "double whammy" to emphasize last week's disastrous announcement. However, a third major megaproject should properly be added to the list. I am speaking of the Cold Lake heavy crude megaproposal of Imperial Oil. It is of the same magnitude in its implications. It is perhaps understandable but most regrettable that Imperial's technical resource team for Cold Lake has been quietly disabanded and dispersed. That entire project is at least unofficially dead.
The tragedy of this triple whammy and these final failures is the enormous negative impact on our total Canadian struggle to live with and overcome the present serious economic recession. That negative impact translates quickly and directly to lost jobs by the thousands and lost opportunities by the billions of dollars for two regions in Canada. First, the three western provinces are affected, especially Alberta, with respect to energy exploration, production and the value added industries. Second, the huge industrial potential opportunities of Ontario, and to a lesser degree of Quebec, are now gone. This triple energy collapse will delay for years the possible reality of Canadian energy self-sufficiency. The tragedy is that Canadian self-sufficiency is possible; I do not think anyone would argue that.
With respect to the eleventh hour attempts of federal energy officials and Alberta to save the project, there was a joint 50 per cent offer by the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada. It seemed like a reasonable and responsible offer, but surely the entire episode begs the question: Why
could this proposal not have been advanced and proceeded with at least two years ago?
Turning to the northern natural gas pipeline setback or even demise, because two years which have been suggested at the setback on that particular project are as good as the kiss of death, I remind the House of the specific admonition of President Reagan when he spoke to our Canadian Parliament on March 11, 1981. He specifically warned us that while the United States government supported the giant pipeline project, financial responsibility for the American portions must be with the private sector, and that private sector responsibility has now failed. Of course, this is another example of lost jobs by the thousands and lost opportunities by the billions for all Canadians. The negative implications suggest that Canada has a moral responsibility to urge the United States to live up to the terms of the formal pipeline treaty between Canada and the United States, dated September 20, 1977.
All southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan are vitally affected by the megapipeline hold-up amounting to a demise. In southeastern Alberta there are thousands of capped gas wells awaiting-some of them for many years-an opportunity to produce and contribute to the eastern leg of the pre-built section of the northern gas pipeline. The eastern leg crosses the Alberta-Saskatchewan border in my riding, continues southeasterly across the southwestern corner of Saskatchewan, and enters the United States at a point called Monchy on the Saskatchewan-Montana border. This portion of the eastern leg is now completed and capable of transporting natural gas to Montana in the United States. The western leg of the main line is now completed and is transporting gas across the southeastern corner of British Columbia and into the United States.
Turning to my own constituency, I suggest that if there is a single identifiable commodity which could be associated with the city of Medicine Hat, it would be natural gas; it has been so for 99 years. We will celebrate our centenary throughout next year. Natural gas has been our lifeline from the very begining; the first gas well in western Canada was drilled at or near Medicine Hat 100 years ago. For many years visiting dignitaries were treated to a special gas-well flare at the CPR station in Medicine Hat as a special indication of our underground resource. Rudyard Kipling, on a visit to my home city, was moved to suggest that Medicine Hat must surely have "all hell for a basement". The city of Medicine Hat has always owned, produced and distributed its own utilities, including electrical power generated by natural gas.
The new taxation on natural gas in the National Energy Program has now resulted in substantial increases to all home owner utility bills. Most of them have been increased by over 100 per cent in the last one and a half years. Commercial users have seen their costs increase by as much as 400 per cent due to natural gas taxes. This 400 per cent figure applies to the greenhouse industry, one of our earliest and most important industries which depends almost entirely upon natural gas. This industry has shipped cut flowers across western Canada
May 6, 1982

for many years, and it may very well not survive this punitive federal tax.
Some people will remind me that we have always enjoyed cheap natural gas in our corner of Alberta. This was true until now. However, the percentage increase in utility taxes is much higher than it is in any other location across Canada. These gas tax costs translate immediately into much higher total costs for retired people and all industrial users of natural gas. A great number of retired farmers, especially from Saskatchewan, have for years enjoyed coming to Medicine Hat to retire and enjoy the benefits of natural gas.
On April 19, 1982, it was my pleasure and duty to present a formal petition to Parliament on behalf of 12,689 concerned citizens of Medicine Hat and adjoining Redcliff who were justifiably outraged over the hardships and illegality of the gas taxes. It was a carefully prepared petition which emerged rather quickly, mostly as a result of spontaneous effort on the part of housewives to demonstrate their desperation and sense of urgency over this tax provision of the National Energy Program. It should be noted that all signators to the petition were at least 18 years of age or over.
The petition also fully supported the legal action of the Medicine Hat city council against the federal government which is now underway. It questions the legal and constitutional right of the federal government to tax another government, as provided for in the BNA Act, on the assumption that city-owned and distributed utilities are in reality an extension of provincial government authority. This legal action is presently before the Alberta courts in the city of Calgary.
On another somewhat related legal issue involving natural gas in southeastern Alberta, it is appropriate to mention the status of the Smith-Coulee natural gas case. Briefly this case involves three gas wells drilled by the government of Alberta on Crown land in the extreme southern part of my constituency near the United States border. These wells are presently connected by pipeline to export natural gas to the United States, and the Alberta government is prepared to do just that. Last year the Alberta government asked the Alberta appeal court to rule on the question of the constitutional right and legality of the export of gas by Alberta from Alberta land to the United States. Five judges of the Alberta appeal court ruled unanimously in favour of Alberta. Now the decision has been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada by the Government of Canada. The Supreme Court referral has been argued by Alberta, and a decision is still to be announced. I mentioned the Smith-Coulee case because there may well be a direct relationship in the final court decisions of both the city of Medicine Hat and the government of Alberta.
Before concluding my remarks, I should like to make a brief comment on the heavy crude production situation in southwestern Saskatchewan. This is a small but worthwhile energy development of extremely heavy oil. It has been completely shut in for some time now, at least up until about a week ago. It has been shut in due to the negative and discriminatory aspects of the National Energy Program. It was simply uneconomic to continue producing these wells. They were losing money on every well because of the low price and the
fact that the heavy crude had to be moved to the United States to be refined. Of course, this made it very expensive.
Very recently, perhaps only a week ago, some of these wells had been allowed a 57 per cent production quota, which may help somewhat. An added negative factor is that the heavy oil upgrading plant which was scheduled for Saskatchewan-I do not know if the location was actually made public-had either been cancelled or set back indefinitely, again as a direct result of the National Energy Program.
Finally, I want to make a concluding comment about the entire energy program and its negative implications for the gas and oil well servicing industry. Brooks is a town in the northwest corner of my constituency. It had a population of 9,000 until the tragedy of the National Energy Program hit them. I am sure that many people have moved away. This town had become a hub of activity for the gas well, and some oil well, servicing industries. Almost without exception they were privately owned by small entrepreneurs who were Canadian. It was a joy to visit Brooks to see this activity which flourished for three or four years until the tragedy of the NEP and the current budget hit that town. These businesses were extremely hurt. I am sure there are other areas in Alberta and the Edmonton area in particular where this situation has happened. However, I single out Brooks because it has been dealt a crippling blow. A good many of these small Canadian entrepreneurs have either moved or gone into receivership.
I conclude with that comment because I think it exemplifies how critical the situation is in my province and my constituency. I am sure it is even worse in other areas. I appreciate the privilege to be able to talk about the implications of the National Energy Program for my constituency.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before addressing the issue of this debate under Standing Order 26, I would like to say how pleased I am to have an opportunity to participate in this debate and to commend the House leader for the government on the motion he put on floor this afternoon. I think that all of us on this side feel that this place is the better for his gesture. I believe he has restored a great deal more faith in the parliamentary democracy process which should take place here.
On Friday, April 30, 1982 it was announced in two separate statements that the Alsands megaproject had collapsed and that the Alaska pipeline had been postponed for two years. The House will know that this represents an unprecedented disaster for the Canadian economy. This disaster can be directly traced to the National Energy Program.
Canada has been relying on the megaprojects to accomplish two goals; to guarantee energy self-sufficiency, and to provide employment and stimulation to the Canadian economy. In short, it would provide jobs.
As a result of the collapse of these projects, our party requested this emergency debate in an attempt to focus the

May 6, 1982
attention of this House on the necessity for jobs in the Canadian economy and the need for energy self-sufficiency. I suggest that in all of our speeches we wish to trace what we feel this meant to the Canadian economy and to suggest some solutions.
There is no question that these megaprojects were important to the Canadian economy since they created 4,800 permanent jobs, 7,000 jobs for construction workers during the construction peak and 14,000 indirect jobs. Many of those jobs were in Ontario steel mills and manufacturing plants. The plan was considered important to our overall goal of self-sufficiency, one which members on all sides of the House believe in.
It was estimated that in 1990 the Alsands plant would produce 11 per cent of this country's estimated oil production. As well, there were spin-off effects in all sectors of the Canadian economy. These effects would have ranged as far as the east coast. Oshawa was particularly affected because that is where pick-up trucks were manufactured to supply the workers in the oil fields. I have visited Alberta and I can appreciate that jobs were created out there but as a member from Ontario I think in terms of the jobs it would have meant for the iron and steel companies of Ontario. It would have meant a $600 million injection for the iron and steel companies, $550 million into the transportation sector and $1.1 billion into other sectors of the manufacturing economy of Ontario.
What promise did we have? Why are these megaprojects so important? They were the magic, the engine of the Canadian economy, as was suggested by the Liberal party. They were going to reduce unemployment, provide more satisfying job opportunities for Canadians and increase our participation in the work force. It would mean growth in Canada at a time when we are either in a recession or depression-depending upon which economist you talk to.
Lest my remarks be totally partisan, I refer to job estimates put out by various government bodies. The suggestion is that there would be created in the pipeline projects 19,000 direct employment jobs and some 71,000 indirect employment jobs.
There are other projects which have been cancelled or deferred as a result of the National Energy Program. For example, there is the Polar gas project, the Kitimat project, the tar sands III project, the Syncrude expansion and many more which have been cancelled or postponed because of the National Energy Program.
Why has the industry lost confidence in the Canadian government? I think there are several reasons and I would like to point them out to the House today. First, there is the grab for federal revenue. It is an effort, through the massive legislation which we have seen, to view energy and our natural resources as simply a tax producer rather than a job producer. I believe that is the essence of how it is regarded on the other side of the House. In our party, we view the megaprojects and the pipelines not as an investment opportunity for some multinational, not as an investment for someone who does not live in Canada, but as an opportunity to put Canadians to work. I suggest that the other side of the House looks at it as
an opportunity for revenue. We cannot have the revenue unless we create the jobs. The jobs must come first.
I will not get into a great debate as to whether the oil companies are foreign-owned, Canadian-owned, half-owned or quarter-owned. That does not interest me. What interests me are jobs in Canada, jobs that cannot be taken away once they are created. I do not care who creates them.
I do not like the discrimination in this energy legislation against the foreign companies. We find the national energy policy confiscates petroleum rights. You will know, Mr. Speaker, that during the debate on the Constitution, our party put forward our feelings about property rights because we were worried about property rights. We felt that they should not be confiscated. We felt they should not be taken away from the people of Canada, nor from companies which are owned by Canadians.
Basically, it breaks down to this: Canadians feel that the government broke its word to the oil companies concerning tarsands oil prices. It is basically a matter of trust. Frankly, the people of Canada no longer trust the Liberal party.
We voted for the Alaska Highway natural gas pipeline. If we ever bring it back, I think we should shorten the name of it so that I can remember the order. We voted for it because of the representations of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), who said this:
In our view, exports of natural gas to the United States should be authorized only on the basis of, first of all, an ironclad commitment regarding the building of the whole Alaska gas pipeline. Everything has to be signed, sealed and delivered, particularly the financing plan and the financing guarantees, before we start exporting one cubic foot of gas out of this country to the United States.
Then we have the expert from the other place. It is rather unfortunate that we find ourselves dealing with people from the other place once we get west of the Manitoba border, but that seems to be the only way in which the government can show any sort of understanding as to what happens to the other half of the country. The Hon. Senator Olson said:
We are satisfied that the United States is committed to build their portion of the line by 1985-
Given the nature of U.S. assurances, the government has decided there is minimal risk of non-completion or long delay in the construction of the entire Alaska Highway gas pipeline system.
Well, on Friday it collapsed. I want to emphasize the fact that we voted for it because we could foresee jobs on the pipeline. We could foresee jobs created to make the steel and everything which would go into the construction of that pipeline. We make no apologies for that vote. I know that reference has been made today by the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) to the fact that the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) was not present during the vote on the pipeline. Since that hon. member wished to bring up voting records, I would like to state for the record that during votes 122 to 169, the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap was absent 23 times. He was present for exactly one half of those votes.

I am sure that everyone would want that on the record so that it could be considered.
What has the Liberal party told the people of Canada? In 1979 and 1980, it campaigned on the theory that it would not raise the price of gasoline by 18 cents a gallon. However, it has raised it 17 times, to 28 cents a gallon in tax and some 78 cents a gallon in total. By September 1, barring something we do not know about, which is always a possibility with this government, the seventeenth increase will bring the price of gasoline to well over $2 a gallon in most Canadian cities.
The people of Canada know they were told a lie. The people of Ontario know they were told a lie. The people of Simcoe-North, in my riding, know they were told a lie. What has this National Energy Program done for Canada? Drilling activity was down 25 per cent in 1981 over 1980 in contrast to the fact that it went up by 25 per cent in the United States during the same period. Well completions are down 25 per cent in Canada. Exploratory drilling, which employs people from right across the country, is down 19 per cent. Development drilling is down 28 per cent. Since the introduction of the National Energy Program, 226 drilling rigs have left Canada.
I had the opportunity to go out west to Alberta to find out, as an Ontarian, just exactly what is involved in moving a rig. I saw some of those trucks, as I understand it, it takes between 20 and 40 trucks loaded with steel to take a drilling rig across the border.

That is just one rig. And it is quite obvious that once you set one of those rigs down, you do not move it back too quickly. So that is what we have lost as a result of the National Energy Program.
Lest one thinks it was just steel that we lost when we lost that rig, let me read into the record a letter from one of my constituents:
Dear Mr. Lewis:
1 never thought I would be writing to my federal representative but unfortunately 1 feel that I must express my extreme displeasure with the current energy policy. I feel that being a voter I should let you know how it is effecting us.
I am a third year undergraduate enrolled in geology at McMaster University and I am extremely interested in petroleum exploration and as such 1 am looking for summer employment in the industry. My search for employment has involved sending out hundreds of resumes along with interviews with the major oil companies. To this day I have received nothing encouraging.
You might say that I am not qualified to get an offer but I disagree with that. 1 am enrolled in the honours program and my marks are good, and on top of that I have a summers experience in mapping Cenozoic and Tertiary elastics in the Yukon and Alberta with Gulf Minerals. I do not think it is entirely my qualifications because everyone in my program has been experiencing the same problem.
I feel that the problems I am having with employment are due to one thing and it is summarized quite nicely by Union Oil and I quote:
No doubt you are aware of the restraints of the new federal budget. The effects of these restraints have substantially reduced our staffing requirements.
Not only does this predicament effect my summer employment but it effects my Bachelors thesis. I want to become a petroleum geologist but if can not do my thesis in Alberta this summer my chances for a full-time job next year will be even more severely limited.
It is pathetic that a country like ours which is gifted with copious amounts of fossil fuels can not develop these resources which could make us energy self sufficient. You would think that the government would want to help the economy.
Hopefully people will see how detrimental the present government is to the economy and will give sensible people like yourself a chance to run the country before it is too late.
That is not political rhetoric, that was not a letter invited from a constituent so that he could say exactly what I wanted him to say. That letter came into my office on January 29, 1982. There are firms in my riding which supply the petroleum industry. The people of Simcoe-North want jobs in that industry, whether by going out to Alberta or by making what we make very well in Ontario and sending it to Alberta. I am referring to Fahramet Limited which produces the reformer tube assemblies which are sent to Alberta for the petroleum industry.
I would like to finish my remarks by suggesting what can be done. I suggest that what is needed is a change in attitude. What is needed from the Liberal party is a decision to cooperate with industry rather than to coerce it. What we need to do is expand the Canadian energy industry, not contract it. We should end the confrontation that exists in Canada with the energy industry and get this country back to work.
The government and the Liberal party should realize that a business deal must be good for both sides. A business deal that sticks it to one side is no good. Both sides must be happy with the deal and have an opportunity under that deal to go forward. If it sticks it to one side, it will break down. I do not care how many signatures are on it-and I have seen this time and again in business-it has to be good for both sides. I suggest we look at the petroleum industry as an opportunity for jobs, not revenue. That is what should be important.
The government should focus in that way on the industry. It should listen to my colleagues, who are more knowledgeable in the industry than I, in the committee. I suggest, as I have often done in this House, that the budget be withdrawn so that we have some incentives for Canadians to invest in their economy.
I say all of this in a spirit of entering into a debate under Standing Order 26 which is not granted very often. Madam Speaker felt this subject was important enough that we take this time to address it. I ask the government, and I plead with the Liberal party, to put the country ahead of their interests and do everything possible to get this country back to work.

There they go, Mr. Speaker, before I even start! My friends on the other side are obviously getting ready to go.
I listened with interest from time to time to members opposite in this debate, including the hon. member for Simcoe

May 6, 1982
North (Mr. Lewis) who just spoke, on the collapse of the Alsands project and the delay of the Alaska Highway pipeline.
There is a question we have to assess honestly. Members opposite have said that the entire difficulty with these projects was caused solely by the National Energy Program. They say that is the only reason, that if it had not been for that program, the projects would have gone ahead without any doubt. That is not factually true. Major projects in the energy field are being cancelled in countries all around the world, no matter what government is in place or what kind of energy program they have.
We heard from the hon. member for Simcoe North and other members opposite about how exploration and development is booming in the United States. However, the oil shales project in the U.S. was cancelled; it was set aside by Exxon.
The Alsands project was certainly a major megaproject. Last night members were talking about the cost, saying that the project had gone from an estimated cost of $5 billion in 1980 to $14 billion. I have talked with people in the industry who have indicated that was probably a low estimate and that it would go much higher. I am sure that was one of the motivating factors which caused the private oil companies to decide not to go ahead with the Alsands project.
There is the historic experience with the Syncrude project. That project was supposed to do certain things, such as produce a certain volume of oil. It is not producing it and in fact never has produced it since its inception. It has been plagued with problems, not necessarily technological, with the way things were being done or the type of thinking and engineering that went into it, but because the equipment produced to work the oil sands depreciates very quickly. An individual at the head of Syncrude indicated in conversation last week that the oil sands eats the equipment alive. The replacement cost of the equipment is enormous. Therefore, it is much more expensive to extract oil from the sands than had been thought.
Shell, Gulf and the other companies involved in the Alsands consortium went to school on Syncrude. They looked at the Syncrude experience and the accuracy of the cost estimates. Indications from those in the industry they talked with were always: "No, the estimates were not right; yes, the estimates were too low and were escalating very rapidly".
Syncrude indicated that its costs were increasing by at least 20 per cent per year. When inflation was increasing between 10 and 12 per cent in the worst situation, which was last year, their costs were increasing at nearly double the rate of inflation. Certainly the companies involved in that consortium were looking at what was happening to Syncrude. They wanted to know the experience, how long it took to come on stream, how much oil was being produced and how much the costs were escalating. That was factored into the decision.
The other major factor which caused the demise of many megaprojects in countries around the world was the fact that world prices of oil have fallen dramatically. Educated opinion
in the field indicates that the world price of oil will fall substantially from the point it is at now. Estimates I have heard indicate that under the Alsands cost structure, a barrel of oil coming out of that project would be in the range of $40 to $45. If world prices were going up as they were, on average about 2 per cent per year, by the time Alsands came on stream, even with escalating costs, the price that could be obtained for a barrel of oil from the Alsands project would be greater than the cost of producing it.
All of a sudden the market turned itself on its ear. Instead of going up, the world price of oil dropped. In the past six months it has dropped by 25 per cent or 30 per cent. That changes the economics of all major energy projects. I am sure that is the second major factor that entered into the calculations of the oil companies in deciding not to proceed. They were not going to put their shareholders' money at extreme risk.
There is no indication that this would be a profitable venture given the economic conditions that face us today, the cost of the project and the price of paying for the product at the other end. The people involved in the Alsands project had to look not only at those factors but at the alternatives coming on stream. What are the alternatives? The oil industry estimates that Hibernia can probably produce at between $25 and $30 a barrel and the Beaufort in the range of $25 and $30 a barrel as well. It was felt that Alsands could produce oil at $40 to $45 per barrel. That is a substantial cost difference. Faced with that, I am sure people in the oil industry were saying that not only could they not be guaranteed a price sufficient to cover their costs, but that they would also be facing competition from a substitute which costs much less to produce. The Alsands people felt they would not be able to compete. Those factors had to be going through their minds.
I would not suggest for a minute that the National Energy Program did not create a situation of uncertainty for the industry. The government has been working very diligently to reduce that uncertainty and to put in place the incentives necessary to get exploration and development back on track. The government has been working to reduce that uncertainty, but we cannot fight economic facts. Economic facts indicate that there were some very real economic uncertainties having nothing to do with the National Energy Program which led to the demise of the Alsands project.
An hon. member opposite spoke about the Alaska gas pipeline. It is beyond my ability to understand, but somehow the two-year delay in that pipeline project is also the fault of this government. I do not understand that. Hon. members on both sides of the House voted in favour of the pre-build. We did everything we possibly could to see that it would go ahead.

They have delayed for two years because of changing realities in the energy business. I have heard it estimated that the cost of completing the project has gone up from $50 billion to $60 billion. What would be the cost of gas coming out of that line? That is an economic fact of life.
On top of the costs of the Alsands project and the gas pipeline there are present world economic conditions to consider. Apart from the cost of the Alsands project, apart from the price for the product which could logically be received and apart from the cost of producing the product- and the quite substantial negative differential-we are faced with another crunch, and that is general world economic conditions. There is declining demand. Very high interest rates would drive the financing costs of the project to astronomical levels. All these factors were involved in the decision by the private oil companies not to go ahead.
Hon. members opposite would say this government did nothing to try to preserve the jobs and the wealth creation which would result from proceeding with the Alsands project. That is just not true. The last offer put on the table by the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada was to tell the private sector participants in the project that the taxpayers would absorb virtually all the risk and guarantee an extremely high rate of return. The rate of return would have been about 20 per cent. To all intents and purposes, Shell Canada would not have paid any taxes for years and years. The offer put forward was extremely generous, but Shell looked at the situation and said that even with that generous offer the project would hinge on whether it would be economic to extract oil and whether Shell could get a price for oil which would come close to covering its costs. If you lose money, you lose money. It is not a matter of taxation or no taxation. If it is a losing proposition economically, one does not go ahead no matter how attractive the tax package or the guarantee. The package offered by the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada was extremely attractive, but a decision was made not to go ahead with Alsands on the basis of very sound and rational economic facts of life.
