speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to enter this emergency debate. I would preface my remarks by quoting Charles Dickens' opening line of "A Tale of Two Cities": "It was the best of times and it was the worst of times".
As usual, under the present administration it is the best of times if you are rich and have no worries; but most Canadians, not just the very poor who have always been badly off but middle-income Canadians, are finding it has become the worst of times.
I do not know how much longer Canadians will be able to tolerate the setback the country is suffering. We have very high inflation, very high interest rates, very high unemployment and lowering personal expectations. Our young people find it increasingly difficult to get work. High school and postsecondary students are advised that for the most part they will not be able to find full-time jobs this summer to help pay for their education. We have widespread uncertainty in the business community; we have widespread frustration in the labour force; we have widespread insecurity in the workplace and we have growing anger in the community.
The Liberals may say that this is a negative approach, but it is reality. In a country rich with resources, with a skilled work force and an abundance of capital, the Liberal government has brought us to the point of despair and stagnation. It has gone from one crisis to an other since coming into office two years ago.
This emergency debate is about the collapse of the Alsands Project, but what we are really talking about is the collapse of the main thrust of the government's economic policy. Alsands was just a part of it. For a long time my party has argued against making resource-based industries the major thrust of an economic policy. That is traditional Liberal policy-a quick-fix, easy policy. It does not require many brains to import talent and money that will rape our resources.
We have been doing that since at least the 1920s and it was done again in the 1950s and 1960s. In order to pay for our imports we allow foreigners to come in and develop our resources, ship them out of the country unfinished or partly finished and then we pay for manufactured imports. That worked in the 1920s, in the 1950s and until the late 1960s and it contributed to a rapid rise in our standard of living.
Because of the economic times in which we find ourselves now, the harsh reality of the weakness of this megaproject
May 6, 1982

based policy-in this case energy, but it could have been mines or any other area of our natural resource bases-and because of the financial realities, we suddenly realise that the main pillar of the Liberals' economic thrust in the eighties has been pulled out from under the government and indeed, the entire country.
We have seen the death of the $14 billion Alsands project and the end, we assume, of the $30 billion Alaska gas pipeline. Hibernia and Venture off the east coast, while viable in the technological sense, will cost $6 billion and $3 billion respectively. We are talking $43 billion, the big eggs the Liberals have put in one basket.
At the same time what has the Liberal government allowed? Inflation soaring at 11.6 per cent with no indication whatever that it is going to come down substantially. High interest rates of 16 per cent or 17 per cent for the bank's safest customers, 19 per cent or 20 per cent for consumers. In addition, the government has been putting all its economic thrust into capital-intensive resource megaprojects, we have soaring interest rates and a constriction on economic development. In other words, a tight money policy-Reaganomics-which incidentally is supported by the Conservatives. The Conservative financial spokesman has said this outside the House. Their leader, just the other day, indicated very strongly that there was no approach to our problems other than continued high interest rates. The irony of this debate is that it was the Conservatives who demanded it, and there is no difference between Conservative monetary policy and Liberal monetary policy. The people of Canada know it.
It is not nice to say "I told you so" because it sort of puts that halo around your own head, but two years ago my party was very concerned that the Alaska gas project was going to be yet another giveaway, because we had no guarantee that the Americans would or could live up to their end of the bargain. So we voted against the pre-build section. We did so not because we were against the whole project; indeed, had it gone ahead Canada would have been a net beneficiary because there would have been the swap later on of American natural gas from Alaska at comparative prices.
But what are we left with? Alsands is dead and we are left with the pre-build, which takes inexpensive Canadian gas to the United States. Only fools in the U.S. would now try to raise the horrendous amount of money required to go ahead and build the American portion of the line to bring out their own gas. The Americans have always worked on the principle that if you can get a non-renewable resource offshore, that is where you go first. You bleed another country until there is nothing left and then use your own resources. From their point of view it is a good and wise policy. They do not have to reduce their own natural resources on which their entire industrial complex is based.
Why can't we be just as intelligent? When you have a hot item to sell and a tremendous world demand for it, why do you have to act with such indecent haste in trying to get rid of it?
Why not be smart and make the best deal? Is it because the Liberals are so inexperienced; they have not been in office very long, they do not have many contacts in Washington, they do not know the name of the game? Hardly the case, Mr. Speaker, for a political party which has been in office almost continuously since 1935.
Therefore, there is something wrong across the aisle and I do not think it is just a lack of intelligence or savvy. I think what has happened is that they have lost the will, on the one hand, to protect our national heritage of resources, and on the other hand they have lost the will to find innovative and dynamic new approaches to a sagging economy. There are muchmore eager to say it is world stagnation or recession and we are just a small part of it. It is much easier to blame somebody else. But if the American economy should come back in three to five years, as U.S. congressmen are now predicting, and if there should be some spin-off north of the border, then of course the Liberals will be the first to jump on the U.S. bandwagon and say: "We told you so; we pulled our nation through."
There is really not one creative idea anywhere on the opposite side that I can see. There does not seem to be any kind of dynamism left in that haggard and worn-out cabinet. What do they do when there is unemployment? The answer of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is: "Share the misery by sharing the unemployment, by going to a three or four-day week". I think it is disgraceful that workers have to behave in 1982 the same as they did in the 1930s by outbidding each other for the lowest paying job in the community. The Liberals have taken us back 50 years because their creativity is impotent. They just lack the will, Mr. Speaker.
The latest reports coming out of Rutgers University and the OECD just last week indicate very strongly that there is the beginning of a turnaround in France and Japan, and to a lesser degree in the U.K. The rest of the major industrialized nations have bottomed out and will commence a recovery within the next six to eight months. Canada is the only industrial nation today which is still sinking deeper and deeper into depression. This is because of the lack of will and the loss of direction in the Liberal government.
We have heard the Conservatives lambaste the government, Mr. Speaker, in a rather narrow way by stressing the collapse of Alsands, by saying it was not profitable and that the private sector could foresee financial disaster if they continued. All of which is no doubt true. But I would like to remind my Conservative friends, as has been alluded to already, that we have a situation in Colorado where the $6 billion or $7 billion shale operation of Exxon was shut down the other day, again the victim of falling world oil prices resulting from an oil glut and high interest rates. I remind them that there is no NEP in the U.S. In fact, the Americans are bragging, in their right-wing bravado, that they are rapidly deregulating the oil industry. Yet here is a major energy enterprise which has, I will not say collapsed, but been terminated at least for the foreseeable

May 6, 1982
future. So it is not really the NEP, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that is the cause; it is high interest rates and an oil glut which has caused the decline in oil prices.
There is a very interesting point here. The hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) who has just finished speaking-I believe it was he, but I stand to be corrected-implied that two years ago we could not foresee this oil glut. We could not anticipate a decline in oil prices. I am quite sure that if he and his Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) had followed the discussions of the OPEC ministers in Vienna and in Caracas, Venezuela and if they had been listening to Sheik Yamani's speeches that he made throughout Europe and the Middle East beginning as far back as 1979, they would have realized that the thrust as early as 1979 on the part of OPEC was to stem research and development in the western industrial world in areas of alternate sources of energy. They would have realised the fact that conservation would have an impact on oil prices and they would have heard Sheik Yamani say to his colleagues in OPEC: "Look, fellows, we cannot keep flooding the market with oil because there will be a decline in demand, traditional customs in Europe and the western world." Anybody who read the headlines of a newspaper two and a half years ago could foretell with a considerable degree of accuracy that there would be a deliberately planned world oil glut and a consequent decline in prices. There is no excuse whatever, Mr. Speaker, for the Liberal government not to have been aware that the price of world oil would decline as a result of a glut on the market.
The problem here, and I alluded to it at the beginning of my remarks, is that the government has got everything the wrong way. We are not opposed to the rational development of our natural resources, even for export. We are not opposed to the Alaska natural gas pipeline. We are not opposed to Hibernia or Venture on the east coast. But we in the NDP have maintained for many years, long before this crisis and certainly long before this emergency debate, that the only way to get this country back on the track in the long term-and for any longterm solution you have to start yesterday-is to make sure the major thrust of economic development is in the industrial areas of our economy. That does not mean Ontario and Quebec only; it means right across the country from the east coast to the west coast.
We should be putting a greater emphasis on manufacturing. We should be creating jobs in the machinery industry, in all facets of transportation and in housing. Without creating a strong industrial and manufacturing base in this country, we will be constantly at the mercy of offshore prices of natural resources. That is a major problem and it is the major weakness of the Liberal position. We would not be in this mess today if the Liberal government had forced the multinationals in the industrial sector, most of which are foreign-owned, to manufacture up to sales in our country. We would not have that tremendous net deficit in trade and manufactured goods which has gone from $2.4 billion in 1970 to $21 billion in 1981. That means a loss of 200,000 jobs in those industries.
I know my time is up, but I wish to sum up by simply saying that I hope this government opposite, before it drives the entire country into a quagmire of economic depression, not only finds some new ideas, which have been positively put forward by the NDP, but regains its sense of direction and its will to govern, something which it has lost.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) in closing his speech said, "before this government drives the country into the quagmire of economic depression". Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, it already has.
Last Friday was a black Friday. On that day the Alsands project was declared finally dead. On that day we at the same time lost any benefit, certainly for some considerable period of time, that we might receive from a new pipeline project running to Alaska. It was a black Friday, not because one industrial project was declared by the owners of that project as no longer viable but because Alsands was symbolic of the disasters that have befallen our country, starting with the election of the government in February, 1980, strengthened by a budget of disaster on October 28, 1980, strengthened further toward disaster by the activities fomented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and our minister of lack of energy, throughout 1980 and almost right through to September, 1981. Through that period the government made sure that the golden ring that Canada had available to it in energy was lost.
When the Liberals took power, by misrepresentation and fraud in February, 1980, there was opportunity and hope in Canada that we could be energy self-sufficient-indeed, that if we could capitalize on our energy wealth, that energy, the oil and gas business, the hydro business and the coal that we have in Canada would propel us through the 1980s and give opportunity for our young people, develop our manufacturing, our expertise and the chemical industry. It would make Canada grow, it would give Canadians employment, hope and opportunity. It was there.
The world was looking everywhere for new and better opportunities to develop energy in opposition to what OPEC had created. We had the chance at the golden ring, and this government threw it away. It threw it away in policies of confrontation with the provinces. It threw it away with an attempt to grab, steal and expropriate the private property of people who would develop. This government would not let people do their own thing and use their entrepreneurship to make and create the country.
This government threw away our hopes and aspirations regarding how to pay off financial debt, almost in one year, by new and destructive forms of taxation. We have a government that promised this country oil prices would be forever lower in Canada than anywhere else, that 18 cents was extortionist. But we now find that 78 cents is not even enough. It is not even enough for its greed. We threw away the golden ring that was there. We threw away the opportunities for the 1980s. We ensured that a recession in this country and in the world would
May 6, 1982

not remain a recession but in this country might well work into a deeper depression.
The government says that Alsands is gone but there are possibilities on the east coast. Only a few months ago a supposedly unsinkable oil rig sank like the Titanic off the east coast. Also the government says that there is oil in the Beaufort Sea, but there is every conceivable regulation and every conceivable ecological problem associated with getting that oil to market. The government says that we should not feel too badly because we have the Norman Wells pipeline, but it has been held up for two years with regulations and red tape. Then it says we have the Q&M pipeline, but as someone said during this debate, the pipe gets smaller as it goes to a market; in any event, it is tied up with labour problems in the province of Quebec and is not proceeding.
Every alleged megaproject or mini-megaproject, every potential development which could have taken place, from the development of the Cold Lake project by Esso to the tertiary recovery in the Judy Creek field, has gone by the boards. Some people wonder why, but I do not. When the government was first sworn into office I was asked to comment upon the persons who were appointed to various cabinet positions. When I found out that the present minister was to be Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, I said, "Goodbye energy in Canada; too bad Canada, you've had it!"
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) cannot obtain co-operation from anywhere. He has only one purpose in mind; it is his whole being and his whole approach. I spent an entire afternoon in a committee meeting with him, so I know well his approach. It is to control, to regulate, to tax, and to try to centralize all decision-making in any department of government with which he has had anything to do. This is probably because of his philosophy which is the philosophy of the four key people in cabinet-the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. They want to change the nature of Canada from an enterprise society to a state-controlled society.
Their philosophy suggests that we should get rid of incentive and entrepreneurship in Canada, except to the extent that it can be controlled by people in an ivory tower in Ottawa. Of course they can be controlled by making businessmen crawl to Ottawa for grants of assistance, by regulations so horrendous that even a fleet of Philadelphia lawyers cannot get through them, and by bills such as the ones introduced in the House which allow the minister to tax one company in one way and another in another way, to change and treat things retroactively or retrospectively as he may desire.
Is it any wonder businessmen and entrepreneurs no longer trust the government, why billions and billions of Canadian capital has left Canada, with more following every day as the lifeblood of the country leaks away, why Canadians must pay high rates of interest on their home mortgages, why farmers go bankrupt and people are out of work?
The philosophy of government ownership, of government control and of government direction of our lives-the way we build and create-as is propounded in the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and in communist countries.
It has ensured that those countries cannot feed themselves and that their people live in poverty and desperation. It is a philosophy which causes Canadians to realize that some day in the not too distant future they will be part of the Soviet of Canada.
I should like to refer to some of the things the minister has done over the period of time he has been in office. I should like to shed some fresh light on the minister. I looked up some correspondence I had with him in connection with Suncor.
The first oil sands plant in the country was built by a subsidiary of Suncor, GCOS. This company had some Canadian shareholdings but it was largely held by the Sun Oil Company of the United States. Suncor went into the tar sands area of northern Alberta near Fort McMurray. It experimented and spent a lot of its hard-earned money to develop oil sands technology; it very nearly bit the bullet. It worked hard, but it lost money in every year from 1963 to 1978. In 1979 it started making money for the first time. These pioneers gambled with their own money. If they had known what was to happen with world prices, with technological problems, with fires burning up compressors, with frost, and with equipment breaking down, I suppose they would not have become involved. They gambled and developed tar sands technology which Alsands would have and Syncrude is using.
Suncor started making money. It was doing very well because it entered into an agreement with the Government of Canada whereby it would always obtain world prices for its oil. Then the vicious, greedy minister came along in October, 1980, and said, "Ha, we've got them now! They are making money, so we will only give Suncor the same payment for oil we give anyone who happens to drill in a good field; we will give them $16.75 per barrel for their oil and treat them as if they were someone using ordinary Texas technology to drill a hole and pump oil." Suncor was financially ruined.
With respect to the agreement with Suncor concerning world prices, the minister said that he could avoid it and did not have to live up to it because it was too rich, in his opinion. The minister wonders why the Shell Oil Company and Mr. Daniels and the people involved in Gulf Canada do not want to trust the financial offer which he made at the last moment. Why do they not trust him? Would you trust someone who made a promise in writing to give you certain concessions and then, when he felt in his opinion that the price was better than it should be, he would unilaterally break the deal? That is what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has done. How any company could trust him is beyond belief.
The New Democratic Party said that the offer was exceptionally rich. The New Democratic Party is part of the Liberal party. They certianly have the same philosophy. They were upset over the alleged offer that the Minister of Energy, Mines

May 6, 1982
and Resources made to Alsands. They said that if the government were to put up any guaranteees or money it should expropriate the whole project. They want it all in their pocket. They want socialism absolutely. This minister does not want absolute socialism. He justs wants absolute control. Eventually, by eating away at the companies, he will own everything. But the NDP want it all right away.
As we said before, the NDP are really the Liberal Party West. They prefer to call themselves the New Democratic Party but sometimes even they call themselves liberals in a hurry. They are part of the same party. Properly, they should be called the "Liberal New Democratic Party", or the "New Democratic Liberal Party" or perhaps just "Liberal Party West". That way they can differentiate themselves and pretend to take a western stance on issues. There is no real difference between the NDP and the Liberals-they are certainly the same as those who control, and manage and direct the Liberal party.
We need to build this country and we cannot accomplish that until we change the attitude of the government. The government must encourage entrepreneurs.
While preparing for my speech, I was reviewing some material. To conclude my remarks I thought I would relate to the House a statement made by the leader of this party in 1978 at an industrial strategy conference. I am pleased that the minister in charge of industrial strategy is here. I want to quote to you what the leader of our party said at that time. He was referring to the Hudson's Bay Company. He said:
(The) Company (that opened up Western Canada) was not just called the Hudson's Bay Company; it was called the Company Of Adventurers Trading Into Hudson's Bay. i think that there is a lesson about our history in that phrase. When we are at our best as a country, it is when we are a country of adventurers. What we have suffered in the last decade, when there has been such an emphasis upon the re-distribution of existing income rather than the generation of new growth and new income in this country, has been an undervaluing, a disrespect for that sense of adventure which is at the very centre of our success as a country. We clearly have to begin the process of rewarding success in this country and encouraging initiative.
It is time that we began to turn this country around. It can only be turned around if we throw out the concept of state ownership, state intervention and state economy. Those concepts have been demonstrated time and again not to work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the Canadian economy is in a severe economic crisis. It is appropriate that this emergency debate has provided us with the opportunity to examine the situation in depth.
While it focuses on the immediate crisis which has been precipitated by the disappearance of the Alsands project and the Alaska pipeline project, I think we have to admit that the
economic crisis in the Canadian economy has been a long time developing. It is all the more tragic because Canada, with its rich heritage of resources, should be one of the most prosperous countries today.
Just to demonstrate that it is not a figment of opposition imagination, that the depth of our economic crisis has been dreamed up by it, there are reports which can be quoted from many sources which indicate that while there might be other economic downturns in other countries, the recession is worse in Canada. Results from a survey done by the Centre for International Business Cycle Research at Rutgers University in New Jersey, for example, have said that the indices:
-show restrictive monetary and fiscal policies are now taking more of a toll in Canada than elsewhere.
It goes on further to say:
"In Canada, the Government is basically waiting for things to happen elsewhere."
This is the state of affairs which has brought about the necessity for this emergency debate. The government has become completely out of touch with the reality in our constituencies. In the short time that I have, I will spend some time relating just how difficult the situation is out there in the constituencies. I can read a few excerpts from local western newspapers to cite some examples. In the western Manitoba area which I represent, a businessman was interviewed. An article in the Brandon Sun on May 3 began:
Strong, dry, prairie winds buffeted A1 Cormier's hardware stone as he talked about closing up shop this July.
"I'm not going to stay here and lose money every day," Cormier said. "People have much less money, much less than four, five, six years ago."
The article says that this merchant is:
-among many rural businessmen in southwestern Manitoba caught in a declining agricultural economy.
It is not only a crisis in energy or in the resource industry, it is a crisis in our basic industry of agriculture. The article went on to say:
Low commodity prices, rising production costs and high interest rates all have taken their toll, forcing farmers to hold off on spending, sometimes putting seeding plans off altogether.
Because of the state of the economy, there have even been instances of cattle farmers allowing their cattle to starve to death. When we get to that point in the western agricultural economy, it is high time that the government, rather than just sitting back and waiting for something to happen, takes the initiative and changes its disastrous economic policies, which in the space of 14 years have reduced Canada from a buoyant, prosperous economy to a disastrous economic situation where all the indices are downward.
I know it is true that even ministers have made their complaints. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister of State (Mr. Joyal) have even written to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in an attempt to impress the
May 6, 1982

disastrous state of the economy upon them. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has burst into bold print, trying to get the message through to the powers that be in the government; but nothing seems to penetrate the thick skulls of these people who have the responsibility of running the economic affairs of the nation. Hopefully, this debate and the growing protest of the people might be able to do what even ministers of the Crown, breaking cabinet solidarity and suffering no consequences for breaking solidarity, have attempted to do.
This situation did not develop overnight. When the government came into power in 1968, Canada was a prosperous country, with a strong dollar, with no inflation, with low debt and with little unemployment; yet, in the short space of 14 years a country which should be riding high on a crest of the wave of prosperity has been reduced to a situation where leading international economic authorities have described our recession as the worst of any industrialized country in the western economy.
The crisis that we are focusing on today, to bring it all into focus, is the crisis in energy which has been precipitated by the loss of the Alsands and the Alaska pipeline. I would think that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), who is in the House this evening, would be particularly distressed and disturbed over what has happened with the petroleum industry under the misdirected guidance of the Trudeau government because we all know that prosperity in the automobile industry is directly related to prosperity in the energy industry. One of our most critically depressed industries has been the automobile manufacturing industry which is primarily based in the constituency and City of Windsor, represented by no less than three ministers. One would think that with three ministers in the cabinet raising their voices, we should be able to get some action out of a government which seems to be totally indifferent, almost oblivious to the damage it is doing to the Canadian economy.

speechtext:
A troika. Certainly, no three wise men. The irony is that Canadian prosperity should be based on our rich resources. If we hope to come out of the depression in which we find ourselves today, it will have to be based on the wise management of these resources. They have been very badly and unwisely managed. If one looks back over the recent history of the management of our resources, there is no reason the goal of self-sufficiency was not reached a couple of decades ago.
We have heard references to frontier oil from the government side of the House during the course of this debate, yet frontier oil was under exploration 20 years ago. I remember being in the Department of Northern Affairs when the search was taking place for frontier oil back in 1960 and early 1961.
Interestingly enough, it was Dome Petroleum which was leading the search for frontier oil and resources. Back in those early days we had a slogan printed on interdepartmental memos circulating within the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources which went something like this: "Woe unto them who sit on their frozen assets." For all of the 20 years since the government of John Diefenbaker in 1963, succeeding governments have been sitting on their frozen assets, with the result that we are still talking about the potential of frontier oil, rather than realizing the benefits of frontier oil brought to market and being a part of the whole self-sufficiency scheme of the Government of Canada.
In those days when there was visionary talk about what could be accomplished by developing oil on the frontier, the response of the Liberal party was that development beyond the sixtieth parallel, or constructing roads to resources, was nothing more or less than building roads which would go from igloo to igloo. Where there is no vision, the people perish. It was at that period that Syncrude came into production. Syncrude has been on stream ever since. Alsands was to be another long-delayed source of attaining self-sufficiency. Tragically, it has gone down the drain.
There is another aspect of the development of the economic tragedy which has now emerged in a critical state as a result of the megaproject disaster that we are debating here these days. If we are to bring resources into production and if we are to develop resources to the benefit of the whole Canadian economy, we must work on a co-operative basis. Unfortunately, the whole story of energy under the national energy policy and under the leadership, or lack of leadership, of the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), has been one of confrontation. In 1962, realizing that was to become one of the most difficult and sensitive areas of federal-provincial co-operation, a "Resources for Tomorrow" conference was held in the City of Montreal. The City of Montreal was chosen because one of the most sensitive areas of realizing co-operation in the resource field lies in the province of Quebec. It was particularly difficult at that time because the minister of resources was none other than our friend who is the present premier of the province of Quebec, the Hon. Rene Levesque.
In October, 1961, all the resource ministers of Canada sat down to work out a plan with regard to the fabulously rich resources, most of them in western Canada as far as energy is concerned, oil, gas, potash, and the resources that we now know are in the northern frontier area. They sat down with the federal government to work out a program of co-operative development through co-operative federalism that was called "Resources for Tomorrow."
Out of that "Resources for Tomorrow" conference came a resource ministers' council. It was established in the City of Montreal because it was understood that, if you were going to work out a national program and policy, a really effective

May 6, 1982
national energy policy, we must have the co-operation of the province of Quebec. Remarkably the first general chairman of the resource ministers' council was the same Hon. Rene Levesque. It shows what can be done to achieve co-operation if the spirit of co-operation prevails in the deliberations and discussions.
One of the first actions the Trudeau government took when it took office in 1968 in a great wave of emotionalism and hysteria known as Trudeaumania was to disband the resource ministers' council and throw the whole process of intergovernment, interprovincial co-operation back into confrontationist disarray.
I did not understand it at the time. It remains incomprehensible to me at the present time. Of course it does not make economic sense. This is one of the main reasons why we are wrestling with this economic tragedy. Today if there is going to be any buoyancy in the Canadian economy, it has to come from a buoyant petroleum industry. From the moment this government took power in 1968, it was confrontation, until we reached the ultimate just a month ago when the Prime Minister went so far as to say that co-operative federalism is dead.
I listened to many speakers from the government side talk about the wonderful projects and programs that are still in the mill. I think it is fair to say that the government which deliberately destroys, through an ill-conceived National Energy Program, the prosperity in the oil industry of western Canada, does not have the interests of national development and national unity at heart.
We know what happened in Saskatchewan a week ago. The premier there got caught in a hopeless situation. It was the typical western protest. The national energy policy in all aspects is confrontationist tactics which have gone on since 1980. It is an attempt to grab a greater share of the revenue, almost an attempt to pay off the national debt through the revenues being generated by a prosperous petroleum industry in the west. One would almost think the government deliberately tried to kill the goose that lays the golden egg.
If this country is to survive, the only way is through cooperation at all levels, certainly at the level of resource development. The premier of Saskatchewan was caught in a posture of close relationship with the Government of Canada. He himself said that. When westerners protest, they protest in no uncertain way. It was a massive protest. It was like the Progressives of the twenties, the Social Credits of '35, and the CCF of '44. It shows hopeful development in this regard which demonstrates a growing political maturity in western Canada. Instead of biting off our nose to spite our face and starting another protest movement, such as joining the WCC, it was a massive protest in support of the Conservative candidates in Saskatchewan. In other words, the people decided to join the mainline party so that they would be in the mainstream of economic development. It is an indication that they want Canada to work. They realize the potential of this country even though they are frustrated beyond endurance.
Every time the minister responsible for resources goes to the west, he insults the west. Every time the Prime Minister goes to the west, he does the same. In spite of that, the people of
Saskatchewan had the wisdom to support a party which has the only chance of bringing the economy back into a state of prosperity. More important, it can get rid of confrontationist federalism and return to co-operative federalism. We will remove the divisiveness that has tended to shatter this country in recent years.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I could say it was a pleasure to take part in this debate, but this is a sad period for Canada, particularly for the younger people of this nation. The much-touted energy self-sufficiency goal we were hoping to attain did not self-destruct, it "Liberal-destructed".
The Alsands megaproject, which was to be the saviour of our energy situation in Canada, has been cancelled. The Alaska Highway natural gas pipeline has been delayed by at least two years. In fact, it is in essence as dead as the dodo bird. It is conservatively estimated by some people that approximately 100,000 people will be added to the well over one and a quarter million people now unemployed in this nation. If the figure were more realistically calculated, it would be in the vicinity of 150,000 to 200,000.
The real tragedy of the unemployment situation is that the youth of the nation is being adversely affected. I refer to young people coming out of schools this year and graduating from universities. I refer to skilled workers and unskilled workers looking for opportunities to gain skills. They will now be denied those opportunities. We all noticed what our youth have been doing. They have been going west to gain skills. The party opposite is controlled predominantly by hon. members from Quebec. I point out to them that the automobiles with yellow licence plates they used to see in their province did not belong to tourists. They belonged to young people who had come back from the west either to enjoy vacations or to gather up their belongings so they could go back out west again for employment. Those people had a vision of future opportunities in Canada, but now those cars will not be returning to the west because of the policies of this government. I suggest hon. members opposite take a long, hard look at those policies and a long, hard look at the difficulties they are inflicting on the youth of this nation. Hon. members opposite should take a long, hard look at their own future because of their stubbornness.
We have heard much rhetoric over the last several years about what this government intends to do and how it intends to make things great for everyone. We heard about how the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would wrestle inflation to the ground, how new energy programs would create employment and what a great future we have here in Canada. During the 1980 election campaign we heard about how the Canadian public could not afford to pay an extra 18 cents a gallon for gasoline. If this were not so tragic, it would be a joke. But it is tragic. To this date the price of gasoline has increased 77 cents a gallon. How can hon. members opposite face themselves, let

May 6, 1982
alone their constituents? They knew full well their programs could not possibly be implemented without an increase in the price of gasoline, yet they told the Canadian people they could not afford an extra 18 cents a gallon.
During that campaign hon. members opposite put out various pieces of propaganda. The one 1 have in my hand says: "Vote Liberal and the price will stay down". The price will stay down to what? The Canadian public has had to get used to this kind of thing. Why were hon. members opposite not frank with the people of Canada? Why did they not say they would increase the price of gasoline? Why did they not say they would also increase the price of home heating fuel? That was one thing we on this side of the Elouse were not going to do.
This is a cold country. There are many elderly pensioners who enjoy the warmth and security of their homes, or they did until now. Those people like to stay warm. I receive a lot of correspondence in my office, and I invite hon. members to come and look at some of it. People ask: "How am 1 supposed to heat my home?" "How am I supposed to keep warm?" "How am I supposed to feed my family?" "How am I supposed to take care of my wife?"
Why did hon. members opposite not say in the last election campaign that they would eliminate 20 per cent of the VIA Rail services in this country? Rail is one of the most efficient modes of travel. Why did hon. members opposite not tell the people down east they were going to take away the Atlantic Limited? That was one of the most popular trains in Canada. Let me read from a letter I received from a young university student about VIA Rail cuts. He said:
As a Canadian I cannot see how the Liberal government could justify the deleting and cutting back of the VIA Rail routes across Canada ... As a university student here at Mount Allison, 1 had the opportunity to travel home ... on this train a few times and I always found it to be very crowded ... Let Mr. Pepin, in his eternal wisdom, decide this route is not being used enough-or making money-so it has to be deleted so we, the ever-shafted Maritimes, can support new trains in the corridor between Quebec City and Windsor.
The perception of maritimers and, I suspect, Canadians all across the nation is that yes, we have been shafted by this government.
Why did hon. members opposite not tell us during the last election campaign that they would introduce a budget which would effectively strangle us in our economic beds? Why did they not tell us during that election campaign that they would introduce an energy omnibus bill which would raise taxes on a gallon of gas without their ever having to come to Parliament for its approval? Why did they not tell us they would introduce in that same bill a measure which would allow them to expropriate land in this country without ever coming and seeking approval from Parliament? Why did they not tell us they would create Crown corporations, if they were able to get away with it, without ever coming to Parliament?
Why did hon. members opposite not tell us they would introduce an emergency measures order which would give the government the power to build virtual concentration camps across the nation and put any Canadian it chose into those
camps without ever making the matter public? Why did they not tell us that under that order the government could effectively muzzle the press so that no one-not a neighbour, a brother, a sister or a cousin-would know what happened to detainees at such camps?
Why did hon. members opposite not tell us it was their intention to leave the right of an individual to own property-a basic fundamental right in this country-out of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms? People have fought, shed blood and died for that right. Why did hon. members opposite not tell us they would not include that? They did not tell us because they knew that if they were truthful with the people, they would be so far back in the boonies that they would be sharing the same fate as all their provincial counterparts. They would become a party of extinction.
Why did they not tell the people in Chatham, New Brunswick, that they would close CFB Chatham down and add another 3,500 people to the unemployment rolls? Already some 40 per cent of the employable people in that region are unemployed. Why did hon. members opposite not tell us that the minister responsible for New Brunswick would not even show the people of the towns of the area the courtesy of meeting with them? Those people were kept sitting cooling their heels for months before the minister finally relented. He is an uncaring minister, a callous minister, a minister who should be dealt with effectively, and I trust he will be dealt with effectively in the next election.
Why did hon. members opposite not tell us they would ram and jam metric conversion down our throats through order in council? Why did they not tell us it would not be voluntary, which is what this House agreed to a few years ago? Why did they not tell the fishermen of Atlantic Canada that their energy costs would be doubled? Why did they not tell the farmers of that region that their energy costs would be doubled? Why did they not tell the older people of the nation that the cost of heating their homes would be doubled?
Coming from Atlantic Canada, what I find disturbing is that a number of members on the other side of the House from that part of the country must have had input into the budget, into the decision to close CFB Chatham and into the 20 per cent cut in VIA Rail, yet they were silent on these important and critical issues. These things were happening in their own constituencies.
Every motion of non-confidence put forward by this side of the House to censure the government was voted against by members opposite. They should hide their heads in shame and should never have the privilege of representing people in this House again. By voting against these non-confidence motions they have approved in principle every move taken by this government since the election of 1980. We do not intend to let them forget it, nor will their constituents. They have supported a rise in the cost of gasoline almost three times that proposed in the Crosbie budget.

May 6, 1982
Let us go back to 1980 and see what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had to say. In an address to the Halifax Board of Trade on January 25, 1980, he said:
Energy security is the second issue, and here the Tory record is a disgrace. They have hurt exploration efforts at home and imperiled supplies abroad.
Then he talked about the 18-cent tax, saying:
That tax wasn't brought in for energy security or energy conservation.
He went on:
So if that tax had been implemented ... every time every Canadian bought gasoline he would be helping to pay for a policy that benefits only one segment of the population. That tax is particularly onerous on Nova Scotians because many in this province have to use their cars to get to work.
What a magnanimous statement-people use cars to get to work! The inference is: "We won't do it because people have to use their cars". Then he goes on:
What is the result? Under the Clark energy plan the average Nova Scotian household would be paying over $200 more in gas and fuel costs this year, rising to over $600 in 1982.
I should like to hear the Prime Minister refer to these comments now. Then he said:
The Liberal plan seeks to achieve energy security at a fair price for all Canadians.
What a laugh that is. Among the things he said the Liberals would start doing at once were these:
Achieve energy security through the accelerated development of Canada's domestic potential and the ensuring of Canada's off-shore supply.
Then he talked about the "made in Canada price":
The made-in-Canada price will result in a lower price to consumers than the one proposed for the next four years in the Clark budget.
That is an untruth, Mr. Speaker. He goes on:
It will be a lower price because we will not impose an 18-cent excise tax on gas and diesel;
He was winding up when he said:
-a Liberal Government will take immediate action to ensure the full cooperation of all parties in the construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the Maritimes. The pipeline will have reversible capacity so that Maritimers will have the opportunity, both to use Western natural gas now and to send off-shore gas to Central Canada later.
I should like to know how you can reverse a pipeline that is two feet in diameter in western Canada, goes through Quebec and narrows to six inches in the maritimes. If you were to put a sleeve on it from the other end and try to reverse it, you would have the biggest jet engine in the world! The thing would blow sky high, just like the energy policy.
Time and time again we have seen broken promises, scattered dreams. We have seen a country torn and fragmented. There has never been a more arrogant, uncaring administration in the history of this nation. No government in the past would have had the brass or the gall to stay in circumstances such as these.
This government should be thrown out of office, Mr. Speaker. Its ministers should resign because of the disaster they have perpetrated on the Canadian people. They should have the courage to call an election based on their record. Let the record show what they have done. An hon. member opposite shakes his head-nods his head in agreement. Let us see him
use his influence to make it happen. I hope he will have enjoyed his stay in Pariiament because he will not last.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not a pleasure to speak in this debate but I feel obliged to do so. Perhaps I should start by stating that this party has been informed by what we believe to be accurate sources in Calgary today that the CanStar project, which was a $14 billion project to go down beside the Alsands project on an adjoining lease- it is a joint project of Nova and PetroCan-was going to announce today that it was not going to proceed. For some reason that I do not know they will not be making that announcement.
According to yesterday's Globe and Mail the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said that the government felt Canada and Alberta did their level best to support and facilitate this particular project but that the situation has resulted from private business decisions made as a result of factors operating in the world's economy. In other words, private industry killed the project. In my respectful submission, you can only say that private industry killed this project as you can, in a similar sense, say that the fellow who was condemned by Robespierre's reign of terror, in declining to put his head under the guillotine, killed the executioner's killing, so to speak. The killing of the Alsands project was, in large measure, at the hands of the National Energy Program.
1 should like to speak about how the situation affects real people in my part of the country and, doubteless, in other parts as well. Recently I sent a questionnaire out in my riding asking what the effect of the National Energy Program was on the citizens of southeast Edmonton. Fully 57 per cent of the respondents indicated that their jobs or business had suffered as a result of the NEP or that they knew directly of someone who had. One example is a person in the business of supplying electrical parts to the oil trucking industry who came to see me a few weeks ago and told me that last year he earned roughly $3,000 gross per month. In the two weeks before he came to see me as his representative, he had earned $15.35.
At least four or five substantial trucking firms involved in the oil patch in Edmonton have gone out of business recently. There was a young man in his twenties who came to see me not long ago to say he had recently lost his job in the oil service industry in Alberta; he blamed the National Energy Program for that.
On the plane last Friday from Winnipeg to Edmonton, there were 15 people for 102 seats. The stewardess told me that in 13 years with Air Canada she had never seen flights throughout western Canada so empty. I am told that the population of Swan Hills was 3,500 two years ago and everyone was doing well. The population is now down to 2,300 and I am told that virtually everyone in the community is doing badly now. You will appreciate that Swan Hills lives by the oil industry.
May 6, 1982

April 30 has been referred to as black Friday, but in my view it will be remembered as the beginning of the end of the Liberal party as the party of moderate voters across Canada. The 5 per cent of the rate which they obtained in the Saskatchewan election I predict will be the range they will receive federally throughout the west in future, and it will go further east than Ontario. With respect, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party has given up its historical role as a moderate party of the centre which favoured a mixed economy and helping people in need. It is now not a social democratic party in the sense some in the NDP are social democrats, it is now simply a socialist party. That is sad for Canada because when the Liberal party disappears-I believe not very long from now-we will be left without a party which has offered a great deal to this country in the past and for which some of us have had immense respect over many generations.
Time is awfully short so let me relate what some people in the west have said about Alsands. The Edmonton Journal said in its lead editorial on May 1:
"Alsands dies
Thanks, Mr. Trudeau. Thanks, Mr. Lalonde. In January, 1980, Alsands was under way. In February, 1980, the Liberals won re-election from their base in Central Canada. In March, 1980, the Liberals headed down the tragic road to their so-called "National" Energy Program. Alsands caught a chill. Alberta headed for cover. And yesterday Alsands finally died."
Or a quote from a recent Alberta publication. I might say that I do not always agree with the publisher of Alberta Report, but I think Mr. Ted Byfield spoke for a lot of people in western Canada when he said on March 15:
We know that little more than two years ago, before Mr. Trudeau and his-
I will leave the next word out. It goes on:
-menage were revisited upon us, our province verged on its finest era. Two gigantic heavy oil projects were all but ready to begin. We were embarked upon the greatest search for self-sufficiency in energy that our technology could devise. Our cities hummed with vigour, industry and prosperity that had drawn the attention of the world. Our artists flourished, and our farmers produced more food than they had ever produced before. Agreements were being worked out by all levels of government that would have launched us into a shining decade. All this is scarcely a memory. One heavy oil plant lies in ruins; the other seems all but doomed.
Of course, it was doomed on April 30. It goes on:
Our drillers desert the country, our rigworkers line up for the dole, bankruptcy haunts our truckers, our developers fold, our cattlemen face foreclosure, scores of houses stand empty because no one can afford to buy them, and a pall of loss and uncertainty hangs over the very decade which held such promise. For all of this, we can thank that repulsive-
I do not know whether that is a parliamentary word. It goes on:
-clutch at Ottawa in general, and the bungling insanity of their National Energy Program in particular.
It is absolutely beyond belief that they can kill this project. I represent a riding which is named after Lord Strathcona who was very much connected with the building of the CPR. That was a project so vast that it acted as a tide which lifted all economic boats in Canada. Unemployment ended in Ontario and Quebec. The spin-offs were enormous. Your parents, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the parents of many of us, came to the west because of that project.
I believe that every western and central Canadian believes the Alsands project had a lot of the CPR project within it. How the government could garrot Alsands, as it has done, is something it will answer for, not just in the next election but for decades to come.
Alsands would have produced 137,000 barrels of oil a day and provided an estimated 50,000 jobs across Canada, half of them in construction in western Canada, half in central Canada manufacturing, and 7,500 permanent positions. Members opposite say there was only $13 billion involved. Some of them have suggested that is not so much. But what about the estimated $450 billion the project would have put into our national economy over its 20-year lifetime?
Why did it collapse? Members opposite say it was because of world conditions. Here is what the president of Alsands Ed Czaja, said in announcing its death:
An atmosphere of confidence and trust in government must be restored before projects such as Alsands can proceed.
With respect, I think the person who pinned down the real reason was John Stoik of Gulf Canada, who said in March, 1980:
"Over the years the government has so strained its credibility with retroactive rule changes that those of us in the industry must now ask ourselves, 'how can we undertake to make huge investments in long-term megaprojects when we have good reason to fear that the government will come along again and pull the rug
on us?' "
One example of so many rug-pullings is the fact that the Liberal government reneged on a signed contract it had with Suncor to give it the world price for its expensively expanded facility at Fort McMurray, and forced it to sell its product for some time at $16.75 a barrel. I am not talking about sanctity of contract, Mr. Speaker; I am talking about a government which cannot be trusted to honour signed contracts in matters of oil sands production.
What is said about the project by those who are looking at it reasonably objectively? Mr. William Empey, vice-president and director of economics at Data Resources of Canada, stated a few days ago:
The Alsands failure will reduce business investment spending in Canada by $360 million this year and set the stage for a steady loss of real output, employment, and foreign investor confidence.
He went on to say:
The investment spending loss will rise to $2.7 billion in 1985.
What did Mr. Empey, whom I have just quoted, say about the effect, for instance, on the dollar? Mr. Speaker, I think you know that the Alsands collapse has already caused a drop of one-fifth of a United States cent in the value of the Canadian dollar. He said:
The project's failure might be widely interpreted as a business-government relation that would temporarily reduce the value of the Canadian dollar.
He sees the dollar going down to 81 cents U.S. quickly.
What does Michael McCracken, president of Informetrica Ltd. an Ottawa consulting firm, have to say? He spoke about

May 6, 1982
the psychological impact. "1 think it's going to be a watershed year or two for the Canadian economy."
Mr. Speaker, it is the psychological impact on Canadians right across the country that is so serious. I mentioned CAN-STAR and the possibility of that project being cancelled. Other projects have been referred to by many speakers. The Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) told us the other night not to worry about the Alsands or the Alaska pipeline because, she said, there are lots of other projects going ahead. One of these she named was the Trans-Quebec & Maritimes Pipeline. My understanding is that that project may go ahead. I very much hope that it will, but that pipeline is having troubles at the moment in the provinces which you represent, Mr. Speaker, and there is a possibility that that pipeline may not proceed.
She also named the Beaufort Sea project as one that is going ahead. I understand that that project is so expensive to the taxpayer that every dollar invested there costs the investor about 7 cents under the PIP plan. It is hugely expensive. Also, how are we to get all those products down to market? The cost of the pipeline is vast and the native claims are unsettled and the Beaufort Sea project is not that simple at all.
How about Hibernia? The Minister of State for Mines mentioned that as one project still going ahead. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that that project is not so certain, because instead of co-operative federalism we have two governments fighting over it. Newfoundland was a dominion at one time when it came into confederation. I believe that it brought all of its offshore resources with it. Unless we can get those problems solved between the two levels of government, that will be a big uncertainty also. There will also be a problem getting the oil from the sea to the markets. Whether it is by a pipeline or by tanker, which seems more sensible, I do not think that project is exactly an early bird in the hand either.
The Norman Wells project was named by the minister as one that is still going ahead. We know that there will be at least a two-year delay with respect to Indian land claims there. "At least two" I am told by the member for Provencher (Mr. Epp).
In regard to the Montreal heavy oil upgrader, she cites that one but I understand there is some doubt whether that will go ahead, or how quickly it will go ahead.
So psychologically, the loss of this project will gnaw at the soul of every Canadian who believes in economic growth, in jobs for young people, in decent pensions for old people, and, of course, in energy self-sufficiency. Those of us who are affected directly, as we all are in the west, are made so mad that it is very hard to be calm about it.
Mr. Roy Phillips, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, said of the cancellation that it is "a real blow to manufacturers". His colleague went on to say that "the rate of bankruptcy among the members will increase". It will hit the men and women of Ontario and Quebec as well. Of course, the other problem is that if the dollar goes down, as Mr. McCracken points out, the interest rates will have to go up even more.
I can only put it that it is a disaster. It is a disaster akin to the loss we would have had, if the CPR rail line had been cancelled back in the 1880s when some people said we were building a rail line that would never pay even for the axle grease. These cancellations are a disaster for this country.
I would like to end on a positive note, Mr. Speaker. Everything could be so different. This project could be underway if we did not have a government more committed to ideology, to blind government control for government control's sake. As so many people have urged, I, too, urge, that some of the members on the opposite side come across. I say: "There are places for you here, your voters will re-elect you as members of the Progressive Conservative Party, I am certain of it, if only some of you would have the courage to vote, as quickly as you can, against the worst government in Canadian history. We will have an election, we will have a new government, and you can join us in building the best and the most blessed country on the face of the earth."

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all express concern about the lack of planning and organization in the present government of the country. I can sense that the people are frustrated and disappointed about the lack of leadership and lack of vision. The country could be in such a high state of progress if we only put our imagination and resources to assist in that progress.
We live in a country with resources of unlimited potential, with people who are well experienced and well equipped to make the country prosper. We all know that our country has almost everything we could possibly want. However, unfortunately we have a tremendously high unemployment rate, we have an inflation rate which is much higher than that in the United States, we have an interest rate that is literally driving thousands of small businesses into bankruptcy and driving people out of their homes and farmers off their land.
Across the way on the government benches we have ministers who are relying on immense megaprojects as the engine or the motor to get the economy moving. They have not succeeded. The Alsands project has been canned. There is a delay now in the pipeline and I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that that pipeline is not just delayed but we will never see it in existence.
Other megaprojects have been cancelled. It is worthwhile, Mr. Speaker, for us to pause for a few moments and reflect on the number of dollars that the government across the way wants to spend on megaprojects. These megaprojects-there are about 234 of them-were planned to operate over the next eight or nine years, up to the year 1990. They were to be worth over $100 million apiece between now and 1990. That totals some $440 billion worth of megaprojects up to the year 2000. That is a lot of money.
The Alsands project was worth about $13.5 billion to $14 billion. It would in the construction stage have provided for 35,000 person-years and would have meant 4,800 operating jobs after it became operational. That project is gone.
May 6. 1982

The Cold Lake project has been suspended indefinitely. It would have been worth some $14 billion, provided some 28,500 construction jobs and some 3,300 permanent jobs once it was operational.
The Alaska gas pipeline has also been suspended and will probably be cancelled. It would have been worth $40 billion and provided about 12,000 construction jobs and about 400 permanent jobs once it was operational.
If we total these projects, we find that the master plan of the government cancels or postpones megaprojects which would have been worth some $78 billion and provided some 70,000 construction jobs and about 8,500 permanent jobs.
These are not the only projects which are unlikely to continue. Other projects were planned which were dependent upon the Alsands project. For example, there were projects in the Peace River area and others in Alberta which would have been worth billions of dollars if the Alsands project was onstream and underway.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is saying that we should not worry because we have other immense megaprojects underway. If we look at his list of other megaprojects, we realize that they are not big and only total about $94 billion. This is way below the projections, the hopes and the aspirations of the minister of energy and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) when they announced the megaproject strategy a few years ago.
In my few moments remaining I want to express a fundamental concern about putting all our eggs in one basket in the first place. It is a very dangerous philosophy to rely upon a few megaprojects, with current high interest rates and the tremendous investment required, for a few jobs in order to stimulate the economy of Canada. I say this for a couple of reasons. First, if we look at megaprojects in terms of jobs, we find that it takes about 40 times as much investment per job in the megaprojects to create one job than it takes in the ordinary manufacturing sector. I wonder from that point of view whether or not it is worthwhile spending so much money on megaprojects. I ask government economists to take a close look at the situation before planning or rebeginning more megaprojects in the years ahead.
My second concern is the philosphy which has existed in Canada since the days of Cartier back in the 1600s. It has been a philosophy of exporting our raw materials to be processed in other parts of the world and of importing manufactured goods. Back in the days of Cartier it was the export of beaver pelts and the pelts of other animals in terms of the fur trade to Europe. In more recent days it has been the exporting mineral resources, non-renewable resources and many renewable resources in an unfinished state to such countries as the United States, Europe and Japan, and in return importing finished goods. This means the exportation of jobs in the highly labour-intensive manufacturing sector. Once again I question putting all our eggs in the same basket in terms of huge resource megaprojects.
Another of my concerns is the whole question of Canadian content. As I look at these megaprojects and talk with people regarding the trade issue, such as General Electric and other companies in the country, I find that there are no guarantees of Canadian content or Canadian jobs in most of the projects and that many of the industrial spin-offs will not benefit Canada but will benefit countries such as the United States, Japan and western Europe. All of us in the House should be concerned about the lack of ironclad guarantees of Canadian content in terms of jobs in these megaprojects.
I should like to raise another point which was mentioned by Peter Loughced, or as they call him on the prairies, "Peter Moneybags", "Peter the Red", or whatever. He is one of the guys who hops into bed with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) time and time again, or with the Prime Minister and the Tories.

speechtext: What about the infamous photograph?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
I am sure the photograph will make interesting campaign fodder in the next Alberta election.
In any event, the other day Mr. Lougheed was talking about small being beautiful. I am not sure that absolutely everything should be small, but I think we would be much better off if we spent billions and billions of dollars on smaller projects helping people become energy self-sufficient in their own communities. We could have conservation programs which would result in the saving of a barrel of oil and we could spend the money saved from that barrel of oil on creating jobs in the small business sector or expanding co-operatives. We could spend some of those billions of dollars building houses, on the national transportation system, and on upgrading our raw materials and resources.
Now that some of these projects have been cancelled or postponed, we will have the time to look at the possibility of planning a real industrial and economic strategy, so that we will have a more decentralized economy and equal and uniform development from coast to coast, rather than relying upon large megaprojects in a few parts of our great country.
These are a few of my concerns. Now that we have had a chance to conduct this debate, I hope we can sit down as parliamentarians and try to persuade the government opposite to use its imagination to provide the country with some leadership and vision. I hope we will be able to convince it that it must have courage to get out there and use our resources,
May 6, 1982

process them at home, provide jobs for Canadians and work toward the future. Also we should put more money into research and development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are engaged in an emergency debate tonight which began approximately 28 hours ago. I have been impressed by the attendance in the House. Since the people who watch us on television see only one speaker at a time, they may not be impressed but the
handful of people in the galleries and others who are here may be impressed.
We are engaged in a debate which has been approved by the Speaker of the House of Commons. The representations made by our leader were such that the Speaker felt that the collapse of Alsands was a serious enough problem to grant us this emergency debate. However, the response to this emergency by government members has been rather bizarre. At the moment there are three Liberals sitting in their places, which represents about 1 per cent of their membership in the House.
I sat through about eight hours of debate when we were sitting all night and it was much the same then. There were only two or three members in their places at that time. This tells me that the government members either feel there is not a serious problem in the country with respect to Alsands and the National Energy Program or they are so naive that they do not realise that there is a problem in the country. That surely cannot be true because two of those members sitting on the other side come from my area of southwestern Ontario and I know they have been receiving representations from their constituents indicating their concern about the National Energy Program and the economy in general.
There is a third possibility why there are so very few Liberals in attendance. It may be that they are so disrespectful to our Speaker that they are unwilling to be in the House for this debate and are refusing to recognize the fact that this is indeed an emergency which should be taken seriously. I hope that is not the case.
I would like to begin by giving the reaction of people in my constituency of Oxford to these unenlightened economic policies of the government which have culminated in the National Energy Program. I will illustrate some of the ways it has affected my constituents. I will subsequently touch on a few reasons why I think this emergency debate was required.
I can reflect the views of the constituency of Oxford by referring to three sectors in Oxford. Since my constituency is about half urban and half rural, there are many farmers who are greatly concerned about what is happening to them. I would venture to say that there is probably no other sector in the Canadian economy that is worse off than the agricultural sector. While farmers in Oxford may not be in as much difficulty as those in the Bruce-Grey area, they are still having a real problem. In fact, Ontario farmers are so concerned that they came here just yesterday to see government members and members of our party in order to discuss the problems they are experiencing. While discussing the small business bond, which was to have been one of the economic answers to the problems of the farmers, it was pointed out in an article written by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, referring to the small business bond, that it was a "cruel deception on farmers who greeted the policy with hope only to find it a delusion".
I believe that is very true. Canadian farmers have been very disillusioned by this economic policy which has played havoc
May 6, 1982

with them and certainly no less so in the constituency of Oxford.
With respect to unemployment, the largest city in Oxford- Woodstock-normally has a fairly high employment rate and a not too serious unemployment rate. However, unemployment is at a record level and I do not believe it has been worse since the days of the Great Depression. Unemployment in Woodstock is now 14 per cent. That situation gives me cause for concern. These economic policies being pursued by the government, such as the NEP, will obviously have an effect on employment in Oxford. Since people in Ontario tend to forget, it is fortunate that some hon. members remind us that in Ontario and Quebec-where you come from, Mr. Speaker- there is a real impact from programs such as the NEP when they come into effect, causing disastrous results for the country.
Let me cite some industries which are suffering and will suffer from these disastrous economic policies. For example, FMC is a significant company in Woodstock where it manufactures heavy equipment known by the trade name of Link Belt. I dare say that had Alsands and the pipeline projects gone ahead, they would have had a significant impact on that company since it could have provided equipment for those projects.
Another company in my constituency is Standard Tube which is probably the largest employer in Woodstock. That company has laid off many employees and is working significantly below capacity. Incidentally, FMC is only working with a skeleton staff.
Holland Hitch is another company in my area which produces heavy equipment. It is working at greatly reduced capacity as well.
Finally, Kelsey Hayes is a foundry in Woodstock which produces the basic raw materials for many of our steel companies. Again, they are having great difficulty trying to obtain sufficient orders. Those were just some references to the industrial and farming community in my constituency.
When the industrial sector in my constituency learned of the survey being conducted by the official opposition, led by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) last January, they came to me with the proposition that they would be glad to report to the travelling panel on the situation in Oxford. They presented a brief to that panel which illustrated how the economy was affecting Oxford. I would like to quote from this brief dated January 11, 1982:
Drops in the housing market in Canada, caused by record high mortgage rates, have had a drastic effect on local industry in Woodstock.
It goes on to say:
In Oxford County workers with up to twenty (20) years seniority in large, well established firms are finding themselves laid off and without a job. Even though our area is directly related to the automotive and housing market, industries producing high cost capital goods are also facing reduced markets and further lay-offs.
They give further evidence of the economic woes we are facing in Oxford because of these very inappropriate economic policies of this government.
It is evident that the average constituent of Oxford county is feeling the pinch as well. He is suffering because the government has refused to introduce any kind of mortgage interest deductability scheme such as we offered when we were in government. As well, there is no energy tax credit such as we offered. In fact, the government has added an increased tax on heating fuels that we as a government felt was absolutely unnecessary. This government has felt that they had to draw extra money from Canadians in order to fulfil some of its programs which it wants to pursue.
We now have the background to the situation in a typical southwestern Ontario constituency and I suggest it is not too atypical for all of Ontario.
I would like to talk a little about the causes which I think lie behind the collapse of Alsands and the various other projects we have seen going down the drain. I think it can best be explained by relating it to an interesting quote which has already been alluded to by the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), I believe. It has also been referred to by others during this debate but it warrants repeating. I refer to some comments made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) back in the spring of 1969. I think he set the backdrop for what we have seen happen in the last 10, 12 or 14 years. At that time the Prime Minister was speaking about the ship of state. That was the simile to which he was referring. I think this bears very close attention because his words were very carefully chosen and had much impact. Retrospectively, what he had to say then was very true and I do not believe it has come to its full fruition yet. Back in the spring of 1969, the Prime Minister said:
One has to be in the wheelhouse to see what shifts are taking place. I know that we have spun the wheel and I know that the rudder is beginning to press against the waves and the sea ... but perhaps the observer, who is on the deck and smoking his pipe, or drinking his tea, sees the horizon much in the same direction and doesn't realize it, but perhaps he will find himself disembarking at a different island than the one he thought he was sailing for.
