It is something that I

May 6, 1982
want to call the rape of Parliament. This should be of serious concern to all hon. members of the House, whether on the government or the opposition side. When I refer to the rape of Parliament, I am referring to what has happened to the ordinary backbenchers on both sides of the House who make up the bulk of the elected members of Parliament. When I refer to government, I am not referring to all government members. I am referring to the executive branch of the government on the other side, not to the supporters of the government. In my view, the government has been guilty of raping the backbenchers in terms of their ability to function the way they should in order adequately to represent their constituents.

There are people on the government side on the backbenches-there have been a couple in the House in the last hour or so-

There is one there now, a neighbour of mine down in southwestern Ontario, there are a number of backbenchers in the House who are fine gentlemen and I have a lot of respect for them, but they have one defect. Their one defect is their unwillingness to stand up in public, namely in this chamber, and speak out against their government. They are prepared to say things back in their ridings in the hope that what they say will not be heard here and get into public view. They are basically unwilling to come out clean and, when the chips are down, they refuse to be absent when some of these abhorrent policies of the government are put to a vote before the House of Commons. It is this coercion of the backbenchers, particularly on the government side, to which I referred as the rape of Parliament. It has been part of the problem leading up to the disaster with the Alsands project.
Therefore, I believe hon. members on both sides of the House will want to take a serious look at this in the months ahead to see if we cannot make some reforms in Parliament which will give meaningful opportunity to backbenchers to become more involved in the policies which the government finally puts before Parliament. Let us allow Parliament to decide whether or not government policies are good. Let us not leave it entirely up to the executive branch.

The other big component underlying the present economic situation is the loss of business confidence to which many hon. members have previously alluded. We must only acknowledge the fact that the National Energy Program
is a very good example of why the business community has lost confidence in our government, indeed in the elected people of Canada. We must provide them with the confidence they need in order to invest in the future. I would like to speak at length on this problem but because of the shortage of time I will be brief.
The second matter to which I wish to refer which also causes a lack of confidence in the business community is our tax policy. For a number of years I have been convinced that we are in the midst of a very antiquated tax system which is becoming more complicated. My hon. friend, the member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), gave a speech in this House to which I have previously referred. It is difficult to get the financial experts in the House to see any wisdom in it. However, if one keeps track of the writings in the press and in the journals, one finds more and more reference to the need for some changes in our antiquated tax system. We should be giving more serious consideration to changing our tax policy from one based on the ability to pay to one based on the value received. Of course, this subject must be expanded and discussed at another time. However, this is a great opportunity for giving our business community a sense of security in the future. It would certainly simplify many of the problems we as taxpayers face at the present time.
Another problem which lowers the confidence of the business community is government intervention in the private sector, which is growing by leaps and bounds. Again, it was anticipated by the Prime Minister back in 1976, at a time when he was "musing" that there would have to be more permanent controls on big business. However, in his typical way of vacillating back and forth, his view had changed by 1978 when he then promised to:
-remove the intrusions of many government policies and regulations from individuals and businesses; in some cases this will mean returning functions to the private sector, in others it will mean removing the heavy hand of government and its drag on personal initiatives.
That did not last very long. It lasted until 1980, when the election campaign came along and he played a different tune. At that time he said government was going to be "an active player, not a passive bystander". In other words, he was saying the government would become an investor. Sure enough, in the last two years that is exactly what has happened. The government has become one of the big investors in the country. Again, this government intervention is causing a great deal of difficulty for our private sector and for industry in general.
I think Your Honour is about ready to say that my allotted time has expired. I just want to conclude by saying that one must acknowledge the fact that there is much distrust in the business community and in the private sector. In my view, the one solution to this problem is to promote policies which will ensure some cash flow to our business community so that we can get our economy going again. Hopefully, we will then have a more prosperous country.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ottawa's oil strategy is in a shambles. In the 1980 federal
May 6, 1982

election, the Liberals made some great promises concerning what they would do for this country and they managed to take the people in on those promises. But to date they have come through with absolutely nothing with regard to their promises. Just one example of the ridiculous statements they were making is that they would hold increases in government spending under the GNP growth rate, they would have an industrial strategy to create jobs, and they would increase Canadian ownership.
No jobs were created. We have seen record unemployment. The government said we would achieve energy security at a fair price. This has not been achieved. Gasoline prices have increased by approximately 80 cents a gallon whereas the government claimed it would hold these increases down to 14 cents. There has been a mass exodus of funds with the Petrofina purchase which has not assisted this country in any way.
The government claimed it would ensure prosperity and economic growth in every region. The only place we have seen any growth is in the federal public service. It claimed it would help first those who need assistance. The people who have been helped the most have done very well under these policies, the OPEC countries, Venezuela and Mexico. They have really benefited. Senior public servants have benefited as well.
The federal government's ambitious plan of achieving Canadian oil self-sufficiency by 1990 appears in shambles today following the collapse of the giant Alsands project. The plan, unveiled in the controversial National Energy Program 18 months ago, banked heavily on production from new oil sands projects, particularly the $15 billion Alsands scheme that died Friday and the $13 billion Cold Lake plant shelved late last year.
With the death of those two energy megaprojects, Canada now will likely still be importing nearly 300,000 barrels a day of crude oil by the end of this decade, a bleak scenario that would result in billions of dollars in imported oil costs being drained annually from the besieged Canadian economy and adding to our massive federal deficit. That is what they call energy security.
We were informed yesterday by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) that he would stick with his National Energy Program regardless of how disastrous the effects are on this country. It is plain stubbornness.
For consumers, Canada's failure to attain self-sufficiency may mean extremely high gasoline and heating oil prices as the cost for what may well be ever-costlier foreign oil imports. In addition, federal energy planners are now praying consumers will conserve energy at possibly unrealistic rates for the rest of the decade.
Hans Maciej, technical director of the Canadian Petroleum Association, says the cancellation of Alsands means Canada will have to replace the lost production with expensive imports, which will hurt the Canadian economy and further erode the
country's balance of payments, already saddled with expensive foreign oil costs.
I now wish to quote from the CPA Review. This is a group of Canadian oil firms, not multinationals. 1 will read some of their comments into the record:
In many ways, the great strategic flaw in the National Energy Program was that it failed to consider the international marketplace. By providing totally inadequate netbacks to Canadian oil and gas producers, it effectively forced those companies to leave Canada for international markets.
The flight of drilling rigs to the United States is the best documented example: with the market for rigs strong in the U.S. and weak in Canada, there was an absolute inevitability about the movement of rigs to that market. It could easily have been predicted. But the government either failed to do so or just didn't care.
Had the program been any good from the start, the rigs would have stayed in this country. It is very costly to move an oil rig. I again quote:
This is happening because the National Energy Program failed to look at the international marketplace. This was brought home to me most dramatically by an analysis prepared by a company with operations in Canada, Indonesia and Australia.
According to this report, if a company were to spend the same number of dollars to find the same amount of oil in Alberta, Indonesia and Australia, it would receive a 10.4 per cent return on its investment in this country. It would receive a 21 per cent of return in Indonesia. And it would receive a 38.6 per cent rate of return in Australia.
From a strictly economic standpoint, Australia's program-unlike the NEP

is clearly the kind that will generate investment and exploration.
The National Energy Program in this country has done the exact opposite.
In fact, this was borne out several weeks ago, when it was announced that Australia's 1982 exploratory drilling would include nearly twice as many wells as were drilled in 1981.
But that is only one part of the international marketplace which the National Energy Program ignores. There is another international aspect-reciprocity- which is just as important. Over time, international trade and economic arrangements depend on reciprocity and, more particularly, equal treatment which does not create different classes of corporate citizens. However appealing the policy of economic nationalism may be in the short run, it eventually carries a heavy price for those who have to do business outside their national borders and in terms of foreign investor confidence. Canada's reputation for a responsibly managed regulatory framework has suffered heavily in international investment circles as a result of the National Energy Program and that, too, holds consequences for our capacity to finance our internal department.
To sum it up, we are on a disaster course. I do not know what is next for our energy minister. It is no secret he is becoming tired of the energy portfolio. The glory days of grand planning are over. Now it is down to the nuts and bolts work of haggling over dollars and cents and minor projects, a prospect that minister must shudder at.
Insiders say the minister will not seek re-election. I guess all the news is not bad. He will either return to law practice, where he will starve to death or make money, or be appointed a judge. If he resigns before the next election, he will probably be appointed a judge. I certainly hope it will not be in my province. For now, the minister must struggle with a bruised reputation and a battered energy policy.
This party presented sound policies when we were in government. I see the chairman of the veterans affairs committee in the chamber. He does a good job there and should stick to it. I do not think energy is his field.

May 6, 1982
Our government promised energy self-sufficiency and we would have been on the road to it had our policies been allowed to be implemented. We would have gradually Canadi-anized the industry without forcing foreign-owned companies to suddenly leave the country en masse, taking with them huge amounts of technology, expertise and potential employment. Our policy would have created employment by giving incentives for further exploration and research. The way to tell a good program is whether it attracts investment and keeps what you already have in the country, such as drilling rigs, expertise and so on.
Our policy would have made Canada self-sufficient in oil and gas by 1990. The National Energy Program has obliterated that. Our policy would not have increased taxes on heating oil. It would not have cost Canadians 60,000 jobs as the National Energy Program has done. Most of those jobs are in the Ontario and Quebec region. It would not create a situation in which over $20 billion in potential investment has left the country since the October, 1980 inception of the National Energy Program. That is a clear indication it is a complete and total failure. It would have kept drilling rigs working in Canada instead of forcing hundreds of rigs to greener fields in the United States.
The National Energy Program is nationalizing, not Canadi-anizing, the energy industry. More and more government involvement in the private sector is not good for industry but, more importantly, it is not good for consumers. Let us always remember the Conservative energy policy of Canadianization.
Actually, the industry itself was working toward more Canadian ownership and, if it had been left alone, eventually we would have achieved 50 per cent or 80 per cent Candian ownership.
I want to explain the great exodus of capital. We will never recover from $20 billion having left the country. That is impossible. The National Energy Program has stimulated a great exodus of Canadian capital and manpower to the United States. It no longer pays to stay in Canada. Reports from Alberta state that the oil patch brain drain, or so it is called, is seeing hundreds of the best technical people in the oil industry leaving Canada for greener fields in the United States. They are leaving because the National Energy Program is forcing small, independent oil firms to cut costs by laying off their technical staff.
In another report, the Liberal government was even congratulated for having assured Canadians the same success in the energy field as we have experienced with other government monopolized sectors such as the post office, the CBC, the CNR and Mirabel Airport.
The oil industry, as many riggers themselves will say, is being chased out of Canada. The industry that is staying in Canada has a very skeptical outlook on the country's energy future. The Canadian Petroleum Association recently stated:
The National Energy Program of October, 1980 was a disaster for the petroleum industry and made oil self-sufficiency for Canada by 1990 impossible. The C.P.A. does not believe that the recently concluded Alberta-Ottawa pricing
agreement will materially improve industry's ability to make the country selfsufficient in oil within a decade.
These are the people we should be listening to because they know the industry. They are the type of people the Liberal government should have drafting its policies. The man who drafted the National Energy Program is referred to by the industry as a communist. His scholastic background and the types of subjects on which he wrote when he was in school clearly indicate that. I also understand he is a personal friend of the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). They probably worked this disaster out together.
All these developments and statements fly in the face of the government's declaration that the National Energy Program promotes opportunity, security and fairness. Is opportunity enhanced when the oil industry migrates to the United States, taking with it hundreds of jobs Canadians could be holding? Is security ensured when self-sufficiency in oil and gas may never be realized? Is it fair when Canadians are forced to sit idly by while billions of potential investment dollars are sent out of the country? I hardly think so.
I have here a list of firms which have been affected by the National Energy Program. I will refer to it in a moment.
I have listened with great interest to the contributions to this debate by members of the New Democratic Party. They have made it quite clear they have the answer for everything; they would just wave a magic wand and we would be well on the road to energy self-sufficiency. We would have full employment and so forth. However, the disaster we have under the Liberals would be ten times worse under members of the NDP, if that were possible, because they cannot communicate with the private sector. There is no way the group down there to my left could meet with the private sector eyeball to eyeball to work anything out because the NDP is against business. It is against profit. It is against the free enterprise system. Members of the New Democratic Party like to go around kidding the Canadian public that if the government looks after everything, somehow we will be on the road to glory. That is not correct.
The NDP has tipped its hand. The federal Leader of the NDP and the leader of the NDP in Manitoba, who is now the Premier, have both called for exchange controls. That is a clear indication they do not have an answer for anything. The only time the introduction of exchange controls is necessary is when a country has no policies to attract business or investors. If Canada had the right policies, we could keep money here and attract investment. The two leaders of the NDP to whom I have referred are not contributing to energy self-sufficiency or getting the energy industry-or any industry in the country- back on its feet when they call for exchange controls. They are throwing up their hands. They really do not know what to do. They have no answers.
I would like to comment on the multiplier effect of the National Energy Program. A recent survey prepared by the Nisku Businessmen's Association demonstrates in a practical way how the National Energy Program is affecting companies
May 6, 1982

across Canada. It clearly shows how the slowdown in the energy field is bringing hundreds of other companies to a grinding halt. I will read a list of some companies from Alberta, Ontario and other eastern areas which have suffered cutbacks or outright contract cancellations because of the National Energy Program. Let us remember that this is only a partial list. It is growing almost too quickly to maintain an up-to-date count of the companies hurting as a result of the National Energy Program. 1 will list just some of the firms affected by the National Energy Program as follows: Algoma, Allen Bradly Canada Ltd., A.M.P. of Canada Ltd., Arnie's Trailer Sales, Atlas Chemicals, Atlas Steel, Border Brokers, Brown Boveri (Canada) Ltd., Browning Manufacturing, B & W Heating Treating, Canada Cement Lafarge Ltd., Canadian General Electric Co. Ltd., Canadian Industries Ltd., Canadian Liquid Air Ltd., Canadian National Railways, Canadian Timken, Cessco Ltd., Cooper Energy, Dacro Industries Ltd.
I hope all the Liberals are listening, especially the ones from Ontario. Some of these businesses are in their ridings. There are many of them in the Hamilton area. The list continues: FAG Bearings, Federal Mogul, F.M.C. Linkbelt, Ford Motor Company, Gates Rubber, GMC, Hays Truck, I.H.C. Truck Assemblers, Ken worth Trucks, King Tractor Manufacturing, Nelson Building Components, Penn Dome, R.H.P. Canada, Roadmaster Trailers, Safety Supply Company, Steelco Steel, Stelco Canada Ltd. I spoke with a gentleman from that firm just today, and he says he has never seen business so bad. That is in the Hamilton area. I told him he had better get used to it. The list continues: Steldoor, S.K.F. Canada, Timkin Ltd., Tarrington Inc., Volcano Boilers, Westinghouse Canada Ltd.
The following are some general industries in eastern Canada: electrical suppliers, fittings manufacturers, hose and fittings companies, lumber firms, oilfield equipment and supply companies. The Hamilton area in particular is in dire straits because Hamilton is a major steel-producing city. The people of the city of Hamilton are very, very concerned.
It looks like my time is up.

Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of this debate-I have had privilege, but also the misfortune to be in the House during the all-night debate from Tuesday evening until early Wednesday morning-I have heard a number of speeches, both good and bad. To me, a good speech is not necessarily a speech of substance or arguments. To me, a good speech is when an hon. member rises and speaks
17117
from the heart, frankly and honestly, to a motion by his leader, and believes in what he is saying . I think a speech is bad when a member rises to spread hate. I have said before that hate has no place in the House of Commons.
Comparisons are being made with communists and dictators and it was even said that the Liberals hated the Canadian people. I am sorry to say this, but the member in question was the member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek), a champion skater. Maybe he was a champion on ice but he is certainly not a champion politician. The energy program is being criticized, and it is the opposition's duty to do so. Some facts have been brought forward, but not necessarily all the facts. Did they mention Petro-Canada's positive role? Did they mention the price of gas in other countries? Did they mention the position of the Progressive Conservative Party when they were in power in 1979? Mr. Speaker, what did the Conservative Party want to do in 1979?
[English ]
My government has initiated action to reduce the size of the federal public service and to offer for private purchase and ownership Crown corporations operating in areas where direct government intervention is no longer necessary-
Our government will be an example for Canadians to follow. It will not be a case of substituting "Do as I say" for "Do as I do". A promise was made to privatize certain Crown corporations-
The government itself is proposing action which questions certain long-held assumptions concerning, for example, the notion that Crown corporations, once established, must stay in the public domain forever.
A question was posed to the prime minister of the time, now the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), as follows:
As I indicated earlier today, there will be no significant action with regard to Petro-Canada without the approval of Parliament.
A question was asked by another member:
Will the Prime Minister assure the House that whatever course of action the government does propose with regard to Petro-Canada, it will not accept the principle that the private sector should be given that which is profitable, or potentially profitable, and that the people of Canada should be saddled with long-range public debts?
The prime minister of the day replied:
The hon. member is asking me to rule out the possibility of the people of Canada taking a direct ownership role in the direction of a major corporation. I will not, of course, rule out that principle.

On October 15, 1979, the then prime minister tabled a report by the task force on the privatization of Petro-Canada. At page 225 of Hansard, November 16, 1979, it is reported and I quote:

In relation to Petro-Canada generally, we are very much attracted by the proposal put forward by the task force which would allow individual citizens to participate directly in a significant Canadian oil company with the capacity to operate in a very major way here and perhaps beyond here. We are very much attracted by that idea.

May 6, 1982

That, Mr. Speaker, was the final collapse, the end of Petro-Canada. In 1979, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the then Minister of Finance-

-can the Minister of Finance tell us whether we will be advised of the future of Petro-Canada prior to the budget speech on December 11 -
The Minister of Finance replied:
Mr. Speaker, the world and Petro-Canada will unfold as they should, and there will be an announcement on Petro-Canada.
On the same day this question was posed to the then minister of energy:
-does the government remain committed to dismantling Petro-Canada and thus tossing away our best chance at long-term security of energy supply and independence from petroleum multinationals?
The then minister of energy, mines and resources replied:
If in his statement there is reference to any dismantling of Petro-Canada, it is misleading. The fact is that we intend to strengthen this corporation to make it more viable.
No wonder the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) is not the energy critic any more, nor is he the critic on finance. They could not get their act together. The then minister of finance continued:
When we return PetroCan to the private fold, it will be paying taxes and will not be a Crown corporation sheltered from paying taxes in the future.
That was the position of the Tory party when it was in power.
[ Translation]
And what did we, the Liberals, say during the 1979 election campaign and in the 1980 Speech from the Throne? We promised that we would keep and strengthen Petro Canada, and increase its powers. That is what we promised and that is what we have done! Mr. Speaker, let us deal with prices now. During this debate, many hon. members of the Official Opposition criticized the government about the 18 cents tax which the Progressive Conservative Party meant to levy on Canadians through its budget. I should like to refer to a question which was asked by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde), the current Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, as reported in Hansard for November 16, 1979.

-the more the Prime Minister speaks about energy policy, the more confused the Canadian public becomes.
I can understand that. He continued:
He said this morning that the policy was toward self-sufficiency. 1 would like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government's policy is still to achieve selfsufficiency by 1990. Secondly, he said that his target was not the Chicago price or the international price.
Will he confirm at least that the price is going to be what he said in his opening statement at the conference, that this preference has been brought down from a $6 annual increase in the price of a barrel of oil to bring us quickly to 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the Chicago price which, as the Prime Minister knows, may very well be higher and is actually higher than the international price?
The answer from the prime minister of the day was:
The proposal we put forward, which the hon. member has accurately read, is 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the Chicago price. There has not been a final decision taken as to whether it would be 90 per cent or 95 per cent.
Whichever is higher.
Mr. Speaker, we often hear about the price of gasoline in the United States, but we never hear about the prices of gasoline in Europe: in the United Kingdom, 82 cents a litre; in France, 81 cents a litre; in Italy, 94 cents a litre; in Germany, 71 cents a litre.
Let us talk about gasoline prices in the United States. It is true that it costs $1.15 a gallon and even $1.00 in some areas, but we must not forget, as certain members on the other side realize that the American gallon is only 4/5 of an Imperial gallon. By using the rule of three, it is very simple to figure out that this means $1.44 an Imperial gallon in U.S. dollars, which converted in Canadian dollars, amounts to $1.75 a gallon or about 38 or 39 cents a litre. Hon. members opposite should listen closely to this. The American states now charge a tax up to 4 cents a litre while the provincial tax in Canada varies unfortunately between zero and 14 cents. If we subtract 9 cents from the price charged in my province on the other side of the river, for instance, which is really shocking, we get 42 minus 9 equals 33 cents, the same price as in Alberta where there is no tax. I congratulate the members from Alberta. They are lucky, they have gasoline, they have oil. We have none in Quebec, but we have tax fiends. We have tax fiends in abundance. However, hon. members opposite are way out when comparing Canadian with the American prices. First, they forget the difference between the Imperial gallon and the American gallon, and then the value of the American currency.
Mr. Speaker, this bothers them, I can hear them mutter across the way, and I admire them because I believe that I can see one member opposite who is sincere. I did not intend to take my whole 20 minutes, but there is one thing that I want to repeat, and I said it at the very beginning and in an earlier speech. For heaven's sake, for the sake of politics, we have to set an example for our youth and stop spreading hate in this House. Those who watch us on television are people who will eventually come to this place, and they will say: If this was allowed in 1982, why should it not be allowed in 1997 or in 2005? I shall close with this comment, Mr. Speaker. I beg hon. members opposite to stop acting this way and to fulfil their role as opposition members. If they are not satisfied with what we do, they can criticize. We can accept criticism, but we do not need anti-French or anti-Quebec comments in this place. We do not need discrimination or racism in this place, and it is with these words that I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker. Let us leave hate and muck for the muckrackers, for those who thrive

in it. 1 may not always be very happy myself, but some politicians would rather play with muck than make speeches. That is all 1 wanted to say, Mr. Speaker.

We did a tremendous job when one looks back because we convinced even the Liberal opposition that it was a worthy policy and objective for the Government of Canada. The Liberals adopted it. They adopted it in opposition and they adopted it in the next election that came along when they were successful and back in the driver's seat. It was a borrowed policy maybe, but at least they said then, and they are still saying today, that energy and petroleum self-sufficiency in this country is the main objective and is what they are after.

May 6, 1982
S'. <9. 26
Self-sufficiency was the objective of the so-called national energy policy of the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). But I want to give you a little background with regard to our research and work in developing that policy.
We scraped the bottom of the barrel to come up with every conceivable project so that we could match the petroleum and energy demands of this country with what we thought could be achieved. It was a potential that could be achieved and we really scraped the bottom of the barrel to do it. We were looking at every conceivable project, program and policy of government. We were looking for assistance, help, co-ordination and co-operation from other governments here in Canada. We were also looking for assistance, of course, from the industry itself. We produced the figures and we produced the objective that this was a potential that could be achieved. I will not bore the House tonight with the actual numbers or names of all the projects that we thought could be achieved. But I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that as we entered into the 1979 election and as we entered into government in this country in 1979 we were really flying. We were really flying with very little margin for error as far as what could be done for this country.
In our view, oil and energy self-sufficiency by 1990 could be achieved just by the skin of Canada's teeth. There was very little margin for error. There was very little margin for cancellation.
I suspect we were so successful in putting forward that objective of self-sufficiency by 1990 that it was adopted holus-bolus by the present administration, which did not really know what it was adopting. I cannot conceive of any group of people who were obviously more determined to wreck that policy and frustrate that objective than the present administration by what they have done.
I just want to remind you again of my phrase "by the skin of Canada's teeth" as far as the margin for error was concerned. Since then some of the major projects that we thought were achievable and which would be added to that potential in order to achieve petroleum and energy self-sufficiency by 1990 have gone out of the window.
What has happened since then? Cold Lake has been cancelled. The Judy Creek program has been cancelled. The Kitimat pipeline has been cancelled. The Syncrude project has been cancelled. The Dempster pipeline has been put on hold. Alsands has been cancelled and the Alaska highway pipeline has been postponed. There are many, many others. In total they amount to millions of dollars of potential investment in this country. They amount literally directly and indirectly to hundreds of thousands of jobs. That is why I am concerned tonight. I do not know what is the experience of my friends on the government side when they go home on the weekends. I suspect that some of them do not do that now because they cannot face the music.
I can tell you that after almost 25 years of public life in this country I have never witnessed a more dispirited attitude in the people than right now. I do not know how Liberal members
can stand to go home on a Friday night and find, as I do, anywhere between half a dozen and two dozen telephone calls waiting for me from my constituents who are facing a very real financial tragedy of one type or another. These tragedies are usually attribuable to government policy or lack of government policy in this country. I have never seen or heard anything like it. It affects everyone. It affects farmers, small businessmen, large businesses, people in the towns, cities and in the country. Many of these do not show up in statistics.
For the first time since the 1930s depression I find farmers abandoning their farms and walking out in the middle of the night.

The absolute collapse of the entire national energy policy is directly attribuable to the arrogance, the stubbornness and the unrealistic atmosphere which exists in the seats of the mighty in government in Ottawa. It is unbelievable how these people can be so insular and not realize the harm they are doing to the people of the country. The collapse of the national energy policy-and it is a collapse-is part and parcel of what has been going on over the last 18 months. Obviously it will get worse.
Quite frankly I was hoping that I would be able to goad the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro) into asking, "How can you say the national energy policy is falling apart because of government policies?" Obviously it is their policy and it is something they want to see strengthened and protected, so I do not know; that is the illogical part of the whole thing. The cash flow problems facing resource companies are enough to destroy some of the projects, as are high interest rates, the cost of money and the cost of investment in the country. High interest rates are controllable by government, but its announced and determined policy is to keep them high. Another thing is that the tax bite in regard to resource projects, which we definitely need if we are to fulfil our dream of self-sufficiency, is simply too great. When we couple the enormous tax bites of greedy governments with the cost of investment, cash flow problems, FIRA problems and, above all, the great bogey of Canadianization-which is a fancy word for nationalization-obviously very few international investors in the country will turn to Canadian resource industries for investment. I am as much an economic nationalist as anyone in the House, but there is a time and place for everything. When our future, as far as the great dream of being selfsufficient is at stake, I suggest that each one of these burdens, heaped one on top of the other, means that anyone with

international investment funds in the world today would be crazy to invest his money in the Canadian petroleum and energy industry. It is a sad state of affairs and a sad fact.
On top of this, when people look at Canada and its petroleum industry, they see a great uncertainty due to the unpredictability of the personalities of some of the people who are running government today. They must face this, as well as the great unpredictability due to the discretionary decisions built into present Canadian legislation. Obviously it discourages oil development and petroleum development in the country and results in discrimination. I will not presume too much on the patience of the House. I will conclude my remarks shortly, but before doing so I want to say that at a time when, unfortunately, Canada must attract foreign investment into the petroleum and energy industries, it is the height of folly to come before the investment community with policies which discriminate against foreign investment.
In the long run perhaps that policy will have to be embraced by us all. At the moment timing is everything, but the timing of the moves over the last 18 months has been absolutely wrong. The higher taxes paid by foreign companies in the Canadian resource industry obviously equal a lowering of value of foreign-owned oil assets in Canada. Therefore, they are forced to sell them off at lower values. This is economic discrimination at a time when perhaps the very reversal should be true.
I have one challenge to the government benches. I return to their dream and our dream of oil and energy self-sufficiency by 1990. I have followed this debate closely and I have yet to hear the answer to this challenge. I put it out to any member of the government benches who want to answer it for me. 1 do not believe I am the only one who is asking this question. The challenge is simple. If the policy of the present administration is still energy and petroleum self-sufficiency by 1990, if in the formulation of that policy we were hard-pressed to match production with demand by 1990, and now that we have had the cancellation of large and small projects directly due to the arrogance, stubborness and unrealistic viewpoint of government members, I would like to hear them explain, either tonight, tomorrow or over the next few days, how they mean to meet that objective of self-sufficiency. Where are the projects which will take the place of Alsands, just as one example? Where are the projects which will take the place of Cold Lake, just as another example? Where are the projects which will
take the place of the others I have mentioned and of the many others which my colleagues have mentioned? It is not a terribly complicated challenge. If they still believe in selfsufficiency by 1990, I should like to hear which projects they are now relying upon to meet that objective. I firmly believe that that dream of self-sufficiency by 1990 has gone out the window with the cancellation of these projects and with the so-called National Energy Program which tumbled like a deck of cards around their ears. I challenge them. I should like to hear, chapter and verse, which projects will produce energy and oil self-sufficiency by 1990.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise during this very timely debate which was asked for by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in light of the emergency situation which exists with the National Energy Program with respect to the Alsands project and the Alaska pipeline project.
I am particularly interested in the debate because the National Energy Program has seriously affected my constituency. More particularly, I think it is a sad commentary on the government of this country because the National Energy Program could have been the number one plank in turning around our economy.
If we review the history of the last two years-which seems like 20 years because of the failure of the National Energy Program under the leadership of the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde)-we realize that there was a boom in Canada's industry. When the minister in charge of energy made decisions, they have had a devastating effect in western Canada. Before he assumed his position, there was a boom in my riding. In the Estevan Weyburn area and in Alberta and Saskatchewan, as well as in all of Canada, the almost complete collapse of the oil industry in Canada has created serious difficulties.
I would like to read into the record some of the facts which were laid out in a document entitled, "Conditions in the Canadian Oil and Gas Industry". It states:
Petroleum Information Corporation of Denver recently released comparative 1981 statistics on oil and gas activity in Canada and the U.S. The contrast is startling. It is hard evidence on the damage wreaked on the Canadian Oil and Gas Industry over the last year ..."
Here are some of the facts as stated in this document:
-drilling activity in Canada down 25 per cent in 1981 over 1980 in contrast to an increase of 25 per cent for the same period in the U.S.;
-well completions in Canada in 1981 were 7,183 compared to 9,481 in 1980, a 25 per cent drop;
-exploratory drilling in Canada declined 19 percent, from 3,925 to 3,179;
-development drilling in Canada was down 28 per cent from 5,556 to 4,007.
The next statistic is in metres due to the Metric Commission:
-measured in metres drilled, the decline was from 10.27 million in 1980 to 7.64 million in 1981.
-the number of active rigs in Canada has declined 33 per cent in 1981 over 1980:

May 6, 1982
-the number of seismic crews, a leading indicator of future exploration activity, also declined 25 per cent in 1981 compared to 1980.
This has been very evident in the small towns and communities in western Canada where exploration, drilling and production activities are so important. It has had the effect of bankrupting small businesses and people involved in the service and supply industry and it has driven out hundreds of oil rigs; 226, I believe, to be exact. It has taken jobs from our young people and in its place it has brought stagnation to economy.
I would like to read an article from the Financial Times. The headline reads, "Banks bail out oil firms." The article states:
As many as 100 western resource companies of all sizes might now be insolvent if financial institutions had not come up with loan extensions and deferred payment plans.
A little further on the article states:
One Calgary energy analyst estimates 100 western resource companies of all sizes would be insolvent today if banks had not allowed them to defer interest payments.
All this has happened within a couple of years and it is as a result of a misguided energy policy. In addition, we are hearing comments during this debate about the failure of the Alsands project. It is estimated in the two projects, the Alsands and the Alaska pipeline project, that the loss of jobs to Canada is in the area of 250,000. This will have a very serious effect on our country.
I will now turn to the question of energy security. I believe that the long-term goal of the government was to have security of supply for Canada. This was a commendable objective to have, but what has happened to that energy supply and security for Canada? We know the story, Mr. Speaker. We have been importing from foreign sources while paying compensation to refineries in eastern Canada for that imported oil. I believe the figure is 400,000 barrels per day. However, in my area of Saskatchewan, 80 per cent of the production was shut in in the Swift Current area, and in the west Estevan-Weyburn area 45 per cent of the heavy oil was shut in during the month of April. This has been happening for the past two years.
The actions of this government are almost unforgivable. It is astounding to realize that we have not been using our own production capability, yet at the same time we have been importing oil from abroad and paying compensation of up to $17 on every barrel. In addition to this, we have an artificially high price for our petroleum in Canada. This is causing some major problems for our country, which I will elaborate on further.
With respect to security of oil supplies, I would like to refer to a very good article written by the Canadian Petroleum Association which was given to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation on April 29. They said that the objectives of the National Energy Program at the outset are security, opportunity and fairness, and I agree with that. However, they go on to say that although the most secure position is to be self-sufficient it is, nevertheless, their opinion that self-sufficiency cannot be achieved by the end of this decade under the present circumstances, and that unless major revisions are introduced to the framework under which the oil industry
operates, oil security may even slip completely from Canada's grasp.
That is a sad commentary on a country such as Canada whose opportunities are so great. If you recall, one of the major objectives of our government-when we were in government-was self-sufficiency. As I stated earlier, the industry in western Canada was in a minor boom. Thanks to the NDP-Liberal coalition, our government was defeated, which caused some very serious repercussions in Saskatchewan, which are now history.

Concerning the major issue of Canadianization, which is a Trojan horse in disguise drawn into the camp, which is really the nationalization of the oil industry, which has resulted in driving capital out of the country, the NDP supported the government, not only in committee but also in the House. Concerning the national energy policy, 1 sat for three years in the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. The NDP supported the Liberals every time on most of the issues relating to government take-over of the oil industry. I think that without a doubt, that is the number one reason there is a major problem in the oil industry in Canada today, and I will refer to it a little later.
In terms of oil security for Canada, the opportunity in this country is very great. First of all, we do have the blessing of rich natural resources and the opportunity to provide security of supply to the people of Canada. But somehow it seems that we do not have a government which has the will to make that possible for the people of this great country. If we are to achieve security of supply and make up for the 400,000 barrels a day which this country needs, we must make some very drastic changes to the national energy policy. We must positively address it and completely turn the direction around. Concerning the Canadianization program, we in the Conservative Party completely agree that Canadians should control their industry and receive the benefits of our great resource. However, the direction in which the government is going has caused foreign investors to lose confidence in the country.
The other day in committee I asked Mr. Hopper, president of Petro-Canada, a question concerning the direction of the energy policy, particularly the pricing policy. He answered:
Now, Mr. Gustafson, I am in a position of having some sympathy for my colleagues in this business in trying to make certain people understand as to how prices get to be where they are. Mr. Speaker, in any case, I am very happy to have the opportunity to analyse what happened last Friday. First of all, everyone is wondering what happened to the Alsands project and why it is being dropped. If the members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries had kept their commitments, and if prices that were increasing in 1977 and 1978-in any case had been increasing since 1973-of course, there might have been a possibility to go ahead with the project. On the other hand, maybe the fact that our energy conservation program was too successful caused the project's temporary suspension. I think some of the previous speakers may have given some figures, but in any case, let me tell you that between 1980 and 1981, oil consumption in Canada dropped by 8.7 per cent. If we look at the reasons for this fairly substantial drop, it is probably due to the success of the energy conservation programs launched by the government in 1974 and the home insulation projects in which 170,000 Canadians participated. Just think of the energy savings that represents, and the jobs created by these projects through which modern techniques were used to better insulate Canadian homes. 1 am also thinking of the savings to Canadians who upgraded their home insulation. There are also one million Canadians who converted from oil to coal, wood or natural gas. Here again, Mr. Speaker, there are tremendous advantages and benefits.
First of all, the drop in consumption of oil, a non-renewable resource that is, once it has been used, that is it. So I feel that the oil we keep in the ground here in Canada, the oil we conserve, is more precious to us than the oil we are burning and consuming. In fact, Mr. Speaker, 1,200,000 Canadians have succeeded in reducing their oil consumption. This shows that Canadians were right in following the program or programs launched by the Canadian government in order to reduce consumption of gasoline. Many Canadians are now driving smaller cars with smaller engines, compared with the cars they used to drive.
Our energy policy, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) pointed out once more, has three main goals, including security of energy supply, especially as far as oil is concerned, and I think we have vastly improved the ability of domestic producers to meet domestic demand.
Second, Canadians would be given an opportunity to get involved in the program. I have given some examples where Canadians have participated in the program on a large scale, and, Mr. Speaker, it must be said that Canadians have done their share with a lot of enthusiasm and have made their modest contribution towards saving energy.
Finally, goal number three was to set fair prices. The program had three objectives, the last one being to set fair prices, and this means, Mr. Speaker, that Petro-Canada was created by the government for Canadians, to ensure that we would not be at the mercy of multinationals. To hear some of the speeches made a few minutes ago, canadianization sounds like a horrible disease. I, for one, prefer canadianization to multinationalization. That is what was happening in Canada, and I think that Canadians have a reason to be proud that now, Canadian participation has risen to 50 per cent in our oil industry. We should be proud that Canadians have achieved this degree of Canadianization in an industry that is strategically so important to this country.
1 find it astonishing and quite absurd that my colleagues opposite are outraged by this canadianization campaign. What is wrong with Canada? Are we paralyzed or what? Can't we develop our own industry to meet the needs of Canadians?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are facing difficult times. There are 1.5 million people unemployed, and inflation stands at 11.5 per cent, more than in 1975 when the Liberal government imposed wage and price controls. Farmers are facing increasing costs of production; at the same time they are getting lower prices for their products. Farm and business bankruptcies are at an all-time high. This is the case in a country as rich in resources and with the highly educated labour force we have here.
How does the Liberal government and the Conservative opposition propose to deal with this disastrous situation? Both parties believe that the way to put people back to work is by the rapid development of energy megaprojects regardless of the price and the concessions to Canadian and multinational energy corporations that would be needed to persuade them to participate in the megaprojects.
The only difference between the Liberal government and the Conservative opposition is that the Conservatives would give more and larger concessions to the multinationals and Canadian corporations in the private sector in order to persuade them to go ahead.
The Conservatives claim that the megaprojects which have been cancelled recently, both the Alsands project and the Alaska gas pipeline project, were cancelled because the government was demanding too much from the companies and because of the National Energy Program.
The truth is that the projects were cancelled because the private corporations, which are in business to make a profit- one cannot blame them for that-have realized that these and other projects were only feasible if there was a steadily-increasing price for oil every year. That has not happened. The world price of oil, which was going up by 10 or 15 per cent each year until this year, is actually going down, with the result that energy projects everywhere in the world have been cancelled.
Just a week ago in the United States, a country which has the most supportive free enterprise president in the world, a Republican who is wiping out virtually every social program ever developed in that country in the last 50 years, Exxon announced it was closing down its oil shale project in Colorado.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona made has been repeated probably 50 times by Conservative members in the last few days. As far as my relationship with the Liberal Party is concerned, the hon. member, who used to live in Winnipeg, should know that in my constituency in the last 50 years one Liberal was elected for one term and one Conservative was elected for one term. I am sure that record will be continued.
The United States has de-regulated energy prices and has taken off all the restrictions the Conservatives claim have been put on corporations in Canada. Despite their free enterprise system and de-regulation, Exxon has cancelled its billion dollar oil shale project in Colorado. There is no national energy program in the United States, so why did Exxon do that? Exxon did it because it knows that the price of producing a barrel of oil from shale is so much higher than the price of conventional oil is likely to be in the next 10 or 15 years that it simply could not afford to go ahead. It is for the same reason that the Alsands project and the Alaska gas pipeline have been cancelled.
What happens when that kind of project closes down in the United States is similar to what happens in Canada. On May 4, the New York Times carried a news story about the closing of the oil shale project in Colorado. It ran as follows:
Like most of the others who moved here to work on the nearby Colony Oil Shale Project, Jerry Ferguson Figured he was making a solid investment when he sank most of his life savings last February into a new $72,000 home.
In Calgary you could not buy a house for $72,000. The article goes on to say that he was surprised by the decision of the Exxon Corporation to close down the project. The story estimates that nearly 4,000 workers who worked in the Parachute area when laid off will cause a loss in the payroll of more
May 6, 1982

than $1 million a week. That is on a project which is not in Canada.
That is what is happening in many places because the price of oil, which was going up by 10 or 15 per cent each year for the last six or eight years, has now gone down, although that decrease may be temporary.
It has been suggested by Conservatives that we are not being fair to the oil companies and that we are mistreating the private sector. We know that until recently the Canadian taxpayer was paying 93 cents of every dollar invested in exploration in the Beaufort Sea in the form of tax benefits. How much more should this country be prepared to give the energy companies before they will invest in Canada? The energy companies are doing very well by us.
I have no time to put the figures on the record, but Great Britain does not deal so generously with the oil companies in the North Sea, and the Conservative government in Norway is so much tougher on their companies that we are not in the same league. They get so much more from their companies that we are not even in the same league, yet we hear from the Conservative Party that we are being too tough. The British government has been half-owner of BP since the 1920s. That was not done by some Labour socialist government, it was done by Winston Churchill. If the hon. member wants to criticize that, let him do it.
We have been accused again and again-the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did it in question period today-of being opposed to megaprojects. Nothing can be further from the truth. We believe and have said repeatedly that where the resource megaprojects can be demonstrated to be necessary to achieve benefits for Canadians, we should proceed with them. But they should proceed with a minimum of public subsidy and a maximum of public equity. When the Alaska highway gas pipeline was first proposed, it was described as a means of getting Alaska gas to the United States by way of the Canadian corridor. We were told it would give thousands of Canadians jobs and we would be able to connect the Dempster spur line to bring gas to southern Canada from our Northwest Territories. The NDP warned that the companies and the U.S. government had not firmly committed themselves to the entire project. We warned that the cost would destroy the project, and that has happened. The cost has ballooned from an estimated $8 billion to $25 billion or more. But the government and the Conservatives brushed aside these reservations. The record will show that we were the only ones who voted against it because we predicted it would not fly. We are now told there will be another two-year delay, and I predict it will be much more than that, if ever.
Later it was suggested that we could get the project started if only Canada would permit the pre-build. Again we warned the pipeline would not be built. We said we should not go ahead with the pre-build. We wanted the whole line built so that the cheap Alberta gas we exported now would be replaced with Alaska gas when the project came on stream. Well, who
was right? We built the pre-build, and where is the pipeline? It is gone. We are exporting cheap gas now, and some time in the future Canadian customers will be paying through the nose for expensive gas from the high Arctic. That is what the Liberals and Conservatives have wished on the Canadian people. We told them it would happen, and it has.
What about the Alsands project? When it was first proposed, it was supposed to cost $13 billion to $15 billion and produce 137,000 barrels of oil a day. It was going to produce thousands of jobs and much in the way of economic spin-offs. However, it was only economically feasible if the price of oil rose to somewhere between $80 and $90 a barrel. Of course, it is nowhere near that. In fact, it is now under $30 a barrel. Who can blame the companies, who are in business to make a profit, as they should be, and who, unfortunately, are much smarter than our government? Who can blame the companies if they say no matter what concessions and no matter what tax write-offs, they will not be able to make a profit from oil which will cost us $80 to $90 a barrel to produce? I think I am being quite conservative in that estimate.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Please do not be Conservative.

I have seen estimates that oil from Alsands will cost as much as $120 a barrel. Who can blame the companies if they say they are not going ahead with a project to produce oil at that price when it is now selling for $30 a barrel and there is a surplus? For the first time in more than a generation less than 50 per cent of the oil sold comes from OPEC countries. Production from the North Sea, Mexico and other places has escalated, and OPEC have not been able to increase their prices.
The government put much faith in getting Canada moving because of these megaprojects, but I want to remind my Conservative friends that it was not just the Liberal government which made this proposal to the companies in its desire to keep the projects going. The Conservative Government of Alberta was a partner. Both made very generous concessions- I would say too generous-to try and persuade the companies to continue with Alsands. But, Mr. Speaker, just like Exxon in the United States, the companies said this thing will not make a profit no matter what they are given, so they will not go ahead.

speechtext:
But, Mr. Speaker, despite everything that has happened, we are told by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), "Well, it is not so serious because, after all, we still have projects going."
The projects that were cancelled-the Alsands project, the Alaska gas pipeline project, the Cold Lake project-total in value, estimated, over $75 billion. But the projects which the

May 6, 1982
minister listed as still being viable, which are still going ahead-the Beaufort Sea development, the Norman Wells Pipeline, the B.C. coal fields, the Revelstoke hydro project, the Quebec and Maritimes pipeline-altogether total just over $4 billion-a far cry from the $75 billion vision of a year or two ago.
And yet, as late as December, 1980, the minister was still promising these miracles. He said, and I quote from a speech he made on December 3, 1980:
Our intention is to ensure that these projects go ahead. Whether they are developed by a company owned by Canadians, such as Petro-Canada, or by other companies which have their own technology, what is important is that all those projects proceed in the next few years. That is what we are going to work on.
Well, the minister has worked on them, but he has proved to be a complete failure.
As I said earlier, we are not opposed to megaprojects if they meet the needs of the Canadian people. But we said then, and we say now, that what we need to do is not to concentrate on a few giant megaprojects which are economically unsound; what we need to do-and I find it stranger that it is I, a member from western Canada, a member from Winnipeg, who should be saying what I am about to say and not my Liberal friends from Quebec and my Conservative friends from Ontario, where the manufacturing industry in Canada exists-what we need to do is to stop the destruction of our manufacturing sector.
In the last year more than 200,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector have disappeared. Whether you look at the automotive industry, or steel, or farm machinery, or textiles, every day there are announcements of lay-offs, of plant closures, of bankruptcies.
My Liberal and Conservative friends who come from Ontario and Quebec, where the manufacturing industry is almost completely concentrated, are quiet. They are so mesmerized by megaprojects, they are ignoring the needs of their own people.
We say that what we need to do in this country is to begin to think about meeting the needs of this country. We need to think about meeting the housing requirements. We are building 150,000 homes a year, when we should be building over
200,000.	We are committed to tremendous increases in the exports of wheat, of coal, of potash, to mention just three examples. Our transportation system will not be able to handle the increased movements of those products.
Are we rebuilding the transportation system? No. We are seeing people laid off by the railway companies, the CNR and the CPR. We are seeing people laid off by the firms which build hopper cars, railway engines and so forth.
So, Mr. Speaker, we say, for God's sake, let us stop thinking about megaprojects and get down to thinking about meeting the needs of the Canadian people for jobs, for homes and for better lives.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this speech marathon it is difficult to avoid repeating what was said by previous speakers. I will try to do what Canadian folklore has done and set new words to traditional tunes. We deplore the situation and sympathize with those people who are directly affected by the, I assume, temporary abandonment of the Alsands project. However, there is some question as to how this problem is being approached. Among the megaprojects developed by Canada and by its leaders, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) pointed out, we might do well to recall the story of Sir John A. Macdonald, whose political party was at that time called the Liberal Conservative Party. The Liberal part has been dropped since then. We may have forgotten the lesson to be drawn from Sir John A.'s story, and this evening we should perhaps remember that when Macdonald was struggling to get the railroad built from the Atlantic to the Pacific, it was not because he wanted to fill the pockets of certain corporations. When he got involved in this kind of financing, heaven knows it caused a lot of problems and scandals and even cost him his government. Nevertheless, his ideal was to build a railroad from the Atlantic to the Pacific, which was a way to unite this country.
1 wish that in this debate we could rise above political partisanship and look for an ideal that we can pursue together. Laurier said that the 20th Century would belong to Canada. No one can deny that the next years will be constantly focussed on energy. Perhaps the best way to unite this country is to stress energy development. I am pretty upset, especially at the hon. members on the Conservative benches many of whom are from Alberta and must have some influence on their provincial government, which accepted the same proposal made by the Minister of Energy who added that he wanted the private sector to be involved. And I want to ask the hon. members, why could Alberta not carry out the same project, through a Crown corporation? When Premier Bennett took over the hydroelectric companies and ferry services in British Columbia, was he accused of being a communist or a socialist? Did it ever occur to Quebecers to accuse Robert Bourassa, Premier of Quebec, of being a socialist when he developed the James Bay project?
Yet, the James Bay project was just as important as Alsands. In the final analysis, we must be guided by the common good of all Canadians. Of course, some members opposite are accusing us of harbouring socialist tendencies and others of being conservative and backward, but we are not dogmatic. If we do have a philosophy, it consists in helping the ordinary citizen, in providing security for the workers, in finding jobs for the unemployed and in guaranteeing a bright future to our young people. I am sorry to say that because of the way the rules of this House are used and even abused, we lose a great deal of time delaying the implementation of
May 6, 1982

projects which are extremely important for the future of our country, which is even now envied by the rest of the world. It was Father Lepire who said: "We are always drawing attention to the 5 per cent that divide us and ignoring the 95 per cent that unite us."
Our country is tremendously rich in resources and assets; yet some would create an environment of pessimism by futile dissensions which make us look ridiculous in the eyes of foreign investors, an environment of pessimism which discourages the unemployed and makes our young people skeptical about our future, while we have everything we need if we want to work together because Providence has blessed us with resources so abundant that Canada is looked upon as the Eden of the world. The fact is that foreigners see this image of Canada for if we were to open wide our doors to immigration, everyone would want to come here. What do we have to do? We have to call attention to what can unite us. In this regard, since we are always talking about our energy policy, I would like to see a member rise in this House and say: "I am against energy self-sufficiency for Canada." No member of this House would say such a thing. Is there one single member in this House who could rise and say that he is against the sharing of our resources and our energy? Once again, no one would rise to make such a statement. I ask the question once more: Do the members of this House want us to be masters in our own country instead of being governed by policies developed abroad either in the Middle East or in other parts of the world? Do we want to let foreign interests dictate our policies in our own country? Let the member who has the courage to say that we must not aim at self-sufficiency, at the canadianization of our energy sector, at sharing with those provinces whose subsoil does not contain energy resources, let that member rise and express his views, if really he is against Canadians forming a single nation.
I referred to John A. Macdonald who with the railway, despite all those mishaps, delays and scandals, pursued until his death his ideal of uniting this country from sea to sea. I suggest that today, with our energy resources, we can have the same ideal, but only to the extent where we are willing to share and stop being hypocritical in that respect. Because in the final analysis, as well as self-centered egotists, there are group-centered egotists who would like to keep everything for themselves rather than sharing with others. This country never will stay together unless we are willing to use those resources for the benefit of ail Canadians. And to those who are concerned that foreign capital will not come here under these conditions, I say they are near-sighted. Because from the moment we will have a common desire in Canada to put our resources in common, to accept a policy of sharing, security, participation and, fairness, private capital will come here because it will feel that in this country we have social order, consideration for private enterprise.
Let us not forget that this country was born, because we had people, pioneers who bowed to no difficulty and, although means of communications were almost non-existent, they discovered the Rockies, Louisiana and opened a huge territory full of promises and resources. I therefore submit that if we really want to give security to our workers, give a chance to the unemployed who ask for nothing more than the opportunity to use their abilities, to our young people who would like to share an ideal made possible by our unlimited potential. Who would have thought that some day, in the Arctic itself, we could go and look for resources capable of developing this country? Let us turn now for a moment to the Arctic pilot project, near the North Pole, where we will be able to get not only the natural gas that is already known to exist in unlimited quantities, and of such quality that the president of Polar Gas told me that the oil we are extracting here, without any processing at all, could be used directly in our engines, because that is how good it is, and through that megaproject we could not only I would say establish Canadian sovereignty on that northern continent near the Arctic but also develop our shipyards, develop a whole new technology, a whole new science and in addition get a resource that is now dormant in the North and could be used to the benefit of the whole of Eastern Canada, of Quebec. Again, since I started from that premise, it could contribute to Canadian unity.
I would ask my colleagues opposite whether they will not recognize the writing on the wall that was apparent during the last election. Mene, Tebel, Peres. Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. If they would not remain wanting but make their mark as an opposition, they will have to renounce such a pessimistic policy, those switches and parliamentary gimmicks, they will have to show to the people that they are a united front, not because of contempt for profit, but because of respect for private enterprise. We admire their technology, we want to use it, but when the public interest is at stake, the government must take its responsibilities. This is not being socialist or communist, to do as Bourassa did for James Bay. This is merely using funds, taking the necessary measures and asking private interests to join with us in attaining our ideals. No government would be elected unless it was ready to implement the energy program put forward by this government, because Canadians will never be satisfied with being anything less than the masters in their own country and will disapprove of collective selfishness where each and everyone wants to keep everything for himself and refuses to share with others who have no resources.
Canadians will never accept any ideal other than selfsufficiency and will refuse to be tied to foreign policies and pressures imposed by countries that have no other ambition but their own self-interest. Those Canadian ideals and objectives are widely shared by our people and if you have public opinion polls taken, you will realize that such is the case. A

May 6, 1982
government which would fail to implement such a program would be a doomed government.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona seems to be preoccupied with the nationalization issue. The moment I rose to take part in this debate, I took care to say that there are no fanatics among us and that our only concern is to look after ordinary Canadians, find jobs for the unemployed and prepare for our youth a better future. We accept the common good as being the basis for our action, and if the private sector for whatever reason refused to take chances, then the State should intervene. More specifically, you would like to know what our approach would be concerning larger corporations such as Chrysler, Ford and General Motors. When private corporations are in financial trouble because of a world recession, I feel it would be quite appropriate for the government to intervene and support them, so that they may continue their operations and ensure the progress and development of many Canadian communities, as well as create jobs, something they have been doing for many years.
France nationalized one of its two auto corporations; the two corporations are competing and, as far as I know, they are doing fine; this was done many years ago by a government which could not be considered a socialist government, by any stretch of the imagination, so that we are making too much fuss, in my opinion, about such categories as socialism, communism and private enterprise; our purpose should be to help the unemployed, the man in the street, and to seek the common good, and when the private sector fails to act the State should step in. I am not worried as long as a climate of trust is created within the Canadian government, instead of fostering endless pessimism for the purpose of running an election for mean political gains. So I am saying now: "Do not worry, for all the businessmen in the world are anxious to come and invest their money in this country, because Canada will offer them the best security and best return".

I apologize, Mr. Speaker. It has been my experience on those few occasions when I have spoken in this House that matters of great import are scheduled so as to have an impact at the very end and create a grand finale, so to speak. Time runs out and important elements of the speech may be left unstated. This is particularly so when one enters a debate absolutely overwhelmed by the amount of legitimate bombast that could be aimed at the deplorable and unworthy performance of this government and of those in this House whose support underwrites its endeavours. They support the government without judging the quality of government initiatives.
The consequences of this loyalty are demonstrated by the collapse of Alsands and the failure of national energy policy. In order to avoid this pitfall, I want to begin my brief comments by dwelling on the positive alternatives which can be offered Canadians in place of the chaos which we observe in the nation today.
I am largely going to ignore the NDP in their role because their Saskatchewan experience has forecast their destiny in Canada.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
