subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me state the following as positive alternatives to this government's unproductive policies, alternatives offered to Canadians by Progressive Conservative members of Parliament.
How about a return to a philosophy that recognizes the worth of the individual and of his efforts as an important aspect of Canadian society? How about a return to policies and actions on the part of the government that encourage productive activity as opposed to government activity? That would get the government out of the pocketbook of Canadians and stop penalizing Canadians whose ambition is to build a personal stake in their nation, whether in the form of home ownership, a business, a farm or simply by investing capital in projects that build the nation. How about an alternative that reverses this government's philosophy which is hostile to risk, hostile to incentives, hostile to private ingenuity and effort? How about reversing the philosophy that sees successful business and individual initiatives as enemies of the state and believes that any wealth created is fair game for government confiscation?
May 6, 1982

How about a return to a philosophy of government that will assist Canadians in the realization of their goals and dreams rather than placing in the way of individual Canadians and their goals and dreams a big government that plans to get bigger and bureaucrats who intend to become increasingly bureaucratic?
How would it be if we put in its place the elitist theory that only government acts in the national interest? The fallacy of that theory is the subject of our debate today. Putting that elitist theory to rest is the positive alternative we offer. We offer a philosophy which, when put in place, will give ordinary Canadians a chance to realize dreams that are impossible under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and under this government, a government whose whole ideology seems intent on destroying the spirit of the only productive element of our economic society.
When the spirit of enterprise and achievement is destroyed by the increasing intervention of government, the spirit of the new philosophy espoused by this government acts as a vaccu-um in which to work its destructive role.
The Liberal government places more emphasis upon the redistribution of wealth than upon its creation. The Progressive Conservative government will recognize that if governments wish to distribute more wealth, they must first encourage the creation of more wealth. We believe, unlike the government opposite, that wealth creation will be accomplished most efficiently through the private sector. It will be accomplished through a private sector supported by legislation and by actions of government which produce a climate of opportunity rather than a roadbed of obstacles.
The economic spirit of my party was summed up in a speech given by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) at the 1978 National Industrial Stategy Conference. He said that the company which opened up western Canada was not just called the Hudson's Bay Company; it was called the Company of Adventurers Trading into Hudson's Bay. Also he indicated that he thought there was a lesson about our history in that phrase and that when we are at our best as a country, when we are a country of adventurers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am just wondering whether there is a problem in making a point to the government when there are no Liberal members present in the House.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not the first time I have spoken to empty seats opposite. To continue, my leader then went on to indicate that what we have suffered in the last decade, during which there was an emphasis upon the redistribution of income rather than upon the generation of new growth and new income in the country, has been an under valuing and a disrespect for the sense of adventure which is at the very centre of our success as a country. Also he indicated that we must
clearly begin the process of rewarding success in the country and encouraging initiative.
It is the philosophy of the government and its intervention which damned the Alsands project, the northern pipeline project, the Judy Creek project, and so on. Alsands was destroyed by greed and the ideology of the Government of Canada which put that project on hold two years ago. A different administration following a different philosophy would have seen this important element in Canada's energy supply nearly half completed, and hundreds of thousands of Canadians now unemployed would be working. That is the measure of the emergency. The Government of Canada is the emergency; Alsands is the evidence.
This important and timely emergency debate has been propelled into the House by the announced failures of important elements of the so called National Energy Program of the Liberal government. What a program! The dictionary definition of program is:
A descriptive notice of a series of events; a definite plan of intended proceedings.
God help Canada if this is the best energy plan the government can come up with. What a plan! What a genius of planning demonstrated in the National Energy Program of the Liberal government! The national program of the Liberal government! This particular program was doomed from its inception by its authors, the minister of disaster and the government of failures. The National Energy Program was doomed by its primary motivation to collect revenue for government, doomed by the purpose in the minds of its creators to benefit one group of electors at the expense of another, doomed by the socialist-dominated philosophy which shaped it, doomed by a lack of understanding of what makes Canada tick, and doomed by a lack of appreciation of the basic values which built our nation-the qualities of thrift, initiative and individual effort, which the government rejected. Also it was doomed by a government with a style of morality which includes deceitful and artful appeals to the electorate, which are totally unworthy of a society based upon democratic principles, principles which must be respected if democracy is to survive.
The survival of responsible democracy in Canada does not appear to be a matter of priority with hon. members opposite. The Liberal administration, under the dubious leadership of the particularly ill-suited Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) doomed its own National Energy Program by choosing the course of confrontation rather than the course of co-operation, by raising tempers rather than reason, by pitting region against region, by pitting government against government and by putting the interests of the big government before the interests of little Canadians. The national energy policy was doomed by the revenue-grabbing nature of its policies, doomed by government interventionism which is alarming reasoned Canadians, and doomed by the disgust which the government has earned for itself in the minds and reactions of individual Canadians who ask only for an opportunity to work and to achieve.

May 6, 1982
The government consistently demeans the efforts of individuals to be creative and productive for themselves and for the nation. That is the damning implication of the actions of the Liberal government and its docile aye-saying members. The damaging philosophy of the Prime Minister is the root cause of the unhappiness in the west which has its latest manifestation in the emergence of the Western Canada Concept and the election of its first member to a Canadian legislature.
My impression of the Western Canada Concept and its motivations is that its growing membership is saying to the Prime Minister of Canada and to those who so blindly follow his ideological lead: "Mr. Prime Minister, for too long you and your colleagues have been building a wall between central and western Canada all by yourselves; Mr. Prime Minister, we are not going to help you." This is the spectre the Prime Minister has created in my part of the country.
I should like to speak for a few minutes on the impact of the government's economic program on the area of Canada which I represent. We are focusing our attention and that of the nation upon the collapse of Alsands, the failure of the Alaska pipeline and all other multitudinous evidence which exists that government intervention is the problem, not the solution. None of these examples of failure focus specifically on Okanagan-Similkameen, but the implications affect us very much. The government has as its preoccupation the expansion of its empire. It is big government determined to get bigger despite the consequences to Canadians. The detrimental impact is felt everywhere, including the area I represent. In advancing its philosophies based upon government, government, government, it has lost sight of those positive things which it could be accomplishing for the people of Canada. It is wasting its effort and our financial resources on its own objectives and excusing failure to respond to real needs by saying, "We have no money." What total hypocrisy, what cynicism, what lack of respect for the intelligence of the electorate to discriminate between truth and deceit!
The electorate will not soon forget the government's deceit in objecting to an 18 cent excise tax on gasoline. The electorate will not forget the campaign promise, "Vote Liberal and the price of gasoline will stay down." The present price of gasoline is simply a measure of the credibility and the honesty of the two-faced Liberal administration. While the government wastes taxpayer-generated revenue in advertised chest-thumping, in Constitution-celebration bashes exclusive to Liberal party followers, in appointing royal commissions the recommendations of which are ignored, in a Canadian Unity Information Office designed to extend the talons of government into more and more aspects of our life; while the Liberal government, under its brilliantly-devious leader, continues to pursue its wasteful habits and at the same time spouts platitudes about restraint, the legitimate aspirations of the people of Okanagan-Similkameen remain unattended.
Today I received a letter from the President of the B.C. Fruit Growers Association saying in effect: "Fred, please tell those people in government back there how very important the continuation of the ARDSA Program is to our area". I will tell the government, and it is important. The fruit farmers in Okanagan have a great interest in the maintenance of the cold storage construction assistance program. I talked to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) about this and he indicated there might be some tie-ins with the creation of yet another Crown corporation, namely Canagrex, in making this possible. There is always another agency and bureaucracy created by this government to spread its tentacles.
What about the mines which are closing, the sawmill operations in jeopardy in Merritt, Midway, Princeton, Okanagan Falls and Westbank? They are all in jeopardy simply because this government has its priorities all screwed up. It is concentrating its efforts on expanding government rather than expanding opportunities. What is it that keeps mines and mills in operation? For sure it is not government grants or emergency programs to help the unemployed. It is not taxpayer paid advertising campaigns designed to promote the government. What keeps the mines and mills operating is an economy which enjoys vitality, the very quality this government is attacking. What, may I ask, about the grant to the proposed new art gallery in Penticton, which had the implied support of this government since its conception? It has been abandoned by this government this year-next year, who knows? Why? Because of restraint. What restraint?
The people of western Canada, Mr. Speaker are honest, industrious, ambitious, hard-working and thrifty. I could go on and on in praise of their qualities. Above all, they are Canadian. Their qualities are not much different from those of citizens in other areas of Canada. We are blessed with people of quality. What then is different about western Canadians which gives us a distinction?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this emergency debate has continued for three days let me begin my remarks by reviewing the process which has been followed. The motion relates to the cancellation of the Alsands project and postponement of the Alaska highway gas pipeline. It was brought before this House by the right hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), and 1 want to put on record that he is in the House this evening and he has had throughout this debate the full support of his colleagues in the Progressive Conservative caucus. As a member from Alberta, it must be very gratifying to him to know that we from the east, indeed from all parts of Canada, support him and his colleagues from Alberta in this enterprise, because it must be brought to the attention of the Canadian people that we are all affected by these government errors and mistakes in judgment. These vicious acts lead to these harmful results, not only for people from Alberta but from right across the country.
We are here tonight in great numbers to support our leader in the action he is taking, and we will continue to support him in this and other actions. He recognized the grave economic damage resulting from these decision for all Canadians and the cumulative harm which will be inflicted on the economies of all regions of Canada. It is in that role that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition sought an emergency debate so that all aspects of this economic and industrial disaster could be exposed and be carefully considered and, hopefully, resolved.
It is a matter of record that our presiding officer agreed that this matter required urgent consideration. It cannot be disputed by any member of the House that the cancellation of the Alsands project and the delay and possible termination of the Alaska highway pipeline project constitute a genuine emergency requiring immediate and urgent consideration. So when the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) and other members opposite claim there is no emergency or economic catastrophe, they violate both the substance and spirit of Madam Speaker's ruling.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
More important, they seek to cover up and conceal from public view the errors of fact and judgment which are part and parcel of the National Energy Program.
In order to expose to public light the policy errors which have resulted in the cancellation or postponement of these megaprojects, thereby jeopardizing billions of dollars in employment and manufacturing, it is necessary to examine the energy policies of the government institutionalized in the document called the National Energy Program. That document was presented to this House on November 12, 1980 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and it bears the imprimatur of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). It is time that the government and the Liberal
caucus answered for the mistakes of those two ministers contained in those documents.
What were those documents, Mr. Speaker? They carried three promises made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He said NEP would bring about energy selfsufficiency and Canadian control of the industry. He said there would be fair pricing. Let me dispose, first of all, of his promise on fair pricing. Over the period of time which has elapsed since the introduction of NEP we have seen taxes on taxes, and the price of gas at the pump and oil in the home has doubled and tripled. We are paying higher prices than anyone in North America, while our American neighbours through their policies, concentrated as they are on the private sector, have seen their prices drop. That is the fair pricing set out by the minister: prices escalating beyond anything else charged in North America. He calls that fair pricing.
What is going to be the price of Canadian participation? Experts indicate that in order to reach the level of 50 per cent Canadian ownership, as indicated in NEP, we will have to spend $56 billion of Canadian taxpayers' money.
It cost us, Mr. Speaker, $1.4 billion to buy a share in Petrofina so we could have PetroCan signs across the country. But who is paying for it? The consumers of gasoline are paying for it at the rate of three or four cents a gallon of gas. That was done just to satisfy the minister's desire to own an oil company! What does that company do? The president of PetroCan testifying before the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation said, "Sometimes you make a bundle of money, and sometimes you just go broke." How do you like that, Mr. Speaker? You spend $1.4 billion buying a private oil company for PetroCan and the president of the company says, "Sometimes you make a bundle of money and sometimes you just go broke." Does the president of PetroCan, or anyone else, have the right to do that with taxpayers' money? Do they have the right to go for the long jump to make a barrel of money or just go broke? Do you want your taxes to go for that kind of risk? If you want to take those kinds of risks, there are lots of stocks you can invest in and go broke on. But that would be your decision, Mr. Speaker, not a decision of the government's. That is your risk to take if you want to, but it should not be put in the hands of an organization which says it might make a bundle of money or it might go broke.
If you read on in his testimony, you find he does not consider himself any different from any other petroleum executive in Canada. He says they are a little worried about 1982 and what their profit picture might look like. He says they are working hard on that. Well, when you talk about achieving a Canadian content of 50 per cent, you are talking about risking the taxpayer's money, and I do not think taxpayers necessarily want to put that kind of faith in the minister, considering what happened to his fair pricing policy. I think it is important that we in this House give the message to everyone that the minister's Canadianization program has a price we may not be willing to pay. That is the problem with all the policies of this Liberal government. They mask them in mist, shroud them in a national spirit, and hide them under the flag. They are good,

May 6, 1982
and do not object to it because if you do, you will be against the national purpose of Canada and you will be blocking the future of Canadians. Well, that is not true, Mr. Speaker, but you have to stand up once in a while and be counted on matters like that. You have to decide whether you support the free enterprise system and the good judgment of Canadians to do what they want with their own money, or whether you think their funds should be channelled into a bureaucracy to be used in any way they please. When that bureaucracy supports the likes of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the president of PetroCan, I do not want them taking my money and doing what they want with it. I do not know what my friends on the other side want to do with their money. Maybe they siphon it off into some tax dodge which they claim to have eliminated.
Mr. Speaker, the goal of the National Energy Program, as stated in the documents, is to achieve energy self-sufficiency in Canada. If you read the documents, you will find that the exploitation of the Alberta tar sands was very much a part of that goal of energy self-sufficiency. In fact, the documents themselves detail the proposals for the development of the Alberta tar sands. They make it very clear that that played a big role in the future of energy development in Canada. And so there was great concern expressed as this project, this huge Alsands project, which I personally visited, appeared to be in jeopardy. Questions were asked in the House, Mr. Speaker, on February 25, 1982, by our energy critic-and do you know what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources answered on February 25, 1982, when concern was expressed about the future of the Alsands project? He simply said:
Those fiscal arrangements seem satisfactory to some of the partners. They do not seem satisfactory to some other partners. The remaining partners in the consortium are at the present time consulting with other potential partners. I myself have had discussions with such other potential partners, and in the next few days and weeks we will see how these negotiations will be concluded.
On February 25, 1982, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources knew that that project was in danger. Yet he did nothing. He allowed those people to slip out of his grasp, and the project was cancelled.
Do you know what I suspect him of, Mr. Speaker? I suspect that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources wanted the project cancelled. I suspect that he let it go down the drain. He wants to destroy the energy industry in Canada and then come back and build it up. And why would he want to do that? He wants control. The Government of Canada wants control of the energy industry because it is the source of wealth in Canada, and if the government can control that source of wealth, it can tighten its stranglehold on the Canadian economy and enable it to keep Canada under its own thumb. It will destroy that valuable segment of the private sector forever.
Mr. Speaker, the question is, are Canadians going to allow that to happen? And what kind of help are they going to get from the New Democratic Party? On that very same day, the member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) stood in this
House of Commons and warned the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources not to give any help to the Alsands partners, not to take any special steps to help them preserve this project. And do you know what he said, Mr. Speaker? he said:
-will the Minister give serious consideration either to running this project as a public utility, as has been suggested, or rechannelling a lot of the funds that were intended for this project into enhanced recovery programs for old oil and heavy oil-
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody, a representative of the New Democratic Party, made it very clear that he did not care whether or not the Alsands project was cancelled. In fact, he would rather have it cancelled. And they sit here, along with us, in this emergency debate and complain about the cancellation of the Alsands project!
Mr. Speaker, it is a wonder lightening does not come right into this chamber and strike them all down. They do not seem to realize that they were opposed to the Alsands project; they opposed the measures that had to be taken to keep it operative. And now they have the nerve, the gall, to stand up in this chamber and say that it should not have been cancelled. They cannot live with the result. They cannot live with the result, Mr. Speaker. They want to have it both ways. They want to criticize the project and have the jobs and the expenditure of funds and the stimulus to the economy that would have gone with that project. But they were found out. Their words are on the record. They cannot deny it. They warned the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources not to give any special assistance to the parties, assistance that might have preserved this project. So now they are trapped in their own words-as they always are, Mr. Speaker. They are always speaking out of both sides of their mouths. They always want to have their cake and eat it too.
Well, the jig is up. They cannot get away with that. Everybody knows. Everybody heard them say "Don't help the Alsands project." And so now they have to live with that. The next speaker can get up and explain, if he will, the remarks of the member for Mission-Port Moody when he stood up in this House on February 25 of this year when that Alsands project was in danger.

speechtext: Be patient.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we really have to talk about and be concerned about in terms of the cancellation of the Alsands project and the delay of the Alaska pipeline project, is the failure to create the jobs that would have resulted from the implementation of those projects. That is what we on this side of the House are talking about. I am not here to support the petroleum industry. They do not need my help, they are big boys. What I am here to do is to ask the government to reconsider its decision in the light of the jobs that these projects would create-and no one, and certainly no one on the government side, can contend that we do not need jobs in Canada.
Tomorrow a new unemployment rate will be announced; and I am sure it is going to be even higher than it is now at over 9 per cent. I am sure there will be more people unemployed than the 1.2 million persons now admitted to be unemployed. That
May 6, 1982

figure can be greatly escalated, because in addition there are 250,000 Canadians who have given up looking for work. They know they cannot get a job, so they do not bother trying. Also, there are 250,000 Canadians who are employed at jobs well below their qualifications. We have school teachers working as waitresses. There are thousands of examples like that. That gets the whole rate of employment up another 500,000. Then one has to consider the people working part time. We have 1.5 million people in Canada who have only part time jobs-and most of them, if not all of them, would like to be working full time.
So when we talk about an unemployment problem, when we talk about unemployment in Canada, we are not talking about 1.2 million people; we are talking about that number plus another 500,000 who have stopped looking for work or who are working at jobs below their level of qualification, and another 1.5 million Canadians who are working only part time. The figure is well over three million, Mr. Speaker-and that is in a work force of 11 million. So you know what the concern of Canadians is in terms of job creation, and you know what great harm is done when projects that would produce jobs are cancelled, and are cancelled by actions of people like the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Mr. Speaker, I think you have to get personal in a debate like this. You have to point a finger at who is causing this problem. I have no qualms about pointing a finger at the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, because not only is his theory wrong, his whole approach to problem solving in Canada is wrong. It is a terrible thing that we Canadians must suffer because of his arrogance, because of his stupidity, and because of his lack of knowledge of the realities of Canadian life. Mr. Speaker, you do not only have to look to Alberta to see that arrogance and that ignorance on his part. Come to Nova Scotia, come to the Atlantic coast, talk to companies like Shell that want to explore offshore and develop the great resources of the seabed off Nova Scotia and off Newfoundland and listen to what they say about the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. They know their projects are being held up because of his unwillingness to assist and his unwillingness to work on the problems.
Mr. Speaker, that attitude goes right down through his department, because that kind of attitude at the top encourages the same kind of thinking right down through the ranks. We do not have to look too far to solve our energy problem in Canada. If we get rid of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, we will go a long way to solving it. I can assure you of that. I can assure you that anyone who wants to work in the energy industry in Canada knows of his arrogance and his ignorance. He is the biggest stumbling block to progress.
Mr. Speaker, that same minister on that same program stood up in this House and said that we will have natural gas in Nova Scotia by 1983. Mr. Speaker, the best estimates in terms of having natural gas available in Nova Scotia are 1985 and later. That is the value of his promises; that is the value of his projections when it comes to solving energy problems in Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, what are we going to do to solve this problem? What are we going to do? If we have to put up with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, I am not sure the problem can be solved. But I can give you a few solutions. One is to help the private sector petroleum industry to get out into the Atlantic and explore for oil and to find and prove up the reserves that we know are there-and we can do that simply by taking a realistic approach to the legislation that exists, the requirements that must be met and the financial assistance that is available.
Mr. Speaker, in addition, if the government were to get working on projects like the Arctic pilot project, if it would get working and resolve the technical problems that are associated with carrying gas out of the Arctic region, we might have a solution in that area. But before we take that step, we have to examine very closely what is being said by Dome Petroleum and the other promoters of Arctic exploration, because one might mistake them on occasion for snake oil salesmen; one might mistake their motives and question whether they are really telling the truth and whether or not they know all about the development they are proposing.
Some people in Canada-and I know some of them, and I think they are very sensible people-view some of those developments with a concerned eye. But the fact is, the reserves do exist in the Beaufort, and if we get together, given the reserves that exist offshore, in the Beaufort and in the Arctic, we can solve the energy problem. And that has to be the challenge of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources-to get to work and get the job done.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, Hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). I want to say to the silent hordes across the way that what my distinguished colleague has said, I endorse. I endorse it 100 per cent. What he has said about our friends to the left in this chamber is very true. His comments about the activities of the present government with respect to jobs and job creation, with respect to openness and frankness with the Canadian people and with respect to the price of energy in this country deserve support, and I am very pleased to endorse them.
There is one particular area I want to get into tonight. I want to trace for the benefit of members of the House the events leading up to the decision by this government to go ahead with a gas pipeline across Quebec and into the mari-times. Before I do that, I want to underscore one other point the hon. member for Halifax West made tonight and which has been made by other Atlantic members on this side of the House, who have participated in this debate, and that is the point that centers around the squeeze that provincial governments-Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick particularly-are beginning to experience as a direct result of the economic policies of this government.
Nova Scotia has been not singularly fortunate but among the three or four provinces of this country which have been

May 6, 1982
able to sustain an acceptable rate of growth. It is not what we would like it to be, but it is an acceptable rate of growth, given national circumstances. Elowever, in each of the last five months we have been going downhill. How much longer Nova Scotia can continue to sustain real growth is a matter of serious question. Most observers feel-and I think it is demonstrated by the most recent budget brought down by the Government of Nova Scotia-that perhaps our period of real growth is at an end.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: What does this have to do with Alsands?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
I am asked what this has to do with Alsands. One comment and one observation: the hopes of sustaining the system, in no small way and not indirectly, were pinned, to a large degree, on these two projects' going ahead, simply because they would have placed demands on the central steel producers that might very well have resulted in urgently needed contracts. The future of SYSCO is in some serious doubt.
So much for the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and his concern for Atlantic Canada.
On May 15, 1980, just a few short days before the referendum in Quebec-and I am aware that much was done, and perhaps much was needed to be done to ensure a proper outcome of that vote-the government okayed a gas pipeline extension from Ontario into Quebec as far as Quebec City, but not beyond. Many of us felt perhaps there was some justification in making that announcement to the people of the province of Quebec before the referendum, and that was fine. That was in May of 1980.
Throughout the balance of 1980 and through 1981 up until December 12, pressure was brought to bear by members on this side of the House as well as the premiers of the three maritime provinces, separately and acting as the Council of Maritime Premiers, on this government to bring down its ruling with respect to the extension of that pipeline beyond Quebec, through New Brunswick and into Nova Scotia.
One of the reasons given at the time was that the line could not go further, and this flowed from National Energy Board hearings, because of the absence of environmental impact studies. The most likely reason was to allow a period of time for the expenditure of some $75 million or $80 million to finish the development at Gros Cacouna. That is a fact. Once the money had been spent, the government then found it convenient to allow the National Energy Board to make a decision about the extension.
On December 12 or 13, we saw in the newspapers the headline "Federal cabinet approves gas pipeline to Halifax". It was all right then. I suspect Gros Cacouna will be the terminal in the south for the Arctic gas pilot project. It will be the receiving centre, or defrosting centre, or whatever is done with this enormously pressurized, very cold commodity.
The gas pipeline extension through the province of Quebec that was approved was a single size, the same size in Quebec City as when it came across the Ontario border. Now what do we learn? We have the December 15, 1981, decision by the
government to extend it to Halifax. We now find that the end of the pipeline which will be in Nova Scotia will be half the size of that in Quebec. We had continuous assurances from the government that this would be a reversible pipeline.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: That means you turn it inside out.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
We know what a megaphone is like; it produces noise. If Sable Island gas were placed into the small end of this reversible pipeline and we tried to sent it to Ontario, you would hear the rumble beyond the Rockies. There would be no snow left in the Rockies. With the pressure required to put it in the little end, when it came out the other end there would be one hell of a noise. However, that is all we have had, noise and rhetoric from the government side.
The Arctic pilot project is necessary. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) referred to the four horsemen of the Apocalypse. They and this government together cannot ruin this country. It is too big, too good and too individualistic. We are still pioneers, prepared to risk and be innovative. They will fail. They can do indescribable damage. They can upset us, disappoint us and mislead us, but they will not kill us and they will not kill useful, good projects. There are too many good people in this country.
I now come back to Gros Cacouna, which is the central point I am trying to make. Let us look at the financial history of this country. Atlantic Canada financing was the start of central Canada. The financing came from our wood, fish, early deposits of coal, our trading north-south and, in fact, literally all over the world. Funds found their way into central Canada for its development. That was the right course.
For the last 50, 60 or 70 years, we have not been able to contribute to national development. We have not had the means to develop wealth. With the discovery of gas and oil off the east coast, there is a dim glimmer of hope. It is possible that out of this we might find a way that will allow us to be more than just hewers of wood and drawers of water. Possibly we can use this gas and oil to develop a petrochemical industrial base that would not look inward to compete with existing Canadian capacity in that sphere but, rather, look offshore for sales.
For the last 30 or 40 years Atlantic Canada has asked central Canada for some form of technology that would be exportable, something we could use to develop an export market. Did that technology come? It was never offered. We still have no offer of it. What we have is the guarantee of a feed of western natural gas to Gros Cacouna, probably three to five years ahead of us, unless Sable Island comes ashore first, or any potential work in Nova Scotia or anywhere else in the maritimes. This will permit Gros Cacouna to take an insurmountable lead in capturing what could very well prove over the next several decades to be a real source of new capital for the province of Quebec.
That is Fine. It has to be done somewhere and will be done somewhere. The plants will be put in place, and the technology
May 6, 1982

will be employed. I suggest to the government that what is done in Gros Cacouna will find its markets in the central part of Canada and in the United States. Were that plant to be located on tidewater in Nova Scotia, its natural markets would be south and east. They would be South America, Africa, Europe and the Middle East, not in the already saturated central Canadian markets.
We were told the pipeline through Quebec into the mari-times would be fully reversible. It is not reversible. It is twice the size in Quebec City and Gros Cacouna as it will be at the Strait of Canso, and it cannot be reversed. The cost of reversing the pumps would be millions and millions of dollars.
Premier Buchanan of the province of Nova Scotia told Nova Scotians the other day that we were very close to a viable economic threshold of natural gas reserves on the Sable shelf. He indicated it would be up to industry and those doing the exporting to demonstrate and indicate to Nova Scotians, and indeed all Canadians, when we have arrived at that viable economic threshhold. We are close to it. The gas is there. The drilling that will take place off Sable Island this summer will clearly demonstrate that.
We have the gas and we have it ashore. Now what do we do with it? We have a pipeline that we cannot reverse. We will draw gas from Alberta-God love them-about 3,000 miles to Gros Cacouna when 275 or 280 miles away there is an enormous supply and no place to send it. Is that fair? Does that make sense?
The government wants some positive suggestions. It has heard many in the debate in this House in the last two or three days. We have made useful suggestions about what can be done to help this country achieve self-sufficiency in energy by 1990. Perhaps 1995 would be more realistic. If we have many more breakdowns like this, we will be closer to the turn of the century, but we will achieve it. We will achieve it quicker if the government will redirect some of the funds saved with the collapse of the Alsands and the delay of the Alaska pipeline and make the Q & M pipeline truly reversible.
The Minister of Finance spoke in Mabou. He knew when he spoke there that the pipeline was not reversible and never would be reversible. The government should make it reversible. Give us an opportunity to do something with our gas.
Give us some technologies so that gas that comes from offshore can free up western gas, perhaps for export. Let us build a technological base to build a petrochemical industrial base near the site of the gas. We in turn will use that industrial base to attract offshore dollars, which everyone in this chamber knows are sorely and badly needed. The importance of this was clearly demonstrated in the comments of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) as well as the 45 or 50 other speakers on this side. If it is not clear, I doubt very much if anybody will ever persuade the government away from its destined course.
Yesterday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) suggested in this chamber that the National Energy Program was succeeding. It may be succeeding, but it
is succeeding as all megaprojects. It is not succeeding in revitalizing us and raising our hopes. It is doing quite the opposite. It has resulted in devastating and dashing hopes and prolonged dreams and has unduly delayed economic recovery. It has killed the hopes and ambitions of thousands of people from one end of this country to the other. This has been done without the slightest indication of shame or embarrassment.
Reverse the pipeline. Do whatever has to be done. Do not let these projects die. They are too important to the Canadian economy and the people of this country who have been relying on them and looking forward to them as a means of rebuilding the great economic spirit of which this country is capable.

speechtext:

When the economy slows down we should do something productive for the future. Those workers want jobs; they do not want unemployment. I should like to talk a bit about the Progressive Conservative party. Time after time members of that party talk about members of the New Democratic Party voting with Liberals. The record of the House of Commons will show that the Conservative Party has voted twice as many times with the Liberal government on very, very important issues.
In the province of British Columbia we have a party known as the Social Credit Party of British Columbia. It came about because the Conservatives and the Liberals joined forces to stop the New Democrats from forming the government. This is the type of thing which is taking place in the House of Commons. The Conservatives and the Liberals represent the same multinational corporations. They do not look after the individual Canadians who sent them here. They do not represent individual voters. The alarming thing is that, in the face of the evidence put before the government and members of Parliament by people who are knowledgeable of the petroleum industry, the government continues right through this debate to say, "It is okay; don't worry about it. And consequently now, Mr. Speaker, they have killed the goose that was going to lay the golden egg. They have laid the egg now. But the fact remains that the objective of energy selfsufficiency has now been replaced by energy being seen as a major revenue source for the federal government. And now, as energy usage goes down, as the price of energy drops on world markets, the government cannot respond, because if they respond, they will see their revenues dropping still further.
May 7, 1982

They projected a $51 billion revenue increase for the federal government over the five year plan. Economists now, observers of the scene, will vary this but they will argue that that $51 billion could be ambitious by about $20 billion over the next five years. What happens to the deficit? What happens to the ability to invite investment in this country with those kinds of projections?
What is the investment climate like today? Do I really have to tell hon. members? Where is the confidence? We have discretionary decisions by government.
One thing the industry, which has to have a ten-year plan, cannot afford is for the rules to change periodically at the whim of government. They cannot afford to have investment. That is why we have Canadian investment in the Williston based in North Dakota. They say to Canadians, "Keep on having the National Energy Program, it is the best policy you can have for the United States". We have literally driven Canadian investment into the United States. That is what they are saying to us.
We talk about rule changes. That is why there is no investment confidence. We then come to constraint shares. The old energy supply bill, which has now been split into so many pieces no one knows anymore how many pieces are left on the floor of the House, talks about constraint shares.
I did not know what a constraint share was. I found out. A constraint share is a share owned by a non-Canadian in a company operating in oil and gas or having a share in a company that might invest in oil and gas in Canada. That share would be placed in a constraint share category. It could be sold without the individual exercising his or her rights and get the net proceeds. Why would anyone out of Canada want to invest in that kind of climate? Why should they? Why would they? That is the policy.
What is the cost? What is the cost in jobs? There are members in this House from every part of the country. When they go back to their constituencies, they find that jobs have been lost in the automobile industry and in the supply industry. The multiplier effect cannot be determined by anyone in this House. Jobs have been lost. Why? Because that party was so doctrinaire, following a doctrinaire principle, nationalization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I have touched a raw nerve. I just advise that gentleman to read his own words which he expressed in the House.
The jobs that were there are gone. The lay-offs are a reality. What do we say to young Canadians looking for their first job? What happens to a young Canadian coming out of a university, trade school or high school who is looking for his or her first job and it is not there? What do we do for that young
person in terms of the country and his view of his own value and contribution to the country?
What happened to energy self-sufficiency? It is gone. What happened to the financial cost? I will give just one quick fact. My colleague from Edmonton quoted Mr. Lamont. A speech by Mr. Lamont, the managing partner, Richardson Securities of Canada, to the Winnipeg Society of Financial Analysts was reported in the Edmonton Journal of May 3. Mr. Lamont said:
We have been subsidizing the import of foreign oil out of the public purse to the extent of billions of dollars annually. One might as well pursue temperance by subsidizing the price of booze.
The cumulative cost is estimated at $14 billion U.S. or $17 billion Canadian- $17 billion is more than 20 per cent of our national debt-incurred to subsidize gasoline and fuel oil-indeed, the interest on the money we have borrowed to subsidize oil prices at 15 per cent is $2.5 billion annually, which was more than the entire budget of the province of Manitoba in 1981.
That is the financial cost. What about the cost to the oil industry?
I do not come from an area where there is oil and gas, but I had an opportunity to be in Saskatchewan for certain reasons over the last weeks during the recent campaign. I have been through the oil fields before. All of us have marvelled at the ability of Canadians to find oil in a place where you would think that all that is growing there is forests or wheat fields.
It is an eerie feeling to go outside of Swift Current to the little towns and see the oil wells shut down. They are not pumping. That is the cost.
Maybe members opposite do not come from those areas, but the cost is theirs as well. As the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) said, we hide our head in the sand and say, "Let us import another 400,000 barrels today, again tomorrow and the day after." I want to speak on that.
The Liberal government and the Liberal Party, if you go through the historical record, have never placed a priority on western Canadian oil to be used across the country. Two conditions had to prevail. It was then they started waking up to the potential of western Canadian oil and frontier oil.
Let us go back to 1961. Albertans came here. Their knees were literally raw. They came on their hands and knees, trying to get the federal government to use western Canadian oil. They would not do it. Finally in 1961 there was an agreement that up to the Ottawa Valley line they would use western Canadian crude.
Today one of the Liberal members said we should share. Yes, we should share. I heard one of the NDP ministers in Manitoba the other day say that the problem in Canada today is that the blue suits should not own the resources. Should we all go cap in hand to this government and ask for a future from them? Hardly.
When offshore oil was threatened, this Liberal Party and government woke up to the reality of self-sufficiency for Canada. That was only when security of supply was threatened. They only woke up to that reality when the price of offshore oil was escalating so rapidly that they suddenly

May 7, 1982
thought they would be able to use western Canadian oil and save some money at home.
It has been interesting to watch. As the price of oil is dropping internationally, they are quite willing to continue going to Venezuela, Mexico and the Middle East to buy oil. However, they would not buy it from Alberta. They would not buy it from Saskatchewan. They will buy, but they talk of buying at certain prices.
Now they talk about sharing. Where were they sharing earlier? Where were they in 1905 when Saskatchewan and Alberta became provinces but were not deemed worthy to have their resources? Where were they then? Western Canadians were not considered mature enough or not good enough managers to have the same resources as the other provinces. That is the legacy of those opposite, and they have to live with it.
Then there is the NDP. My goodness, the NDP. Every time there is a proposal, what do they do? Roadblocks, fanned in the gears. They want to be forward looking, yes they do, but always in retrospect, always, "I told you so", always up front.
Let me tell you about the Mackenzie valley. The Mackenzie valley people lost jobs. Natives lost jobs. Why? Go into the Mackenzie valley. On the day Berger closed down the Mackenzie valley, natives had barges full of supplies in the hope that the pipeline would go down the Mackenzie. That is what the NDP supported.
Canada can have a great future, but it will not have a future and cannot have a future with this Liberal government's National Energy Program and its economic leadership, aided and abetted by its socialist friends.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to see so many members in the House. I do not know how they knew I was about to speak. However, I am delighted they are in the House because maybe they might learn something. There have not been enough who have been listening to the brilliant speeches tonight and yesterday and the day before to learn something about what is happening to this country because the Alsands, Cold Lake and Judy Creek projects represent the disaster that this national energy policy is. It is an unmitigated disaster.
Yesterday the member from the Lone Star State came here telling us what was good about the energy policy. Not once in that speech did he mention the fact that the Alsands project had collapsed. He is running around, stumbling over the wreckage of his energy policy, not knowing what he should do and ignoring the fact that drilling activity has dropped 25 per cent, 40 per cent of the rigs have left the country, people have left the country.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: They will come back.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
The hon. member says they will come back. Where has that member been? Take your head out of the sand and look at what happened in 1973. At that time it took four
years for the drilling activity to reach the same level as in 1973 when the disastrous policies of Donald Macdonald came in.
At that time drilling activity went down 10 per cent, not 25 per cent. The number of rigs went down 8 per cent, not the 40 per cent it has gone down this time. He should take his head out of the sand and try to learn what is happening.
Let me give another example of the head in the sand. This is very interesting to me. Tonight we had the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Gray) before our committee. I asked him to tell us his perception and understanding of the effect of the collapse of Alsands.
He scratched his head, wiggled his jowls and said 200 jobs will be lost because 200 people will be laid off who are now on the project. He said there will be no balance of payments impact because the project will not be completed for eight years. He said there will be no effect on research and development activity because it is all a state of the art research, state of the art technology.
The man does not understand the impact of this project and the other projects that have gone before which have collapsed as a result of the program that his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) brought in a year and half ago.
I do not think hon. members opposite understand because the many speeches to which 1 have listened tonight and during the past few days have totally ignored the impact of this on the country.

speechtext: I understand.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
I hear an hon. member opposite indicating that he understands. That is a total admission of defeat. There is nothing we can do with these men. It was as a result of the stupidity, the bullheadedness and shortsightedness of one minister.
Let me turn to the reasons for the project being stopped. Hon. members of the Liberal Party have indicated that it was because of the oil glut, international economic problems and high interest rates. Supposedly these are the only reasons the Alsands project collapsed. They totally ignored the real reasons for the project collapsing. It was because private sector operators had no trust or confidence in the federal government. They were worried that the rug would be pulled out from under them later on and that the rules of the game would change again. These statements were made directly by private sector operators. They feared that the government did not trust the private sector and that it would change the rules again. They were worried about the future of the country. There were two other reasons. One was the fact that cash flows, the moneys going to finance the project, had been siphoned off over the past 1.5 years by the same government to satisfy its greed and need for money, money, money, because of its wild
May 7, 1982

spending over the past ten years. Another reason was the lack of confidence which is necessary on the part of someone moving into a project of this magnitude; it was just not present. I think it was the president of Shell who said that the time for this project was lost. It was lost about two years ago; that is the tragedy of the situation.
The real tragedy is that the Canadian public hear these reasons being given and they know that they are not true. This undermines the level of confidence and trust all Canadians have in their government.
I should like to refer to another illustration of deception of the Liberal government. I refer to the decision of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that Arthur Erickson Associates would be the architects for the new embassy in Washington. The government is a master at deception. When we look at the press release of February 25, we get a good idea of what I am talking about. It indicated that 11 semi-finalists were chosen from some 300 finalists from across the country. From the 11 semi-finalists, four finalists were chosen. The Erickson firm was established as one of the 11 semi-finalists, but it was not named as one of the four finalists; it did not make the final round. The release from the office of the Prime Minister, the most senior political leader in the country, the man to whom people should look with trust and confidence for integrity-but there is no integrity or moral leadership there-indicated the following:
Mr. Erickson's firm was one of eleven finalists chosen from some 300 firms from across the country-
It was total deceit. There was no statement of who the finalists were, but we know from the panel of architects that Erickson was not one of the finalists. There was no mention that Mr. Erickson is a very good friend and strong supporter of the Prime Minister. There was no suggestion that that man was one of the finalists, which is another example of why people are losing trust in the political leaders of the country. This is one of the most serious things with which we must deal in our lives as politicians.
The loss of the Alsands project is a tragedy for many Canadians across the country. Two years ago we talked about the importance of getting this project moving because of its tremendous size and its impact in many, many communities such as Hamilton, Mississauga, Toronto and in a number of communities in Quebec which will be affected by the industrial spin-offs. We were concerned, if the project did not move ahead soon, that we would lose it. We said so on many occasions. I looked back at some of the speeches I made as energy critic. I was amazed by the concerns expressed to me, which I reflected in my speeches. At that time people felt that if the project did not go ahead, a project of this magnitude could be lost, and it has been lost. We should not be deceived for a minute by the statement of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his colleagues in the Liberal Party who said that the reason the project was lost was what was happening today.
The project was lost two years ago, and that is the message which must go out to Canadian people. As the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) said, people looked to members of the Liberal Party because they were good managers. This is
probably the best example of disastrous management of the country from which all Canadians are suffering.
We have talked about the importance of self-sufficiency for all communities in the country. We said, going back as far as 1977, that that should be a primary objective of any energy policy in the country. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources finally saw the light at the end of 1980 and included it as an objective in his energy policy. I should like to turn to some of the provisions of the National Energy Program which bear directly upon the tragedy of the loss of the Alsands project. It was pointed out in the National Energy Program that, currently, about 15 per cent of our oil requirements were satisfied from non-conventional sources, but that looked ahead ten years to 1990, the requirement from non-conventional sources will rise to 50 per cent. A full 50 per cent of our oil requirements will have to be met from projects like Alsands, Cold Lake and Judy Creek, the three major non-conventional projects which have been lost in the last few years. It will be almost impossible for us to come within 20 per cent of oil selfsufficiency by 1990. We hear the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources say that they will bring on Beaufort and Hibernia and that they will get more conventional oil out of the ground in western Canada and that we will be self-sufficient by 1990. That man has his head in the sand. He does not understand the portfolio which he has been holding for the last two years, which is another tragedy we have to bear as Canadians. We will be importing 30 per cent, 40 per cent or possibly 50 per cent of our oil requirements by 1990. We will be exposed to the instability of the Far East and the problems there.
About two years ago, there was a debate in the House of Commons before the National Energy Program was brought in, drawing the attention of the government to the concern of many Canadians caused by over-reliance on imports. The loss of the Alsands project is throwing us more and more into the laps of the people who will sell us oil from offshore. The government has not learned from the past; it has not learned from the mistakes of others.
In 1970, Canadians were 100 per cent self-sufficient in oil and the Americans were 75 per cent self-sufficient. In 1980 we dropped to 75 per cent and the Americans dropped to 50 per cent. Suddenly the light went on down in the United States and the Americans realized that they had a crisis on their hands. They realized that they had to take enormously expensive and disruptive steps to move themselves back to a more secure position. What has the government learned from this? It has not learned from the mistakes of the Americans over the past few years. The minister talks about it and points to the fact that he does not want to have it happen in this country, but he leads us right down the road toward the same thing happening. In 1990 we will have lost about 65 per cent of the non-conventional oil upon which the minister had counted in his energy policy a short 18 months ago. That is another tragedy which we are facing today. It is another reason for all Canadians to be very, very concerned.

May 7, 1982
When I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce a question concerning this matter, he did not even reflect upon the fact that the Canadian manufacturing industry would be more and more exposed to offshore supplies of crude oil.
I have a letter in my file from a manufacturer who said that within reason he could handle any cost for oil because he knew that we were competing with the United States, our main competitor. He indicated that if we could keep somewhere within reason of the price of oil which Americans had to pay- and we are satisfied with 85 per cent-that it was all right, but what he could not live without or operate without was oil. He indicated that he must have oil, that he had to have that energy. He also said that the government should put its priority on security of supply, and that price should come second. Those were the opinions of a manufacturer from the Toronto area who owns a company which has operations in Quebec and in other part of Ontario. Security of supply was the number one problem which he was facing. He was concerned about the viability of his company and the possibility of his company providing jobs for people.
Now I should like to comment upon the document entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s".

I have tried to listen carefully to the members opposite to see if they had a strategy to revive some of these projects or turn in other directions to develop our economy. I was wondering whether they felt it was too late to revive some of these projects-not the Cold Lake project, I know that is dead- which are in a long-term hold position. Are they considering alternatives? What plans have they to revive the economy? That is critically important when we have close to 1.5 million people out of work. When you look at the state of the economy today you see those people have been effectively excommunicated from our economic life because it is hard to find a job. We have all heard that many times over from people who come into our offices or call us up asking for help. That is the importance of moving ahead and restoring economic growth.
I was looking for some flexibility on the part of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to make some changes in the NEP to show us he recognized the folly of his ways, and that he understood he made some enormous mistakes in October, 1980. He talks about frontier oil and conventional sources, but they will not be developed unless there is some cash flow. He has to reduce his tax take. If not, we will not see those projects develop. That is the challenge, and the government has to make those changes. We in the Conservative Party are prepared to meet those challenges. We would make the changes to bring the industry back on-stream to the point of being an important source of economic growth. We understand the problems and we know there has to be flexibility. We are prepared also to look at some of the other changes in the energy program which have undermined confidence and trust in government.
I say to the government that it is far more important for the people of this country to bite the bullet now, recognize the mistakes, make the changes, and if it requires the resignation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources or the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), so be it.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am happy that I am able to participate in a small way in this debate, but it is rather saddening that we even have to have this debate. It seems to me that-I am very pleased to see that we now have four Liberals in the House. For most of this evening we had none and then we had one, and now there are three. Unfortunately, there has not been a cabinet minister here all evening.
1 think it is sad that we have to have this debate. The governing party has put all of its eggs in one basket. As they have dribbled away parts of our economy left, right and center, they have always said, "But wait, here come the megaprojects. That will pick up the slack."
And now, with a flush, down the toilet go the megaprojects.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) had some interesting comments to make. They might have been valid. 1 particularly liked the one in which he indicated that Progressive Conservative Party members only fight against orders in council which they do not like. 1 have never heard of anyone fighting against orders in council which they like, even in his party.
The hon. member has said that our party is convinced on megaprojects whereas his party-granted not the NDP in Alberta-is dead against megaprojects. The hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) spoke in the negative about megaprojects.
I do not think it can be said that the Conservative Party is in favour of megaprojects just for the sake of megaprojects. They have to be profitable megaprojects. They must have a return.
One thing that has to be taken into consideration is the number of jobs they provide, the energy that will be provided to the country so that we do not have to depend upon foreign sources. Some of these megaprojects would have been nice had they gone ahead rather than just depended on hope and prayer, as we must now.
It is interesting to note that the megaprojects were outlined so well by Mr. Robert Blair of Nova Corporation and Shirley Carr, vice-president of the CLC, in their documented paper of the 40 megaprojects that will take place in Canada.
At the time it was said that it was a classic example of how the labour movement and the capitalist entrepreneurs could work together to define what the projects would be. There was a lot of hope pinned on those. It is sad now to see that the first, second, third and fourth of those projects are going down the tube. The reason is government greed on taxation, wanting more money to try to fill its depleted coffers because it has spent so much money foolishly in this country.
We should point out the history of Canada and the way we have treated our oil industry over the years. It has really been pathetic.
Let us talk about Imperial Oil. My friends of the Liberal party west, the little pink rump of the big red machine, always knock Imperial Oil. Imperial Oil started out as a Canadian company. It drilled its first well in Petrolia back in 1888. It was a Canadian company. Under the Liberals, it was sold to the Americans in 1937.
British American Oil Company was another integrated Canadian-owned oil company. It was sold under the Liberals in 1947. It subsequently changed its name to Gulf in 1964, again under the Liberals.
The third integrated Canadian oil company, White Rose, Canadian Oil Company, was sold under the Liberals in 1965 to Shell. Subsequent to that, they allowed Supertest to go to BP in 1970. The list goes on.
We had a Canadian oil company. The reason Standard New Jersey picked up Imperial is that they then marketed the name "Imperial" in all the Commonwealth countries around the world. It is still using that word. They took that name from a Canadian oil company which the Liberals allowed to be sold to foreigners.
In 1979, Alastair Gillespie, the previous energy minister, was so anxious that he ran to Venezuela through the Canadian Commercial Corporation to buy more oil for PetroCan. He went to Mexico and signed contracts for heavy oil, not the light isthmus crude which the eastern refineries need.
The Canadian refineries in eastern Canada cannot use this oil. It has to be converted. Now there is talk of $100 million just to convert this oil which, unfortunately, we are contracted into by the Liberal administration of the time. The list of Mr. Gillespie indicates that megaprojects were going to supply some 70,000 direct jobs in Canada and 255,000 indirect jobs in Canada, over 320,000 jobs. At a time when we have 1.5 million unemployed under a similar Liberal administration, would it not be nice to have some of those 320,000 jobs?
Those jobs were to include the Dempster pipeline, 6,000 direct jobs and 26,000 indirect jobs. It was cancelled. The Alaska highway gas pipeline, 13,000 direct jobs and 55,000 indirect jobs, is delayed. The Polar gas project was cancelled. Tennaco LNG project was cancelled. The Alsands project was cancelled. The Syncrude expansion was cancelled. The Cold Lake project was cancelled. The oil storage project in Waba-nex was cancelled.
The megaprojects, which were so important to previous Liberal governments, raised the hopes of Canadians. There was to be something for us in the way of jobs and energy selfsufficiency. That has all been lost through the mismanagement of the economy by the present government and by the lack of respect for people with initiative, Canadians who want to invest. We find small Canadian companies formed in Alberta and British Columbia, some on the Toronto Stock Exchange. Their major investment is in Oklahoma, Louisiana and Texas.
May 7, 1982

That is where they are going to search for oil. They are taking Canadian rigs with them.
The Canadian government fooled the Canadian people deceitfully in the election of 1979-80. They said they would have budgetary restraint. We have had $14 billion deficits every year since. They said they would lower interest rates. The hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) pledged that he would quit his job if they did not lower interest rates. Interest rates have gone up and he has not quit his job.
They said they would have lower prices than the 18 cents that the NDP voted for. We now have increases of 78 cents in taxes, not 18 cents. They said they would renew employment, encourage Canadians to expand job opportunities in this country. Instead of having six months of declining unemployment, as we had with the Clark administration, we have had unemployment go up. We now have almost 1.5 million unemployed in this country. They said we would have oil selfsufficiency. Now we are told we are not going to have oil selfsufficiency unless, through hope and prayer, they can bring in Hibernia, Beaufort and a number of other projects which we do not have the technological skills to bring onstream.
This government has failed this country and the people of this country with their interest rate policy, their employment policy. All they have done is to create unemployment. They have failed this country and the people of this country with their program of restraint. They have failed at reducing the deficits and they have failed in bringing us oil self-sufficiency. We have been waiting. Now we find everything has gone, all the hope we had with the announcement that Alsands and the Alaska pipeline are cancelled, delayed or postponed.
It is unfortunate that we are going to lose tens of thousands of jobs. It is important to note that it is not just jobs in Alberta and the Yukon, British Columbia or Saskatchewan. Fifty per cent of those jobs will be in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) are supporting a government which will cost thousands of jobs to the underemployed steel companies in Hamilton such as Stelco and Dofasco. They sit quiet. They do not participate. Yet they will vote in support of something that will cost their area thousands of jobs.
We have had a debate which has gone on very long. It has been important for the Canadian public to try to understand how much they have been deceived. We in Canada have been deceived. The present administration has deceived us with regard to interest rates, unemployment, restraint, reduced deficits and oil self-sufficiency. They have deceived us on megaprojects. They have not negotiated in good faith.
They have not left anything for the private sector in the way of return until, perhaps, far too late. They have killed the projects. In a sort of macabre way, it is like an Alfred Hitchcock movie. Picture a scene in which members of the cabinet come in darkness because there is no light in the cabinet. They are standing around like zombies, staring at the cadavre on the
operating table. The pathologist is dissecting the cadaver, which is the National Energy Program. Behind the zombies are those who are even more dead. They are the skeletons, the backbenchers, who just sit there silently as the operation goes on.
The death of Alsands and the postponement of the Alaska highway gas pipeline have indeed been a sad blow. I hope the people of Canada come to realize they have been deceived. I hope they come to understand that we have lost thousands of job opportunities. Indeed, it has been unfortunate that this debate has been necessary. It really is sad that Canada has lost all these opportunities.
This is a country which has every reason to have every hope. We have all the potential in the world. Properly managed, we would not have to cancel the megaprojects. We would have those thousands of jobs. That would mean fewer people on unemployment insurance and fewer people on welfare. There would be more Canadians with a sense of self-satisfaction because they were working to enhance our country.
