speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have no notes prepared for my speech, but I have some very, very deep feelings with regard to this matter. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) presented to my colleagues across the House and on my left a very reasonable proposition. I assure the House that there are many hon. members behind me who are willing to participate in the debate. This is just about the same time I came into the House two nights ago and sat through until morning. Thus, 1 have an early start tonight and, if my voice holds out, I am quite prepared to stay a lot longer.
The majority of the speakers we have heard so far have driven home with great clarity the problems the National Energy Program has caused in this great land of ours.
I wish I had the eloquence to deliver with the same passion and the same emotion the points made by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) when, at about 5.30 in the morning two days ago, he rose in his place and in a voice charged with emotion told everyone listening exactly what was
wrong with the National Energy Program. I do not have his eloquence; I will not try to repeat his words. I recall shortly thereafter how the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott) pointed out to hon. members in the House at that time that it was not just Alberta which was being hurt by the machinations of government. Rather, he listed a number of firms in his riding and clearly gave indication of the harm which was being done to them.
Were I to take a moment, I could give an equal number of firms in Prince Edward-Hastings which are also being hurt, simply because this stubborn block-headed government does not want to deal honestly with Canadians. I could deal with firms throughout the entire province of Ontario. I have the singular honour of representing the caucus of Ontario when we meet, and I can say that every hon. member from Ontario on the Conservative side of the House could refer to instances wherein firms have been hurt by the actions of the government.
I should like to refer to one example. Earlier this year the uncaring government gave away to a firm in Japan something in the order of 380,000 to 400,000 man-days of work which could have been performed by a firm in the city of Belleville, which is in my riding and has been my home for the past 30-odd years. Over the last three or four days, in meetings of the Standing Committee on Transport, I have placed upon the table irrefutable evidence, which was not once properly refuted by the chairman of the National Harbours Board who was a witness before the committee. He did not refute the fact that technically, competitively and promptly a Canadian firm could have provided the necessary equipment for the Ridley Coal handling facility. I proved, to the satisfaction of all who sat on the committee-but perhaps not to the satisfaction of the chairman of the National Harbours Board-that this Canadian company could have built these units. This firm has built 20 to 25 of these units throughout the world. It is presently completing one slightly south of the Ridley terminals in British Columbia. It is completing four in South Africa and is bidding competitively on others in South America. Recently it provided a similar piece of equipment to Korea, in competition with its cheap labour and its policies. In fact, I proved that its bid was technically and in other ways superior, yet the callous, uncaring government opposite awarded the contract to a firm from Japan, taking away jobs from Canadians.
I should like to relate a few facts. Had the job been allotted to the Canadian company, it would have been 96.5 per cent Canadian in production and 100 per cent Canadian in engineering. The Japanese company indicated that it will provide 52.8 per cent Canadian content, but that same Japanese company promised two years ago to provide something over 60 per cent Canadian content in the Burrard floating dry dock which was supplied to Vancouver harbour. This firm has not spent a single red cent or even a yen in Canada on that project. I do not know why we should believe that it will at this time. In fact, I suspect that there is not a snowball's chance that it will
May 7, 1982

spend that amount of money in Canada this time. I would like to go into a little more detail on that particular project, but I do not think it is necessary.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is a reasonable individual. I think he has been completely misled by his staff and his public servants, because he stood in the House and said that the whole project would be some 85 per cent Canadian, and the remaining bid on that project went overseas to Europe. Less than a week ago another part of the same project, a contract worth over $7 million in steel pipe, was given to Japan. I am sure the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth would agree that the Steel Company of Canada could manufacture steel pipe of a nature which will carry the highest pressures in gas and oil. I am sure he will agree that it should have had a chance to bid on this, but the specifications for the pipe were purposely made in such a way that no Canadian company could bid on it. Is it not surprising that the specifications for the pipe just happened to be exactly the same specifications as that which could be provided by the firm in Japan?
As a result another $7-odd million worth of work, which could have gone to Canadians, went to this Japanese firm. This work will be paid for by Canadians. It will be paid for by the taxes of Madam Speaker, by my taxes and, more importantly, the taxes of millions of Canadians. I have nothing against the Japanese. They are a fine and industrious people, but had the project been in Japan, no Canadian would have been given an opportunity to bid on it, never mind supply it or supply it at a higher price. This is what is happening with our uncaring government. The government cares little about Canadians. It takes the taxes of Canadians and spends them in a prolific, wanton and cavalier manner.
As I was entering the chamber this evening, I heard the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) very completely covering the subject concerning the architect from Vancouver who, not on the choice of those who were put in the position of choosing the architect for the new Canadian embassy in Washington, but because he was a friend of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), was chosen for the job. I suppose I must say, "Thank God, at least he was not Japanese; at least he is a Canadian." Perhaps that is some consolation, but it gives an idea of the way in which the government treats Canadians with disregard.
1 am sure a number of my colleagues wish to speak in this debate tonight. I have used up just about all my time, but before returning to my seat, I suggest to hon. members opposite that there are many, many more members who want to participate. After all, it is only 1.45 in the morning. We could continue through the remainder of the night until dawn tomorrow. A number of my colleagues and I sat through the night and saw the sun rise Wednesday morning; I suppose we could sit through until the sun rises on Friday morning. Perhaps in so doing we might get across a message to the unfeeling government that we are no longer prepared to be walked over, stomped on or to have our Canada, this Canada
we love so much, trampled into the ground by a government which has lost all sense of care, of dignity and of reality.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I participated this afternoon in a seminar on parliamentary reform, and one subject discussed at length was why this institution does not work in representing Canadians. It is a subject which can be discussed for hours, but if I needed an example I could not have provided a better one than that which occurred approximately 15 minutes ago. That is the kind of tragedy which sees members opposite assuming that the issue of an emergency debate on the economic future of our people is one with which you play parliamentary games.
Last night and again tonight the members opposite have shown that it does not matter if $50 billion of investment goes down the drain. It does not matter if an energy program destroys the economic future of an entire region. It does not matter if my province loses every day because of programs which led to the collapse of Alsands. It does not matter to members opposite if that causes lay-offs numbering in the thousands. I suppose if you sit here all the time under the bright lights where you do not feel an energy shortage, where you just cannot have any feeling for the problem in a place as insulated as this environment, you can and do lose a sense of what is happening on the streets. I think perhaps this has happened to a number of members opposite.
The collapse of these projects is important because they represented what the government said was a way out of the economic malaise confronting Canada. In good times we could afford the loss of a project, even one as big as this one, but in bad times we cannot afford the loss of any projects. What do you say to a young student who comes in to your office, having been laid off from a company which closed because it makes products related to oil development, and now has no work? This student spent the last six months educating himself to become a computer programmer in a school which has the greatest single track record for placing students in jobs after graduation. How do you respond when he says he was laid off because of the collapse of these energy projects? He went to the best school he could go to and he cannot find work after being on the streets for eight weeks. There is no work, even for those who have taken the time and trouble to help themselves and Canada. All this because we have a government which plays parliamentary games during what has been the longest emergency debate in this House.
Madam Speaker, I am advised by way of a note that there has been an agreement in this matter. Therefore, Madam Speaker, I thank you for allowing me to contribute for even a few minutes.

Canadians want the removal of the most incompetent, arrogant, isolated, and the most power-hungry
government in modern history. The latest example is Alsands, a $15 billion project which would have provided some 50,000 jobs. The shelving of the Alaska highway gas pipeline deprives the economy of a further $40 billion.

So they cannot change their position now. They cannot say they were for the original pipeline concept, because they were not. Well, there was one, the executive assistant to the leader of the NDP at that time. He is now the leader of the Opposition in Yukon, Mr. Penikett. But not when it was going through the committee and through the House. His party's position at the federal level is diametrically opposed to that of the NDP Leader in Yukon, who happens to be the national president of the hon. member's party. It seems to me you fellows should get your act together.
Last Tuesday the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), in an unwanted burst of frankness, used the word "collapsed" with respect to these projects. That was exactly the right word. It was not the project alone which collapsed, but confidence in the government, which in turn brought about a collapse of the project. It was not the decision of the private sector. The uncertain and erratic financial policy of the government brought about internationally and in Canada a climate of uneasiness in which investors were unwilling to continue. The bottom line was that trust and confidence in the government and its policies was found wanting, and it is the government which must bear the responsibility for those disastrous policies which have created that disastrous and deteriorating economic climate and for failing to produce alternative policies when their hopes in the megaprojects came tottering down.
While the major responsibility is that of the government, that does not detract from the nauseating and hypocritical
May 7, 1982

performance put on this week by the NDP. From the beginning their attitude has brought opposition to Alsands on the grounds that it was a giveaway to private industry. I do not think there is anyone in this House who has not observed what we fliers call doing a 180 as the NDP tactics changed here last week. I have no complaint against his opposing the project, nor against any member of his party opposing those projects. But what we have a right to complain about, now that the projects have been wiped out because of the procrastination and ineptness of the government, is members of that party rising in this House and claiming that they were for the projects all along. They cannot do that and still retain any credibility whatsoever.
On November 26, at page 5109 of Hansard, the energy critic of the NDP, the member for Vancouver-Kingsway criticized the government for what he called "overbuilding pipelines". That may have been justified or it may not have been, but it is the height of hypocrisy, for those who charged two years ago that pipelines were being overbuilt, to now claim that those same pipelines are so vitally necessary.
We have sat here and listened for a week now to this 180-degree turn in the tactical direction of the NDP, and I think it is about time to expose some of this hypocrisy, and hopefully force the members over there to display some honesty in this House when looking at the history of these projects.
What did the member for Vancouver-Kingsway say in that debate on November 21, 1980? At page 4955 of the Hansard, he said this:
We would get even more money by developing the tar sands under public ownership. The large multinational companies want a 15 to 20 per cent profit out of the tar sands, and the minister is prepared to allow them to receive that.

As an alternative, the member for Vancouver-Kingsway suggested setting up energy alternative programs at the local level.
Well, perhaps now the minister, if he ever comes back, will be more receptive to that proposal. Nevertheless, the truth is, Madam Speaker, that the NDP has been against these projects from the start, and they cannot now have it both ways and act as though they were supporting them all along. To do so would be the height-the pure height-of socialist hypocrisy. Mind you, I must say that it is in keeping with socialist tactics.

They are reduced to something like the Chinese five-year plan for making iron ingots in the backyard.
The tragedy of this government is that it is destitute of ideas, devoid of principles, incapable of dealing with problems on their merits, or proposing solutions that will be acceptable to those involved. There will be no such thing as a co-operative atmosphere between the government and the private sector while these rascals are over there.
The seriousness of the Alsands cancellation to the economy cannot be overestimated. If investor confidence was at a low ebb, it has now dropped completely out of sight. This project would have given Canada access to over 100 billion barrels of oil-one third of the proven reserves of the Middle East. It would have brought self-sufficiency within our reach, and provided thousands upon thousands of jobs.
It was killed by the budget, killed by high interest rates, killed by the iniquitous nationalization policies of this government, supported by the NDP.
The architects of these tragedies, of these disasters, are the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). Make no mistake-

speechtext:
"The three Canadian destroyers." Make no mistake: it is a disaster of a magnitude from which Canada will not soon recover.
If there is to be a recovery, it cannot be achieved by a government that is so moribund it is not even aware that its time has run out. The cancellation of Alsands is all the more serious since the latest figures show a deliberate drop in OPEC production in the first quarter of this year. Saudi Arabia, OPEC's largest producer, has reduced production by 1.5 million barrels a day.
Alsands was to be the linchpin of economic recovery in this country. It still could be-but not under this government. Now
that the linchpin has gone and the Alaska pipeline has been virtually shelved for the foreseeable future, where do we go? What happens to the great paper program put together by the Meach Lake mugs-the minister from the other place, the former minister of FIRA, who has had his powers removed, the travelling minister, salesman Sam from Cornwall? They put together a program to usher in a new heaven and a new earth. The pot of gold at the end of the rainbow turns out to be a crock-

speechtext: Don't say it.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
It turns out to be a crock of broken promises, shades of broken promises from the last election, Madam Speaker.
I will not weary sensitive ears-ears already wearied by this lengthy debate-by recalling all of those promises, now broken. They would fill many crocks. The list is almost endless. But on the energy question there was one about cheap oil, and I want members to listen to this statement by the Prime Minister, as quoted in a Globe and Mail questionnaire during the last election campaign:
As far as non-conventional oils are concerned-that's the tar sands, the frontier oils and the enhanced production wells-we would have an incentive pricing scheme which would make sure that it is profitable to private and public enterprise to look for and exploit that oil.
That is what he said. Well, that has not materialized, and they are not prepared to look for it and to exploit it. Somewhere along the line, the Prime Minister got sidetracked on other matters-

speechtext:
Double track. He forgot that promise, along with a lot of others. The Minister of Finance was one of the architects of this great economic program, one that never got off the runway. This was going to make up for all of the defects of the budget. People would be so lost in admiration of Phase I and Phase II of the megaprojects that they would forget the budget disaster. Now that Phase I has gone down the drain, what about Phase II? If Phase II was built on Phase I and if Phase I has evaporated, where does Phase II come in?
We are now entering the pie-in-the-sky phase of Liberal self-delusion.
The minister of employment is going around saying-in spite of the budget, in spite of Alsands, in spite of the postponement of the pipeline, in spite of Cold Lake, interest rates, and all of the rest of the Liberal house of horrors-that he is still in the business of creating jobs. How ridiculous! The only jobs that he or his moribund colleagues in the cabinet have created are the jobs they opened up for their friends in government-and there are plenty more of those. Here is the minister of unemployment-pardon the slip-under whose administration the rate of unemployment has gone up by 50 per cent, saying repeatedly in the House that he is creating jobs.
May 7, 1982

I challenge that minister to show us where his policies have created a single permanent long-term job that would not have existed in any case without the government's intervention.

While they have not created any jobs, they have been instrumental in wiping out virtually thousands of jobs, the loss of Alsands-50,000 jobs immediately, and more later; the postponement of the pipeline-the loss of an equal number, and more later. Both of these reversals are the direct result of the crisis of confidence in the government's economic policies, brought about by the flight of capital from this country. Surely even this government must realize that the National Energy Program has been the most destructive force in Canada's economic life. It has utterly destroyed investor confidence. It is the product of theorists removed from the realities of the marketplace. Its genesis was ideological and destructive-capacity unlimited.
We are going through a crisis of confidence that can only be solved by the removal of this government.
